The Witcher 3 is one of my all-time favourite games, but I'll leave this negative review for now, even if that sounds like a wild reaction to a free update.
Unfortunately the remaster is in such a messed-up state, that I can't really recommend playing it until they (hopefully) fix it up. 
I like the visual update itself, but there's no world where it should run like that. 
Trying to get this thing into a stable state for 4k, without sacrificing nearly every setting in sight, is basically impossible on a 5080. I get 60-80 FPS with Balanced DLSS and 2x Frame Gen. This frame rate fluctuates so hard and comes with so much random input delay, it basically makes the game unplayable. Or at least VERY hard to stomach.
As if that wasn't enough, the game completely starts choking to near-death at random times. Often after exiting some kind of menu, but sometimes at random, sometimes mid-combat etc. When that happens, the GPU gets stuck at 100% utilization while the game drops to 20 FPS. Presumably some kind of Frame-Gen choke, but who knows. This sometimes gets fixed by switching resolution back and forth. Otherwise it's a restart. Get unlucky and the game chokes again after 15 minutes.
Turning off DLSS isn't even a viable option anymore apparently, since the game just sacrifices half its pixels or something. I honestly have no idea what's going on there.
Other than that I've had audio issues where characters were suddenly at what feels like 20% volume. Happened right before the long post-White Orchard cutscene sequence too. 
Had NPCs glitch in and out of existence, enemies freeze in place after being hit by finishers, and many many similar glitches that aren't a big deal alone, but really stand out when you're already annoyed at the bad performance.
Being unable to get an uninterrupted hour of gameplay without running into major bugs and having to restart is simply not very fun or immersive. It wasn't actually quite as bad when I started the game, maybe because of the smaller tutorial area, but it's a fact that it no longer runs well, even if I go back to that area.

In theory I'm very happy that CDPR decided to give this game another makeover. In practice this is NOT it and I hope they properly fix it up soon-ish. Especially considering that they want us to buy and play the upcoming DLC.

Elden Ring is definitely one of the most immersive and best gaming experiences I’ve ever had. Literally a massive achievement in every part of game design. Even despite having so much difficulty and frustration through the bosses, dungeons, etc., I still don’t think I can ever get an experience like this from any other developer. It’s packed from start to finish with content in a world that’s so dense and rich.

There’s just something special about simply existing in this world and then slowly understanding the history, conflicts and circumstances that brought everything to where it is in The Lands Between. After finishing the game, I decided to watch a bunch of lore videos. It really hit harder thinking about the grand moments when I understood the actual weight behind them, realizing that the journey through this broken world has ultimately meant. 

Elden Ring’s story is completely outstanding in its own regard. In the fantasy open world, it depicted the cycles in terms of generational and familial tragedy, the cycle of violence and the hope of a brighter future. It's clear that the vision of the story is so well directed, well driven and how almost every mechanic ties into this game. I really love that the game never tells you that there’s not a single correct way to fix everything because either; you’re given this world that’s already been shaped by countless of failures, ideals and conflicts, and then you’re left to decide what kind of future should come from it, even if it means embracing something completely unknown. 

Overall, this game has been frustrating to the max lmao. But it’s overwhelmingly beautiful, mysterious and genuinely breathtaking. An insanely, well crafted game that’s impressive in its technicalities and somehow just those things make Elden Ring truly the experience instead of it just being a game.

This game is great, but it has been such an incredibly frustrating experience getting to the good parts of it. Baldur's Gate 3 is a buggy unstable mess of a game that reminds me of Skyrim. It lacks quality of life features all over and I find myself managing the tedium of multiple inventories, potions, broken pathfinding, etc more than actually enjoying the game. It also suffers greatly of the same problem most "high immersion" games suffer from: it has quips, reactions and dialogs for so many little things happening but when you find a MASSIVE plottwist about the game's story and suddenly nobody has anything to say or think about that, it completely ruins any of that immersion. It also seems to assume in many places you interact with story elements and NPCs in a certain order, meaning you can easily miss out on story or find someone referencing things you have absolutely zero context for quite easily. The combat is as repetitive and one-dimensional as you can expect from anything trying to be D&D, thankfully there's explorer mode to breeze past all that and get back to the good part:
The story, the voice acting and the choices you get to make are all great. At the time of writing I'm somewhere in act 2 and I have to admit it feels a lot like DOS2 with a faerune skin draped over it. But that's not bad because I loved DOS2.
It's a shame I might not see the conclusion of that story as a minor patch, over two and a half years after release, has screwed with one of the mods I donwloaded through the integrated mod marketplace and seems to have corrupted the last 4 hours of saves, so I'm going to put this down for a while.

With any other FromSoftware game I wouldn't have even cared to leave a review. insanely hard fights just for the purpose of being hard and making the player suffer, impossible to comprehend lore, and toxic wannabe philosopher fan bases; but the titular game, ELDEN RING, is really quite different, and quite good.

Though the formatting of incredibly punishing combat has remained the same, the formula of which it is presented is wildly fun and unique compared to other games by the same dev team. Stuck on a boss? You have a massive and deep world to explore and level up in to strengthen yourself before returning. Like character customization? ELDEN RING has one of the best character creators I've ever had the pleasure of playing with possibly hundreds of builds to play around with in the Lands Between.

Graphically the game is beautiful as well, even if turned to potato settings.

Where this game still fails a bit: In terms of actual roleplay there isn't much, most dialogues consist of you just pressing "Accept" or "Decline" with often times the Decline option lacking consequences; There are a few endings to play towards, but a good number of them are extremely similar.
Then onto lore; from what I know the lore and background lore of the game is it written with a lot of passion, with even a helping hand from Game of Thrones writer George R.R. Martin being lent. However like most FromSoftware games, it feels very much as if it doesn't actually want you to learn it. The general information about the world and its characters is all extreme conjecture and bias, which can be good for a complex world; but having no (at least to my knowledge) concrete way to learn the definitive lore is a bit wacky to me.

I played this at launch when it had many graphical and bug issues. I was disappointed with the product at the time, having pre ordered it and was anticipating its release for months. I didn't pre order any game for probably 4 years after that. I came back to this years later after getting the Phantom Liberty deal on sale and sunk over 160 hours into it, played every single gig except for all the NCPD content. 

CDPR have accomplished creating an open world that feels truly lived-in. A lot of open world games have the problem of creating too large a sandbox with not a lot to do outside the more closely designed points of interest. There's something to do on pretty much every street corner of Night City. Storytelling, characterization and performances are top notch. There's many side quests to get involved in, with great characters the player can decide to help or hurt. A lot don't have impact on the end of the game but they're entertaining nonetheless. Main quest follows a similar path where certain choices within them impact the final few missions of the game and give the player up to 7 endings with the Phantom Liberty DLC. 

One complaint about the base game versus the Phantom Liberty DLC is the quality in gigs. Base game gigs are formulated mostly by a short call from a fixer introducing you to a contract that often involves stealing something, killing someone or escorting someone to safety at a particular location. The worldbuilding and storytelling for these side gigs are often limited to reading a shard that you can find on the ground or in buildings. I find the Phantom Liberty gig content having more variety and in depth storytelling than the base game, with a lot more dialogue and player choice on the outcome. Many moderm games do these lore reading dumps and thats fine, but I just wish the quality and delivery was as good in the rest of the game as it was in the DLC.

In terms of player choice, combat is like a Deus Ex/Fallout lovechild. Cyberware, netrunning, stealth and skill trees give the player freedom to defeat enemies however they want. First playthrough i played as a melee heavy cyberpsycho, and on my recent replay I mostly focused on stealth, netrunning and pistol headshot damage multipliers.

 I kinda hated the Johnny character at first but after playing alongside him for 100 hours I started to feel for the guy, especially during Phantom Liberty. I look forward to the sequel and wonder where CDPR will take the world of Cyberpunk next. Its preem content, choom. You should try it. 9/10

The negative review is for this: Do not buy it at full price, especially not if you have a mid-range PC like mine AND especially if you are a completionist like me. I tried to experience all the content the game had to offer in a single playthrough, which led to me "optimizing" it (meaning completing all side jobs, fixer gigs and NCPD scanners). Here is my extensive review:

Six years after its original release, I thought the game would be in a pretty great state, but it is still pretty disappointing. I think most people who praise it, they do so because they compare it to the dumpster fire it was on release. But the game still feels unpolished, even unfinished, and it's still riddled with bugs. Not game-breaking ones, but they are still there. I had to install numerous mods in order to get to a decent playable state (fix for junky melee combat, pedestrian behaviour, quality of life elements for HUD and menus, like filters etc, de-scaled skill checks which were impossible after leveling up)

Gameplay wise, the RPG elements are minimal, the dialogue options are mostly different flavours of the same choice, the combat is repetitive and the enemy AI is extremely stupid, even in Very Hard difficulty. The side content (gigs and NCPD scanner jobs) are all duplicate brain-dead quests (read flavour text, go to location, sneak/shoot, loot chest, read flavour text). And no, the city is not immersive at all for me. All the places feel the same.

Its only redeeming quality, the story and characters, are overshadowed and diluted by the immense amount of mediocre side content that continuously distracts you (text messages, calls, etc) and forces you to engage with it ("wait for a whole day until the next mission objective", "find something else to do until [character] contacts you"). 

As always, I think the level design would have benefited if was a more linear and condensed experience, allowing the player to progress through the map gradually and learning to organically traverse through the levels, instead of blindly following quest markers.

I'm considering playing it again and focusing only on the main mission, just to experience the story in a more condensed way, but I am dreading the thought of having to go through all the tedious character progress and repetitive combat.

EDIT: I played the game again, and engaged only with the main quest. It was a far more enjoyable experience for 2 reasons: 1) I was already accustomed with the in-game universe (slang, concepts, characters) and I realized this was part of why I felt lost all the time during my first playthrough, and 2) I was not distracted by the side content and I was able to focus on the story and characters).

Bottom line: Cyberpunk 2077 is a good game but its held down by the open world elements that feel they were forced and rushed by the devs, because apparently these are the minimal expectations for a AAA release.

Obviously, I knew this going in. I really didn't think that would be that big of a deal, but it is. This is a D&D 5e system... it's a D&D setting... but it is NOT D&D. It's in an unpleasant uncanny valley where, in the end, it just feels like the 5e rules got shoehorned into a game they're not written for. It's all the weaknesses of 5e (unbalanced classes, martial/caster divide) and none of the strengths (flexibility, application of real world ideas into a game system, smooth combat resolution). It's a chimera, with semi-simultaneous action resolution, really high/long jumping for some reason, stripped down leveling (max 12), and lower flexibility for spells (Polymorph).

As of writing, every companion/"origin character" I've met has been unlikeable. Still, they're expected to be the center of the story, as there's no mechanism for you to have a backstory in the game. You might as well have spawned in those pods for all the relevancy your character's history or possible history has. 

The high magic in the game is kind of absurd. You have access to multiple scrolls of revivify at level 1 for game reasons, and you're literally flying around in a giant interdimensional Mind Flayer spaceship that took a wrong turn at Waterdeep, got hit by some dragons, and ended up in Avernus (because everything in D&D seems to end up there). I was rolling my eyes the entire intro because it was just so absurd. Combat is neither good nor bad, but it's kind of unfortunate it doesn't show the dice rolls for anything. Rolling dice in any other setting is a full-screen popup.

Larian tried their best, but I think, frankly, they had an impossible task. You can't adapt D&D, a collaborative story game, into a video game. You can make a [i]sandbox[/i], but that's not the same thing (and it's also not what they did).

The game looks great until something moves in a way that isn't just walking. Nearly every character in every scene is wobbling with mocap awkwardness; nearly nothing looks actually natural. They even have it in the trailers.

If you want an experience somewhat closer to what I think Larian was trying to accomplish, I would recommend Kenshi. You really do feel like you're creating your own story there, not stumbling through railroaded cutscenes. 

If you want a compelling mystery in a game that is both funnier and more representative of how D&D is played at the table, play Esoteric Ebb.

But if you want my honest advice...

[b]JUST PLAY D&D[/b]. This game seems to take over 60 hours to complete. That's enough for [b]ten 6-hour sessions of D&D[/b]. Buy the PHB for half the price of this game and

[b]Just[/b]

[b]Play[/b]

[b]D&D[/b].

The Witcher 3 is one of those games that stays in your mind even after you finish it. You start playing because you want to kill some monsters and do a few quests, and before you realize it, you're getting attached to the characters, making decisions you actually think about, and spending hours exploring places you didn't even need to visit.

The best part is that even some random side quests feel more interesting than the main story of other games. You never really know what you're getting into. Sometimes you accept a simple contract, and somehow it turns into a story that makes you sit there thinking about it long after it's over.

And the world itself? Absolutely incredible. The music, the atmosphere, the villages, the forests, the people you meet, and even the little details make everything feel alive. You can spend an entire evening just riding around on Roach, exploring question marks on the map, and completely forgetting what you were supposed to be doing.

Geralt is also such a great main character. He's not some perfect hero who always does the right thing. He's just a man trying to get through a complicated world, and sometimes there isn't even a good choice to make. That's what makes the story feel so real.

And don't even get me started on the DLCs. Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine are worth experiencing on their own. Blood and Wine especially feels like a whole new adventure rather than just extra content.

If you've never played this game, do yourself a favor and give it a chance. Don't rush through it, don't just follow the main quests, and take your time with the side stories. That's when you'll understand why people still talk about this game years later.

And if you've already played it and uninstalled it, maybe it's time to come back. There are always quests you missed, choices you want to make differently, and moments you want to experience again.

For me, The Witcher 3 isn't just a game I finished and moved on from. It's one of those experiences that makes other games feel a little less special afterward.

I was a day-one buyer of Cyberpunk 2077. I was there for the launch, and I swear I encountered just about every bug that ended up documented online.

So I waited.

I saw what CD Projekt Red had done with The Witcher 3 over time, and I genuinely believed Cyberpunk would get the same treatment. I wanted to experience this game when it was finally ready, rather than ruin my first playthrough fighting through technical problems.

Six years later, I still can't play it.

For me, it's the infamous audio crackling/popping glitch. If you've searched for this problem, you already know the worst part: everyone seems to have a different "fix," which means there really isn't one.

I've changed audio refresh/sample rates. Updated and reinstalled drivers. Turned SFX down and completely off. Disabled spatial audio. Used Windows spatial audio. Tried Bluetooth headphones, wired headphones, laptop speakers, desktop speakers, and monitor speakers. I've verified the game files, uninstalled and reinstalled the entire game, restarted the computer, turned it off and back on, and done all the other obligatory troubleshooting steps. I've gone through forums, Reddit threads, videos, and troubleshooting guides.

Believe me, if you're about to suggest a fix, I've probably tried it.

And before someone points at my Steam playtime as proof that the game must have been playable, those hours are extremely misleading. A huge amount of that time was spent with the game running while I was trying to troubleshoot the problem, testing settings, restarting, loading back in, driving around to see if the crackling returned, and repeating the process. Yes, there were stretches where I actually got to play the game, but I'd estimate maybe 25% of my recorded hours were spent genuinely playing rather than trying to make the game work.

And that's what makes this so disappointing. I *want* to play Cyberpunk 2077. I bought it at launch, watched CDPR spend years rebuilding its reputation, watched the game receive major updates and an expansion, and deliberately waited to give it the experience I thought it deserved.

But I've never once been able to actually play through the game.

Six years of patches, updates, fixes, and second chances, and a game-breaking audio issue that has been reported by players for years still makes the game effectively unplayable for me.

So, for the final time, I'm uninstalling Cyberpunk 2077. At this point, I have to accept that I'm probably never going to finish what I genuinely wanted to be a superb game.

I'm sure Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game when it works. I genuinely wish I could have found out.

I've been trying to give this game a fair chance because I'd heard so many good things about it, but honestly, I just don't think it's that good. To me, it feels like one of those massively hyped games that ended up being far more impressive in reputation than in reality.

The story has been surprisingly difficult to follow and stay invested in, while the mechanics often feel clunky and frustrating. Too many times I've had the game do something I never intended, forcing me to reload a save and replay sections just because the controls or interface got in the way. Instead of feeling smooth and intuitive, it often feels like I'm fighting the game itself.

The characters haven't helped much either. Most of the companions and NPCs are forgettable, and I honestly don't understand the popularity of some of the fan favorites. Astarion feels incredibly overrated and irritating, while Lae'zel spends most of her time coming across as obnoxious and unpleasant. I know a lot of people love these characters, but they simply didn't click with me.

As someone who genuinely loves D&D and runs two games a week, I was expecting something that captured the spirit of the tabletop experience. Instead, this often feels like a game wearing a D&D costume rather than actually embodying what makes D&D special. So many mechanics and design choices just feel off, and the overall experience rarely captures that freedom and excitement that make the tabletop game so enjoyable.

Considering the price, I don't think it's worth paying full price for. If you can pick it up during a major sale, then maybe it's worth giving a shot. Otherwise, I personally wouldn't recommend it at its current cost.

I started playing Witcher 3 some days ago, just before they announced the remastered version. Since my PC is quite old, I downloaded the classic version, which used to run fine. However, after the release of the remastered version, the classic one now fails to launch. I tried both checking the files and reinstalling the whole game; neither fixed the problem. 

Despite having played the game to almost the end of the main campaign, the impossibility of playing it from now on doesn't cause me any frustration – one chore less to do; it is the impossibility of a refund that weights more. It took years in between the purchase and the first time I tested it. 

Now on to what I think of The Witcher 3 as a game. The writing is OK for the most part (anyone used to reading the classics may think it is mediocre at best); the written content, on the other hand, could be less boring, considering it was based on books (books, however, that couldn't reach success on their own merit, and are now widely known thanks to the games, and indeed, when I tried reading one of them, “The Last Wish” I think was its title, it tasted like uninspired cheap porn); the graphics are well done, which is meaningless given that some of the best games ever made have very simple graphics; the background music and ambient sound effects are quite good; as for the game-play, which is by far the most important component of a video-game, it is easily the worst part of the Witcher 3 experience, both combat and walking or riding a horse controls are atrocious; also CD Project Red brutally “ubisofted” the game by making it unnecessarily open-world with lots of question marks marking repetitive tasks, a complete disrespect to the player’s time.

Whenever Geralt hits a physical roadblock, there is a sorceress who just happens to have the exact spell to fix the problem. The only way to lift a curse from character #234 is giving them witcher potions that could kill them? No problem, Yen has the exact spell for helping them survive. Need to swim deeper and can’t hold breath? Yen just has the spell to cover you there too. Bridge is broken? Can’t cross it? How lucky Philippa came along then, she just happens to have the fix-broken-bridge spell. Is the White Frost too frosty to stand and you forgot to pack your sweater? Yen has just what you need, a warm sanctuary spell to keep the frostbite away. The Wild Hunt is very wild indeed, and hunts in packs, wouldn’t it be great to get invisible when there are so many of them around? Guess what? Yen just happens to... Because why bother writing clever quests to solve these obstacles if you can make your mages conjure the solution out of thin air? This way you make room to fill up the game with higher priority content, like sending Geralt after some old man’s goat

Having played the series in order, I was expecting Witcher 3 to be an improvement over the second game; it is clearly a downgrade instead. In Witcher 2, the story starts with Geralt in jail, falsely accused of regicide. In what is arguably one of the most dramatic cut-scenes in the history of video-games, he fails to protect the king and watches powerlessly as the true assassin escapes. He suffered torture and would probably be hanged if not for Roche, who gives him a chance to prove his innocence by capturing the true culprit. The main objective is very clear, Geralt is caught in the middle of a geopolitical struggle and, as a player, you immediately want to see how the story will unfold. As for Witcher 3, well... Geralt starts in search of a woman, and when he finally finds her, or rather is found by her, he is then given the heroic task of – guess what? – finding another woman. And that is the whole plot. A much more fitting title for this game could be “Finding Ciri”. 

Do not think, however, that finding Ciri is going to be easy. The Novigrad section plays like this: find Triss, she may know about Ciri → find Corinne, she may know about Ciri → find Dandelion, he apparently was with Ciri → find the crime bosses, they may know about Dandelion → find Junior, he may know about Dandelion → find Dudu, he knows about Dandelion → find Priscilla, she may know how to find Dudu. Then the infamous butcher of Blaviken and slayer of monsters, Geralt, is required to use his quite specific set of talents to help the professional bard Priscilla to write a play in order to attract Dudu from wherever this undoubtedly very important character is hiding. It was at this moment that my tedium gauge reached stratospheric levels and I unconsciously started button mashing the controller through the cut-scene. I stopped playing the game then, but forced myself to keep pushing some days later, and made it to the Isles of Mist.

I should thank CD Project Red for completely breaking the classic version or I would probably torture myself even more.

EDIT: With respect to the problem of launching the classic version, a user in the comments provided a link that solved the problem. So I went on and finished the game. To my surprise, the achievement for completing the main campaign was obtained by only about 22% of players. So, despite all the universal praise this game received, 78% of its digital renters never even bothered to actually finish it.

The Death of The Cayo Perico Heist: How Rockstar Methodically Killed the Only Fair Content in GTA Online
When The Cayo Perico Heist dropped in December 2020, GTA Online players felt like they could finally breathe. After years of forced cooperative misery, mental breakdowns caused by unreliable random players, and outrageously overpriced properties, Rockstar finally delivered something that felt too good to be true: a highly lucrative heist that could be played entirely solo.

Cayo Perico was the ultimate symbol of freedom in Los Santos. You didn’t have to beg anyone to join, and you didn’t have to waste hours on tedious setups. You could jump in, pull off a slick stealth run, and pocket $1.3 to $1.8 million in just over an hour.

But then, Rockstar realized that players were actually having fun, and—more importantly in their eyes—they weren’t buying Shark Cards anymore. That’s when the methodical, ruthless, and shameless nerfing of the heist began, turning El Rubio's island into a frustrating, low-paying chore.

The Rap Sheet: How a Jackpot Was Turned into Spare Change
1. The Desecration of the Pink Diamond and Primary Targets
We used to cheer when we saw the pink diamond on the security cameras, knowing we were in for a massive payday. Today, Rockstar has practically stripped these targets of their value. Slashing the value of the Pink Diamond—sometimes dragging the total payout of a solo run down toward the $900k mark—is a massive slap in the face to the player's time. Why risk your neck against a private army when you walk away with barely more than what a basic VIP contract used to pay?

2. The Systematic Punishment of Solo Players (The Cooldown Terror)
The most hostile move was the execution of the solo playstyle. If you complete the heist alone, the game now forces a brutal 3-game-day cooldown (approx. 2 hours and 24 minutes) before you can start it again. Meanwhile, team play has a much shorter cooldown. This isn’t "game balance"; it's blatant extortion: “Play with others (who will take a cut of your money), or wait hours to play again.”

3. Guards Suddenly Became Mind-Reading Geniuses (Wallhack AI)
Stealth was the beating heart of Cayo Perico. You followed your memorized route, quietly took out the guards, and slipped away unnoticed. But Rockstar rolled out an update where guards now detect dead bodies. While this sounds good on paper, GTA Online’s notoriously buggy, decade-old AI turned it into a disaster. Guards now frequently see through solid walls or spot corpses on the completely opposite side of the map. Precise stealth has been replaced by a frustrating, unpredictable gamble.

4. Jacked-Up Setup Fees
Just to make absolutely sure you don’t keep too much of your hard-earned cash, they quadrupled the heist setup fee from $25,000 to $100,000. Before you even set foot on the island to scout, you start in the negatives, all while your final payout is actively being gutted.

Verdict: A Monument to Corporate Greed
The current state of the Cayo Perico Heist is a perfect mirror of what GTA Online has become: a game that is no longer designed to entertain you, but to frustrate you into opening your real-world wallet.

They took away the freedom, they took away the fair pay, and they replaced it with a buggy, soul-crushing grind. Rockstar didn't just ruin El Rubio's island; they sabotaged their relationship with their own community. This isn't game development—it's highway robbery.

It started innocently enough—a couple of canceled plans, a few unread text messages, and a growing preference for spending my evenings locked in my room. To anyone on the outside, it just looked like I was going through a phase or slowly falling off the grid.

The real culprit was Elden Ring...

If playing it on a controller is hard, mastering it on a keyboard was pure masochism. Once I stepped into that world, I was hooked. I lost count of the hours spent frantically remapping keys, missing dodges because my fingers slipped off WASD, and throwing myself at brutal bosses for whole nights. Friends called to hang out, but I always had a quick excuse ready. My girlfriend wanted to talk about where we were going, but I brushed her off, too consumed by managing my quick-slots and camera angles to notice how far away I was pushing the real world. Slowly, the invitations stopped, the texts dried up, and my room became completely silent except for the endless, aggressive clicking of my mechanical keyboard.

By the time I finally defeated the final boss—fingers aching, wrists stiff—and watched the end credits roll, the high of victory vanished instantly. I looked around the dead silence of my empty, dark room, hit by a sudden, crushing wave of loneliness. I had conquered the Lands Between on the hardest control scheme possible, but I had completely ruined my life in the process.

Or so I thought.

As I sat there in the quiet, staring at my own reflection in the dark screen, a sudden realization washed over me. I hadn't actually lost a great life. The relationship I had been ignoring was already dead long before the game; we were only staying together out of comfortable habit. The social circle I missed was full of surface-level friends I never really felt connected to, and my daily routine before this had been a soul-crushing, exhausting cycle I hated.

Elden Ring hadn't destroyed my life; it had actually burned away all the noise, obligation, and dead weight I was too afraid to let go of myself. It didn't leave me broken—it gave me a completely clean slate.

I stood up, stretched my tired fingers, walked over to the window, and pushed it open, letting the cold morning air fill the room. I shut down the PC, picked up my phone, and smiled. I was completely alone, but for the very first time in years, I was free to build something real from scratch.

I was never really into CRPG's and found turn based combat annoying. The Divinity series and then this game have completely turned me around. I have absolutely loved playing this game and I am nowhere near finished because it has me by the proverbial shorthairs. The depth of the world, how rich the story is, the items, the characters, it's definitely an acquired taste for some, but for me? This has very quickly become one of my favorite games.

I have to admit, and I do not say this lightly, this game is an absolute masterpiece. In my nearly 20 years of gaming I have never EVER seen anything come remotely close to this in terms of pure love, effort and dedication. The amount of content you get for your money is absolutely mind blowing with very well over 150 hours required if you want to properly experience just one playthrough, and that's not accounting for the unbelievable replayability. Even the smallest, seemingly insignificant side quests have story relevance and multiple ways to go about completing them, everything is made with such painstaking attention to detail and a dynamic world in mind. The writing is utterly phenomenal, the characters believable, the voice actors just amazing and all this with people new to the world of D&D taken into consideration. Everything important is explained and shown to you in the world, with smaller tidbits of lore scattered in books around the environment, painting a complete picture of Faerun. And if that wasn't enough, the combat ties a perfect little bow on the whole thing, it's fun, it's challenging but fair, and rewards you thoroughly for using the environment and making smart choices, giving a true tactical sandbox experience. Overall, I have nothing but love for this game and I genuinely can not think of any way to improve it except to make that sequel. Thank you, Larian Studios, for the unforgettable experience!

I would have to spend a lot of time manually organizing my radials into something usable whereas in Divinity, spells are placed on a hotbar where it's easy to arrange them and see exactly what they do. It's possible some of this comes from the unholy matrimony of D&D 5e mechanics and video game design limitations but it's so frustrating that I just play keyboard/mouse. I guess that's fine, but, like, this game is available (and more expensive) on consoles where controller is the only option. Now something that I know is 5e's fault, is that combat is not very fun. [List]
[H1]Foreword[/h1]
[*]Loved Baldur's Gate 1 & 2 (Shadows of Amn & Throne of Bhaal), including Siege of Dragonspear - they are in my list of all-time best and favorite CRPGs.

[*]Never touched tabletop Dungeons & Dragons, but I considered myself an avid RPG-er (western ones). Advanced D&D 2nd edition and 3.5 D&D are some of my favorite systems.

[*]Played in 2-players co-op.

[*]Played on Balanced difficulty as to avoid excessive metagaming that will break roleplay.

[*]Explored every place and did every content (hence the hours) - as long as it didn't contradict roleplay.

[*]No achievements because of some cosmetic mods used and the absolute necessity of using the Item and Spell Bug Fixes mod. The game is almost unplayable without this imo. Imagine building your character with care and with roleplaying in mind to later finding out too late that half the skills, feats, and equipment your character is using don't work as intended.

[*]Held back from playing the game since its launch so that it could be enjoyed post bug-fixes, dlcs, and polish - biding literally 3 years of time thinking it the 'messiah' of CRPGs from the word of mouth and hype surrounding it.

[*]Played with keyboard and mouse.

[H1]The Good[/h1]
[*]The game is very aesthetically pleasing. The best looking CRPG to date. HDR support.

[*]No loading screen, unless you're changing regions.

[*]Co-op up to 4 players.

[*]Character models are excellent (not including custom-created player characters). The dialogue camera captures this beautifully.

[*]Fully voiced but there are odd fews which are not - probably due to time constraints.

[*]Very accessible and beginner friendly to anyone wanting to dip their toes into D&D or just fantasy CRPGs in general.

[*]Throwback to events from BG 1 & 2 with old characters returning. Jaheira and Minsc are brilliant in this and easily are the most interesting characters/ [spoiler]companions[/spoiler] in the game.

[*]Overall great OST, but somehow not as memorable as the classic ones for me.

[*]Massive amount of content you can sink hundreds of hours into. It is not one of those RPGs that end abruptly.

[*]Non-linear path on which you tackle the main quest and side quests, embark on an adventure of your own making.

[*]All the combat animations, spells, and visual effects are flashy and smooth, not janky.

[*]Pet [spoiler]owlbear[/spoiler].

[*]A conclusive ending.

[H1]The Bad[/h1]
[*]Bugs. Not worth all the wait. Just to list a few: Web (level 2 spell) useless, failed saving throw against it will instead free you. Shatter spell no AOE indication. Combat log showing wrong calculation of spell DC, shove DC, damage modifiers, attack rolls. Tooltips not accurate, Evasive Footwork not lasting one turn, Shield Master feat practically useless. There are many others that I can't possibly list the majority of them but the mod I mentioned in the foreword mitigated this problem to a bearable degree.

[*]Ability and skill checks don't detect who you bring into your party. Want to succeed an Arcana check even though you have a wizard just by your side? Tough luck.

[*]The stealth and surprise system made me want to tear my hairs out. Many unexplained intricacies/ bugs that will make a simple stealth attack fail. For example: successfully killing an enemy with stealth attack will result in the remaining enemies not being surprised.

[*]Master volume is too low. I needed to turn to my headphone external controller to crank up the volume.

[*]As per standard of today's game industry, no beautiful faces to choose from for your human female PC. Resolved this by using mods.

[*]Memory leak - constant micro-stutters - if your game session is on the longer side. Also two instances of buggy dialogue scenes that lock you up and require a restart of the game, only happened when the game's running long.

[*]Initial romance routes are too strict. Not choosing the correct 'thirsty' option in that particular time will make you unable to romance that companion for the rest of the game.

[*]Further into the game, there will be feats that are not listed in the enemies' abilities. E.g. darkvision not listed, [spoiler]Cazador cannot be disarmed despite not having Permanently Armed feat[/spoiler].

[*]The voice acting doesn't cover all the info that is given to the player - you need to consult the journal/ trust the journal more than what's being said to get the full picture. E.g. [spoiler]Investigator Valeria pledging the City Watch help for the final battle was never mentioned in dialogue[/spoiler].

[*]Some subclasses are clear dev's favorites. Assassin is lackluster compared to Gloom Stalker and playing Hunter subclass felt like you have a grenade launcher in your hand - its AOE capabilities far exceed a Fighter's.

[*]Many villain expositions. The villains bored me.

[*]Thematically, no subject deeply explored nor a hard question asked. The game is massive and coupled with high production value, but it is generic fantasy. It will not cause any restless night or contemplation.

[*]Camera controls using mouse and keyboard are janky. Oftimes, the environment will mess your camera up and rotating using Q and E has input delay if pressed successively.

[*]The ratio between combat and dialogue skews heavily towards the latter. Felt like the devs are allergic to trash mobs and encounters - even though BG 1 & 2 had those aplenty. It could last up to 30 minutes - felt like an hour - before the next combat encounter.

[*]Balanced difficulty is not it. It rests more on the easier side and even becoming too easy oftimes. The bosses we faced usually can only act one turn before dying, and the final one didn't even have a single turn.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[*]There are plenty of CRPG goodness here, especially for those not looking to bog themselves in the genre's usual complexities. But if you perhaps are looking for a CRPG that has a well thought-out system, way less bugs in its core mechanics, stays truer to the classics, and most importantly, ask deeply the questions regarding gods, faith, destiny, soul, philosophy, and morality, play Pillars of Eternity 1 instead.

I've beaten it and I've spent over 600 hours with it (probably double that if you count the GOG version as well), but the percent of that time was actually fun is not that high. It's also full of so many frustrating design decisions.
For example:
1. Alert is a top tier feat in normal D&D 5 already, but with a d4 for initiative it's just ridiculous. If they were doing that, it should give only +1 to iniative (and it would still be a powerful feat). Meanwhile, the mess they made of the action economy made the "use your shield to shove as a bonus action" you can get through the feat completely useless.
2. They made a complete mess of the action economy by letting you cast two spells in one turn, jumping is an action for some reason, and they made shove a bonus action instead of an attack (but they also nerfed it so you can't use it to knock someone prone). There's other examples, but that's enough.
3. "Weapon actions" OK, at first glance this makes sense, could be fun. If I have a spear maybe I can rush someone down and... I can only do that once per day? Why is there even a limit to a completely mundane non-magical action?
4. The conversations: There's a distinct lack of options to disagree with a lot of people. Rather it's 3 options like "I agree" or "I agree and apologize" or "Maybe you're right after all" or "Get defensive but don't disagree".
5: The culture in game: There's no consistency at all, and people that are human and look like they belong in that part of the world is a very small minority. I think there *should* be exotic races and species present, especially in the city or in the extraplanar journeys, but not everyone should be an exotic, because then nobody is. It just makes the world building feel flat. Speaking of flat, why does Viconia, a relatively young full-blooded elf look so old?
6: The party members. All the males are completely unlikable. Not "charmingly annoying" or "gets under your skin, so you want to see what bad things can happen to them" (the old version of Wyll was a bit like that). No, you just want them to go home and leave you alone.
7: Character creation: Shield Dwarf should get a +2 to Str and Con. That's what makes them so good at doing dwarfy stuff. But no, someone at Larian has something against dwarfs (that would explain why so many of them in game look nothing like a dwarf apart from their stature too), and every race has the same bonuses. The same thing screwed over humans too, who lose their stat bonuses and their level 1 feat, instead getting weapon and armor proficiencies because every human (and half elf) has miilitary training I guess?
8. Perhaps the most annoying feature, but I almost forgot it, is The Controls: Casting a spell with one character then switching to another often has you clicking 3-4 or more times on the portrait you're trying to switch to before it actually does, and the camera often refuses to follow you "upstairs" when you're trying to get a character to move there. Also, rather than a simple drag to select multiple interface like in the infinity engine games or many RTS games, or Owlcat's Pathfinder games, there's a needlessly cumbersom e "chain" system which makes positioning a complete pain when accuracy or speed matters (which it usually doesn't, but still), especially since if you decouple them, switching between them can take multiple clicks. Using the function keys to switch usually works on the first try, so I don't know why they screwed up the mouse controls so bad.

That's just 8 things - there's dozens upon dozens of large, small and tiny annoyances that collect until there's just a feeling of fatigue trying to play the game.

Luckily, there's mods that fix almost ALL of these annoyances (doesn't fix the controls or the camera, and Realms Restored is a pain to install on Linux), but playing the game without mods is just not a good time.

Now that I finally got to really playing through Elden Ring, I must sadly say that my initial opinion did not change. I know it is a hot take and contrary to the overall opinion, but this has to be the worst FromSoft game I've played (granted I've never played Bloodborne or any of the Armored Core games so those are out of the count). For me, soulslikes are closer to dungeon crawlers than the anime boss rush that they've become. That's why I think that even though Dark Souls 3 is my favorite overall, none of the games have come close to the feeling of DS1.

While the base combat still feels good and far more fluent than any Dark Souls has ever done, the issue is that they've gone head first into the idea that you wait for a combo, then hit once or twice, rinse and repeat. To me, that has become a tedious way to fight, considering how well games like Monster Hunter have perfected the idea that you can take control of the fight and play more aggressive. Yeah, I know that you can do that in most soulslikes too but the difference is that even when I've learned a boss so well that I know almost all the spots, it never feels like I am in control. The only FromSoft game that made me feel like that is Sekiro. The reason this wasn't an issue in DS1 for example is because bosses actually died after a reasonable amount of hits.

And that's the key point, these games focus too much on bosses and with Elden Ring, the idea of visual clutter to make things look cool instead of engaging to fight has been overutilized. There is so many flashy moves that are 100% dodged only with iframes, which to me signals incredibly lazy boss design. When I practically have to analyze the moves like I go through some SDVX charts, I just feel like rather focusing on a game where studying things on paper is actually fun. In my entire playthrough, the only boss I actually felt was fun and I'd like to go through again was Placidusax. Maybe Maliketh too, if we exclude the first phase. Not a huge fan of it but that's mostly just because I suck at it. Radahn was nice as a concept with all the summons and it being a sort of a brawl but the fight itself was pretty meh. Other than that, the bosses were pretty lame.

As for story, I can't help but feel like they just took the original story of Dark Souls, gave it to Martin and told him to just reimagine it with them and then they called it a day. This is almost a carbon-copy clone. And with most NPC's dying and that being a trend of FromSoft's games, I feel far more surprised when someone lives but I find it hard to care for the questlines when they're just "go talk to someone, quit to menu or sit at site of grace, go talk to them again + maybe a summon/invade at the end." It just feels lazy that this formula is still repeated for almost every quest, even after all these years. FromSoft should really come up with something new.

The world design was great though. Places like Stormveil and Leyndell felt really fun to explore. But the open areas and the open world was bad. For me it just doesn't work in a soulslike setting. It is too open and when everything respawns, there's no permanent impact on your actions, which to me is a key point of open world games. Plus when the entire world is practically dead and almost everyone is hostile, I feel like the sense of exploration is pretty watered down.

It just doesn't feel like there's really a need for the open world setup, especially when you realize how linear the game actually is. It's not like you can approach Leyndell from several areas, since the map is extremely linear and there are places blocking your progress further. It is a good thing in this game but makes the open world feel pointless. I feel like it only exists for the same reason that Monster Hunter Wilds is "open world", which is just to fill a marketing tickbox because open world games are trending. You need to sell the concept of the game being massive, not so much the actual amount of unique content being there, so what's an easier way to do that than making your game open world.

All that being said, it is not necessarily a bad game. I just think that it is mediocre when compared to FromSoft's previous products. I started with DS2 then DS3 > DS1 > Sekiro > Nightreign > Elden Ring and before playing Elden Ring, I considered DS2 the worst FromSoft game, which is why I find it hard to believe it would be just nostalgia talking.

Generally speaking, no story is good enough to justify horrible mechanics and playability, and Cyberpunk 2077 is not an exception. It should be noted that I cannot comment on some of the game mechanics that are supposedly redeeming, as by and large the goal of this game seems to be to obscure mechanics and solutions in the most needless and confusing ways possible, and I have better uses of my time than trying to hunt down how on earth anyone is actually supposed to play this game. If you read the positive reviews, they mostly focus on aspects that are positive in passive media and do not comment on the combat or gameplay loop. I am sure the books and tabletop games this was based on are amazing and may devote time to them at some point, but this game itself is a pain to play. Based on my current experience, I will probably have even more complaints if I ever finish hunting down however this game is supposed to work. Given the actual gameplay, this is almost a side note, but I did not buy a 6800 XT that can crank the settings at 1440p just for said cranked settings to make combat utterly nightmarish and more unfair than some horror games due to lack of visibility.

Baldur’s Gate 3 - Overwhelmingly Tedious and Boring

I genuinely tried. Seven hours in, multiple sessions. Somewhere around the middle I had a tiny moment of “okay, maybe I’m starting to see it”- that lasted about five minutes.
This is one of the most boring games I have ever played.

BG3 feels like taking every slow, fiddly, overcomplicated part of tabletop RPGs and turning it into a video game - then making every single action take three business days. An Indian drama...

The introduction is atrocious. You are dumped into a wall of classes, races, abilities, resources, dice rolls, actions, bonus actions, movement, spell slots, concentration, inventory, companions and unexplained mechanics with barely any useful explanation. Character creation somehow manages to be both absurdly detailed in places and bizarrely restrictive in others. I spent more time fighting the character creator than creating a character. I eventually made a Wood Half-Elf Ranger because “stealth sniper -> get spotted -> RAAAAAGH” is basically my natural playstyle, but the game certainly didn't make understanding my choices easy.

Then there is the actual gameplay.

Combat is an RNG simulator where my greatest enemy is apparently the number 1.
Miss. Miss. Miss. Critical Miss. Miss. Miss.

Congratulations, you have successfully spent several minutes positioning your character so that a dice roll can tell you to go f*** yourself.

And the damage progression? Incredible.
Hour 1: 1–9 damage
Hour 7: 4-11 damage
Absolutely revolutionary.

The combat is painfully slow. Every movement point matters, every action takes ages, enemies take their turns one by one, animations drag on... Pathfinding is janky and a single misclick can send your character climbing some invisible wall or walking somewhere you absolutely did not intend. I have played games with clunky controls before, but BG3 somehow makes most games' control schemes look like divine intervention.

Exploration isn't any better. You click on a ladder: “You can't go there.”
Click again: suddenly you can. Click beside a doorway: your character attempts to scale the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Himalayas. Try to scout around a corner: congratulations, you've been teleported into combat.
I repeatedly felt like I was fighting the interface rather than the enemies.


The world itself has not grabbed me either. I explored the Grove, picked up a pile of vaguely described errands that they call quests, fought some goblins, got annihilated by an owlbear, got blown up by a statue, stumbled into fights I wasn't prepared for. Spent half my time rummaging through containers for mediocre garbage. The game constantly tries to give the impression that there is supposed to be something fascinating around the next corner, only for the reward to be another conversation, box of junk or fight.

The loot is particularly underwhelming. Forget about finding cool gear and becoming noticeably stronger. 
You get another item with slightly different numbers, same ugly piece of armor, pile of useless arrows and another 20 minute inventory-management session.

And yes, I understand that the game is about player choice and role-playing rather than conventional power progression. That doesn't make the gameplay engaging.

The story, after seven hours, is essentially: YOU HAVE A PARASITE. FIX THE PARASITE.

FIX THE PARASITE.
FIX THE PARASITE.

I KNOW. I HAVE BEEN TOLD. PLEASE STOP BEING A BROKEN RECORD.

The characters haven't done anything for me either. The voice acting is generally good but great performances cannot make characters interesting if I don't care about what they're saying.
Shadowheart is probably the closest I've gotten to actually liking a companion. Still not enough.
Astarion is entertaining to listen to but insufferable.
Lae'zel is an aggressive noseless ♥♥♥♥♥, any line coming out of her makes me physically cringe and want to put my hands on somebody (the writer or smth...).
Gale is a parasitic f*** who has 3 moves, then becomes utterly useless until you go rest.
And the whole party has so far felt more like a collection of personalities I am managing than people I actually want to travel with.

The romance system also feels hilariously prominent for a game that otherwise tries to take itself so seriously.
Apparently everyone is horny enough to jump you after approximately three conversations. Fantastic.
I'm sure this has nothing to do with the soulless gooners that actually LARP sh** like this.

The music is underwhelming at best. It's competent but repetitive and generic compared with games whose soundtracks actually stick in my head.
I ended up wanting to turn it off, replace it with actual good OSTs, like The Witcher's or Lies of P's...

And then there's the technical side.

The graphics look MEDIOCRE for a 2023 game, yet the performance is absurd.
My PC gets hotter running this heap of trash than Cyberpunk 2077 on max settings with Ray Tracing.
It's artificially big and visually inconsistent. Manages to make my hardware work overtime while I stare at two people standing in a room talking about a spermatozoid...

The funniest part is that I can understand why people like the freedom. BG3 clearly allows variying approaches to situations. That's the only place I can really see effort put in.
But for me, that is not enough. I need the actual GAMEPLAY to be fun.
Not "options to potentially make gameplay exist are vast"... Empty theatre room.


This feels less like an adventure and more like administrative work with dice. Pick up item. Miss item. Open door. Miss door. Walk somewhere. Accidentally climb something. Sort inventory. Equip slightly better trousers. Start combat. Miss. Miss. Critical Miss. Watch six enemies spend an eternity deciding whether to move three meters. Finally get a turn. Use an ability. Miss. Get one-shot. Rest. Repeat.

I have games sitting in my library that give me more entertainment in six hours than BG3 has given me in seven. The Darkness II's entire amazing campaign is shorter than the amount of time I have spent trying to convince myself this game is going to click.

Maybe it gets better.
Maybe Act 2 is secretly the second coming of gaming
Maybe Act 3 gets you a horned girlfriend IRL

I genuinely do not care enough to find out.

Clearly I'm not the target audience. But after seven hours of giving it a completely fair chance, I don't see a masterpiece hiding underneath the geriatric systems. “Overwhelmingly Positive” is absolute insanity.

Pretentous CRPG buried under a mountain of slow combat, RNG, inventory management, awkward controls, weak progression, tedious traversal and endless dialogue.

I didn't ragequit because the game is difficult - it's just tedious.
I rage-quit because I was bored out of my mind, realizing I'm wasting my precious and finite time doing the paperwork/homework equivalent of a "video game".

And when a game makes me look at my backlog and think, “I could be playing literally anything else right now,” that's the end of the road.

I'd rather chew the 40 euro I gave for this game, that might be more fun too.

TLDR: This isn't a good game, it's got nothing to offer other than some pretty graphics.

I decided to give this game a chance (despite the fact that i'm not a fan of RPG games) because I like open world games and this game's city looked cool. And so I started playing, trying to focus on the positives – the beauty of the city, just driving around, doing missions as an excuse to spend some time immersed in it. I did succeed in that – at times the game hit me with some stunning views of the city's architecture. From that aspect I won't deny that some mad talent and hard work must've gone into its creation. The city has no depth to it though, it's just a pretty postcard – whenever I tried to explore it I found that there's nothing there. Can't really have no fun interactions with the environment or the NPCs.

Beyond that though, this game definitively confirmed to me, together with my previous excruciating attempts at playing The Witcher 3, that the developers at CD Project Red have no idea how to make an entertaining videogame.

This game's story is bad. It's generic, it's pompous, event though it has no right to be, since it's a dookie. It's filled with exposition dumping from a bunch of talking heads with stiff animations that explain to you why you should care and why it's essential for you to shoot 30 more guys for the story to progress. The story tries to touch on all your typical dystopian topics like corrupted corporations and governments, the violence, the meaning of life, but it fails to say anything meaningful or impactful.
 
The main character is arrogant and unlikeable. Their immature desire to hit the "big leagues" coupled with the overdone voice acting and terms like "delta", "nova", "choom" etc. really didn't evoke any emotion other than embarassment. I wanna emphasize just how much they dropped the ball with the story and the delivery of the voice lines, because I didn't feel this way about Cyberpunk Edgerunners, which used those same made-up slang terms, but didn't feel nowhere near as cringe, and it also succeeded at delivering a better story and showcasing the beauty of Night City much better.

The gameplay is there and it's just okay – and that is not okay, you know what I mean? There is nothing special, no scratch that – even remotely engaging about the gameplay. It's your typical "choose your own approach" game (similar to the Far Cry or Hitman games). Shooting is generic, driving is generic, stealth is generic. It's all serviceable, it's there, but it leaves you not being able to shake off the feeling that you're playing something you've already played dozens of times before. And let me be clear, I don't mind generic, it's just there's no fun gameplay loop here.

I could sit here a bunch more nitpicking about various things that rubbed me the wrong way about this game, like all the times I was tasked with finding a circuit breaker to restore power to progress a mission, or how a manual save system really doesn't fit an open world game like Cyberpunk and losing minutes of progress from accidentally dying while messing in the open world isn't fun. But I think it's time for a conclusion.

I could write a long video essay on why I do not think this is a good follow up to the amazing souls trilogy. I'll break it down in a summary with bullet points.

The Good:
-The Story. Its fantastic. Far more fleshed out and more interesting than even an entire three games of Dark Souls story.
-The Views. There are some stunning sights in this game. Seeing Raya Lucaria across the Lakes is astonishing.

The Bad:
-Enemies. It feels basic enemies no longer have any real function in the game anymore except to be run past. They're so copy and pasted without consideration that it feels a chore to kill them. There's also usually no reward for the vast majority of them. A boss will give you more Runes than a thousand standard enemies can give.

-The Open World. Despite the sights being fantastic, the Open World kinda doesn't add anything. There's so many extra dungeons with random, copypasted bosses that the Open World feels more like it took away from development time that could have been put towards certain fight mechanics and enemies.

-Fight Mechanics. Look up Zullie the Witch's video on how the heal punishing is not technically input reading but is just as bad because of how poorly they designed it. Its one of many very disappointing combat decisions in this game that makes it feel much worse than many other Souls games including those that came before. 

Overall, alot of people like this game, I get I'm in the minority. I don't blame others for liking this game but after playing several Souls and Souls-likes, this one so doesn't click with me its made me not want to buy any other Fromsoft productions on release anymore. Now, I'll be looking elsewhere for Souls-like experiences like Lies of P.

It’s been over a decade, spanning three entire console generations, and Rockstar is still milking Grand Theft Auto V harder than a dairy farmer trying to pay off a mortgage. What started as a groundbreaking open-world experience has slowly morphed into an exhausting grind-fest. The single-player story remains iconic, but GTA Online is a relentless machine where everything from a basic sports car to a flying motorcycle costs tens of millions of in-game dollars. The economy is so aggressively inflated that it feels entirely designed to push you into buying Shark Cards just to exist in the same zip code as the fun stuff.

If the digital inflation doesn't break your spirit, the public lobbies absolutely will. Trying to progress your criminal empire or complete a heist as a legitimate player feels like a medieval punishment. You're constantly trying to coordinate with randoms who mysteriously disconnect halfway through a setup mission, all while navigating an endless plague of modders and cheaters. It is a daily occurrence to spawn in, immediately get blown up by an invisible hacker, and have a literal UFO dropped onto your character's head.

GTA V is a beautiful relic of gaming history that has massively overstayed its welcome. If you want to experience the phenomenal single-player campaign, it’s still worth picking up on sale. But if you’re hoping to jump into GTA Online today without a dedicated group of friends or a bottomless real-world bank account, you’re essentially just signing up to be target practice for a 12-year-old on an Oppressor Mk II.

Elden Ring is a masterclass in open-world pacing and spatial direction, effectively translating linear Souls-like level design into a sprawling horizontal sandbox without a single traditional quest marker.

The Good:

Horizontal progression: If a boss or area walls you in, the open world lets you walk away, explore elsewhere, and return later overpowered, completely bypassing artificial difficulty spikes.

Environmental cues: Natural landmarks, architecture, and lighting do the heavy lifting of navigation, reducing reliance on conventional map UI.

Systemic flexibility: Spirit ashes, mounted combat, and flexible build paths provide structural options for players of varying skill levels.   
Scribd

The Bad:

Late-game balancing: Endgame scaling sharpens aggressively, narrowing viable playstyles and heavily punishing off-meta builds.

Obtuse quest design: Key triggers and NPC questlines rely on obscure progression paths that practically require external guides.

Verdict:
A landmark achievement in systemic world design, though it inherits and occasionally magnifies FromSoftware's historical friction points.

The biggest issue I have with this game is the writing. In my opinion it's not it's strongest suit. It has a lot of "some races are inherently bad" tropes that I hate in media. There is no better example of this than the fact that one can (if not encouraged as it makes the combat easier) kill the goblin children with no consequences (even Halsin, the contradictory guy who claims to love all of natures creatures, can maul them to death). This weird fantasy racism affects other less popular races as well, including the gnomes, which we can play as. Astarion will often be cruel to your character if you do, and its very apparent that his prejudices affect his worldview (of course he will face no consequences regarding this because when does he ever). This sorta ties into my next point and major complaint; the game has very explicit and violent animal cruelty on several occasions. Blood and violence is one thing, but adding unnecessary animal gore is another. You're even encouraged to crush the animal's skull with your foot to kill it faster in one of these mentioned scenes. This is out of pocket and adds nothing to the game. Due to it being a disliked and often demonized animal, this slips under the radar. This is a cool game to pick up on sale, but it's pretty shallow and the story is incredibly boring and forgettable. I have not played the Phantom Liberty DLC so I cannot comment on that. Worth picking up if it's cheap and you like the futuristic setting.

Pros:
- beautiful city that feels alive
- great graphics
- varied combat systems, with guns, swords and hacking
- skill trees for different playstyles
- runs well, short loading times and easy to jump in and out of
- plenty of content in the city. Lots of stories, side missions and collectables.

Cons:
- the story is boring and forgettable
- the entire game is 1st person and you never see your character which makes it hard to identify with them
- whilst the combat is varied, the actual gunplay is very basic. You soon become OP and there is no reason to use any of the guns you find instead of Iconic weapons
- dialogue is weird. There's a lot of futuristic colloquialisms but the actual dialogue is just odd and easy to miss key details
- the game expects you to know a lot about the setting and ignores the 'show don't tell' rule. There will be loads of times were you're like 'wait, who is that?' 'what is that?' 'why does my character know this when I don't?'
- stakes feel very low and attachment to characters is odd. Everyone is a stereotypical Cyberpunk resident. My character seems to care loads for people she's just met, or form deep relationships with people she doesn't know.

Overall it's a nice looking game if you like the Cyberpunk/Bladerunner vibe, but the story is very poor, the gunplay is basic and there's just not much to do outside of the pretty aesthetics. I'd give it 3/10 as a narrative RPG

Honestly, I don't think I can describe a bigger disappointment for me than Cyberpunk 2077. I know it's considered one of the best RPGs by many people, but after about 5 hours, my experience has been almost the complete opposite.

Let's start with the positives. Night City is absolutely stunning. The graphics are easily one of the best I've ever seen, especially with ray tracing enabled. The attention to detail is incredible, the hacking mechanics are fun, and the main story has been interesting enough to keep me playing. If I had to rate those aspects alone, the graphics would be a 20/10 and the story, so far, around an 8/10.

Now for the parts that disappointed me.

Driving feels awful. Almost every vehicle I've driven feels like it's sliding on ice. Cars, bikes, vans—it doesn't really matter. Taking sharp corners often turns into either massive understeer or drifting when I didn't even want to drift. Traversing the city ended up being more frustrating than fun.

The gunplay also didn't click with me. The weapons look fantastic and have great animations, but actually using them feels bland. Damage numbers often feel strange, and combat never felt as satisfying as I expected.

Another thing that didn't appeal to me was how heavily the game leans into sexual themes. I understand it's part of the world's identity, but after a while it felt like it was everywhere—from advertisements to certain side quests—and it became more distracting than immersive. Some side missions also felt random and forgettable rather than meaningful.

Performance was... acceptable. On my RTX 5060 Laptop GPU at 1440p with max settings and low ray tracing, I averaged around 40-80 FPS, depending on the area. However, cinematic cutscenes occasionally became extremely laggy for me, dropping to what felt like single-digit FPS regardless of whether ray tracing was enabled. I'm not sure if that's a hardware issue or something on the game's side.

I also wasn't impressed with the NPC AI. I frequently saw civilians walking into walls, repeating strange behaviors, or panicking in unrealistic ways whenever combat started. It broke the immersion more than once.

Is the game worth buying for around $12-$15? I'd say yes. At that price, there's definitely enough content to justify the purchase, especially if you're interested in the story and exploring Night City.

Overall, I don't think Cyberpunk 2077 is a bad game—it just wasn't the game I expected. While the world, visuals, and main story are excellent, the driving, combat, AI, and some of the side content kept me from enjoying it as much as everyone else seems to.

I get that this is called cyberPUNK, but for a role-playing game, you don't get a lot of choice in how you want to play the role of V in this story. If you don't want to be a punk, sorry, V is going to be one whether you like it or not. The story insists on having everything be a grey moral to the point that it lost all of its meaning, but puts its foot down and insists that choosing to side with a Corpo is a bad thing, despite dedicating one third of the story to a Corpo member trying to win you over (his story missions also had the best setpieces). All of the endings fall flat because of this insistence that no ending can be happy, but especially the Corpo ending since, despite all of the endings/routes following a theme of sacrificing something for your survival, that ending has you sacrifice the MOST things to receive the LEAST rewarding, most downer ending of them all. The double standard would be funny if it weren't sad.

I have also found the game to still be somewhat buggy, one I remember a lot is that if you save the story quests for last and level up on the exploration content, you end up with quests not triggering because the game tries to space them out but doesn't have anything to trigger them with. There is also a bad bug with pop-in, maybe due to low RAM allocation. Vehicles don't load in quickly enough, meaning you can't drive until they do, and several times during races I fell through the ground due to the map not loading in quick enough. On another note, it's also really annoying how you NEED a cyberdeck to do any hacking, whereas the Sandevistan is really fun for stealth builds, but having one means not being able to do really basic things like opening doors, especially after they nerfed quick hacks into the dirt.

Overall, get this on a sale. It is a passable looter-shooter/immersive sim hybrid but is bogged down a lot by not having enough cool levels to play through and too much time spent on a weak story with a forced moral message. Otherwise this game costs way too much for what it is.

I genuinely don't understand how you take one of the greatest games ever made and somehow manage to make it feel this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ disappointing.

The Witcher 3 is a game that has aged remarkably well, even by today's standards. Its world, atmosphere, environmental storytelling and art direction were already phenomenal. The next-gen update was supposed to take all of that to another level, but instead, at least on my system, it feels like a downgrade disguised as a graphical upgrade.

Let's talk about the graphics first. Without ray tracing, the game looks surprisingly flat. The lighting lacks the depth and natural feel that made the original experience so immersive. Shadows, ambient lighting and environmental details often look inconsistent, and the overall image just doesn't have the visual richness you'd expect from a so-called next-gen update. And the worst part? Turning on ray tracing doesn't exactly solve the problem either. Instead, it absolutely chokes the GPU, turning what should be a visually enhanced experience into a frustrating performance nightmare. For a mid-range GPU, the optimization is genuinely atrocious. The performance cost is simply absurd for what you're getting in return.

And then there are the graphical glitches. Clothes flicker, textures don't always seem to match their surroundings, and certain environmental elements look completely out of place. The weather effects can look inconsistent, and the lighting sometimes feels disconnected from the environment. There are moments when the entire world looks gorgeous, followed by moments where everything just falls apart visually. The inconsistency is infuriating, especially when the game's original art direction was already so damn good.

The whole experience gives me serious pre-Cyberpunk 2077-release vibes. The kind of technical mess where the ambition is clearly there, but the execution leaves you wondering whether anyone actually tested the experience properly across different hardware configurations. It's frustrating to see a game with such an incredible legacy suffer from technical issues that take away from the very atmosphere that made it special in the first place.

And honestly, that's what pisses me off the most. This isn't some mediocre game that needed a complete visual overhaul to become relevant again. This was The Witcher 3. A masterpiece that didn't need to sacrifice its stability and visual consistency just to chase modern graphical features. A proper optimization pass, consistent lighting, stable textures and reliable performance should have been the bare minimum.

I'm not against graphical upgrades. Ray tracing can look incredible when implemented properly, and I'm all for pushing visual fidelity forward. But when the game feels noticeably worse without it and becomes a performance disaster with it, something has clearly gone wrong with the overall experience.

For now, I'm putting this game aside. I would much rather revisit the original experience than keep fighting with graphical inconsistencies, flickering textures, questionable lighting and performance issues that completely ruin the immersion.

It's genuinely disappointing to see one of the greatest RPGs ever made brought down by technical problems that should never have overshadowed the experience in the first place.

An absolute masterpiece of a game, let down by an update that feels like it needed a lot more time, testing and optimization. I'll be coming back when this mess is actually worth playing again.

This game is inbetween for me, but leans negatively.

The positives are the incredible level of visual polish. It's a very polished game. All the technical elements are well done. I'll say that.

The negatives, though, are quite numerous, but they aren't all equally negative. Let's start with the obvious. This game is oozing woke ideology. Never mind that it's an example of going out of one's way to cater to a very vocal and insane minority of people at the expense of reason and sanity. 

The woke doesn't end there though. Every scene feels like a Disney movie poster. They have the perfect balance of "races". Black dwarves, black elves, black this black that.
