They care more about virtue signaling than they do creating cohesive and meaningful cultures. All they see is skin color. They don't see subtle cultural differences, the tendency of certain races to naturally share traits which make sense to be inherited by their environment and nature. They throw all of that away to make sure that every gender and racial make up of humans is represented in every "race" or species in the game. It's stupid, childish, and down right disturbing. 

Because their idea of "diversity" is to throw a paint bucket on one of every character type in the game, it is to be expected that the actual meaningful types of diversity, such as thought, personality, interests, passions etc were ignored. Instead, it's only surface deep. Vapid, vain , and superficial differences are all the wokesters care about because they are what they claim to hate. This leads to very mundane, stale, and underdeveloped characters.

It's so hard to take the setting seriously because of the ridiculous colorswap skin color focused , gender bending characters. They look, feel, and act more like caricatures of real people than real people. Feeling any connection for them is out the window, with the exception of maybe two in the whole game. 

Further still, every character is bi, and every character wants to have sex with you after even a single nice word is thrown their way. It's jarring to be talking to a clearly straight character, only to have the narrator suggest we start having sex with eachother in only two dialogue exchanges. This might not seem like a big deal, but it will totally ruin characters for you when they are presented one way, then instantaneously given an abrupt 180 personality shift. Many such instances of this happening soured my opinion of the character to the point I just don't like talking to them. Add in the ridiculous skin color swapping and gender bending, you end up with a cast of characters better suited for the looney troons than a semi-serious RPG.

Moving on from the blatant political bent, the rest of the game suffers from a similar lack of meaningful nuance. Abilities all feel very similarly. Spells more or less offer different colors of the same few effects. Spamming the same few spells over and over, because they're clearly the most effective, gets old pretty fast. Combat in general begins to feel the same after a while. Fights move along methodically and predictably. Occasionally someone will crit, but the fights feel stale and lifeless. Turn based combat is rigid, inflexible, and creates odd situations.

Effects lack conviction. Most everything is just a couple turns in length. The odds of spells being resisted is high. There's not much satisfaction to the spell system at all really. 

Overall, the game lacks a feeling of urgency and lethality that would make the moment to moment combat more exhilarating. Instead, Fights move along in predictable fashion, with predictable outcomes, and predictable rewards. 

Having to rest every other fight wouldn't be so bad if the player wasn't forced to return to camp, requiring a level load out of their area, where they must then get past a few animations before they can rest. The process to rest adds tedium which quickly gets old, but always forces you to to do it. How great it would be to click a button and instantly just be rested up, with no loss to the challenge or value of the experience. The old BG games worked that way. It was a much better and more streamlined system.

Unlike other great Crpgs, the handholding removes much of the mystery from the game. Virtually every trap is automatically discovered. Their effects are typically minor, and the ability to disarm them is almost guaranteed with a default party. There's hardly anything left to the player's imagination, nor their senses. Hidden switches are easily seen, chests easily opened, most fights easily won. There are few interesting puzzles, though they do exist. The original Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 had far more detailed hidden item searching, where player agency mattered as much as the character. Baldur's Gate 3 does not think highly enough of the player to expect them to overcome adversity, so they give very little of it. 

The camera sucks. Controlling the Camera is tedious. Being 3D, it requires constant re-orientation and positioning. Oftentimes it gets stuck on walls, ramps, doorways or any other background asset.  I can't remember the last time I played a CRPG where the Camera fought me as much as the enemies did. 

Most CRPGs allow for seamless and fast switching of characters. Due to the turn based nature, each character must be resolved in order. While splitting party members up is possible, it's problematic. Characters can't be group selected, so each character must be controlled individually when group  mode is deactivated. Furthermore, every character has their own inventory, which is completely disorganized. It's just one giant x by y grid of item slots. Trying to find a specific item, on a specific character is downright obnoxious. The low contrast, dark color of the UI does not help with this. I've gone hours without even wanting to go  looking for items. It's easier to simply not care.

Finally, my least favorite mechanic by far is the die rolling system. Ultimately, this is what stalled my playthrough more than anything else. The ridiculousness of forcing me to click on a 20 sided die to resolve virtually every in game challenge is unfathomable. The game will have you rolling a die every minute, on average. Some rooms are so full of traps and treasure, characters will be rolling dice for minutes. First, a screen pops up, interrupting your flow. You then have to determine which modifiers you want applied to the roll. Then you click the die to roll it. Now you wait for the die to finish its flashy roll animation. Once that ends, it starts another animation adding your mondifiers together one by one ( could be 5 or more often). After this ends, it gives the result in a final flashy animation and tells you either you succeeded or failed.... this happens every..single..time... you want to open a locked chest, disarm a trap, convince an npc, pull a stuck lever... etc etc. You'll watch this same animation 1000 times over dozens of hours. This should have, and could have been done behind the scenes without the player even knowing.

BG3,despite all of its polish, has only superficial depth in both the setting and gameplay. They cleaned and polished every speck of character out of whatever this game claims itself to be. Whether its the repetitive combat, or the vain, skin deep woke pandering, BG3 just feels bland. While I don't love it, I also don't feel enough about it to hate it.

Apparently calling the people responsible for this a bunch of clowns was enough to hurt their feelings and justify deleting my posts and banning me from the forums.

Fine. You want constructive criticism? Here it is.


[h2]Visuals[/h2]

You ♥♥♥♥♥♥ with the game's color palette and art direction so much that you stripped away a lot of the original grit, darkness, tone, and contrast. The game now looks more like some high-fantasy setting than the gritty world it originally had.

And somehow these visual changes also came with:

[list]
[*]Shadows randomly disappearing and reappearing during dialogue camera switches, causing flickering.
[*]NPCs randomly T-posing, including the merchant during the horse chase quest in the starting area.
[*]Hair becoming ridiculously shiny and staying bright even in dim areas.
[*]NVIDIA HairWorks eating a noticeable amount of performance just to make the hair move around slightly.
[*]Snow deformation being removed.
[*]Grass sway being removed.
[/list]

Igni looks cartoonish and doesn't have the same serious appearance as the next-gen version. The new Quen effect is also ridiculously difficult to see. Yrden is probably the only effect where I can actually say the visual change is a clear improvement.


[h2]Performance[/h2]

Performance is bad overall.

I understand that improving the visuals can make the game more demanding. That's fine. What isn't fine is making the game more demanding while simultaneously making parts of it look worse.

FPS is unstable even with ray tracing disabled, so what exactly was the plan here?

And then there's the biggest problem: [b]the combat.[/b]

The combat is still garbage, if not actually worse.

[h2]Modders Already Most of This[/h2]

A lot of the other changes, such as the skill tree changes, removing the weight limit, removing gear degradation, and various other quality-of-life changes, are things modders had already addressed years ago.

So what exactly was the point of this “remaster”?

You had an opportunity to actually improve the game's biggest weaknesses, especially the combat, and instead you gave us a visual overhaul that makes the game more demanding, introduces visual bugs, removes some existing features, and still leaves the terrible combat largely untouched.

And then you expect people to treat this like some generous goodwill project.

[b]No.[/b]

Elden Ring was a disappointment for me because it tries to combine an open world with the soulslike formula, yet never fully excels at either.

As a soulslike, it relies too heavily on systems and ideas that FromSoftware has been using since Dark Souls 1. After dozens of hours, I often felt like I was playing another variation of familiar mechanics rather than a true evolution of the genre. The combat lacks enough fresh ideas to justify the massive time investment the game demands.

As an open-world game, it also falls short of the best examples of the genre. The world is huge, but much of the content feels repetitive. Similar enemies, repeated dungeon layouts, recycled bosses, and familiar activities create the impression that quantity often takes priority over quality. Instead of being excited to explore, I frequently felt like I was simply crossing another section of the map to find a slightly different version of something I had already seen before.

My biggest issue is that the combination of an open world and a soulslike structure does not work particularly well. What I love most about soulslike games is focused level design, interconnected areas, meaningful shortcuts, and a strong sense of progression through carefully crafted environments. Elden Ring sacrifices much of that focus in favor of scale, and the result is a game that often feels diluted compared to the tighter experiences that came before it.

I cannot say that Elden Ring is a bad game. Its production values, scope, and ambition are impressive. However, as a long-time soulslike fan, it failed to deliver what I personally look for in the genre. It did not meet my standards as a soulslike, and it did not meet my standards as an open-world RPG either.

For that reason, I would not recommend it to players who prefer more focused and replayable experiences such as Bloodborne, Mortal Shell, or Lies of P.

This game is overrated due to the branding of Baldurs Gate" and its close match to D&D mechanics.

Combat is over 50% of this entire game and it feels bland (dialog is the another 40% and movement is the remaining 10%). 1 Action per turn, no cover system, missing 9/10 times when hit chance is 70%, too many gimicks to try to gain a single extra action one turn that just seem like moving tokens around from one panel to another in some cases, you don't even get this option for every class and not until you're a good clip into the game. As a Wizard you get a ton of spells and cantrips but most are pointless to use, you just gravitate to using the same 1 or 2 all the time. I found myself heavily relying on Magic Missile just to ensure that I was actually landing some hits since you miss like your blind most of the time even at point blank range. Cantrips are a last ditch effort when you have no more spell slots but are very weak and never seem to improve in damage as the game progresses. As a Barbarian you just have the option to hack and slash and you whiff a lot so combat really has minimal choice required. As a barbarian it's walk up to something and keep swinging one (miss). action (critical miss). per (miss). turn (15 dmg). at (miss). a (critical miss). time (critical miss).

Yes, they have a "Karmic Dice" feature to help with your attack rolls but this spills over to checks outside of combat too and swings both ways. The result is you make too many rolls you should fail (20% chance of success) and fail too many rolls you should make (75% chance of success). Fortunately this feature can be disabled.

Several mechanics were stapled on and feel hollow and pointless:
Camp supplies - Types of supplies you use don't matter for effect. Not like you gain extra bonus if using different types of supplies (there's like 20 different items that are "supplies" but there is no point). As long as you have 40 supply vlaue you can recover in full. Not even finished with act 1 and I've got 1200 supplies and I've been full resting after every battle. What's the point of even having them in the game as a requirement to rest? Who is running out of these things?

Alchemy - Everything is so finite you get very few materials to craft anything. And seems like pretty much everything you can craft are things you can find and buy elsewhere. No limited unique super power craftables looks like. A huge missed opportunity here to have an alchemy skill that allows you to identify rare components to use for unique things. I just don't see the point - you collect a bunch of random bibs and bobs and eventually after a lot of gathering you can craft a basic heal potion.... OoooOOOoo not like they're 15 gold at any trader infinitely.

Relationships - Everyone seems super sex depraved. You can bone anyone in camp with a few dialog selections seems like. You have this whole "party member approves/disapproves" to build some liking between characters but it just seems the only end goal is to bone like we're playing Leisure Suit Larry.

Leveling - Leveling is a joke. While you have a TON of options at initial character creation, you don't really get much choice at each level (the few level ups that there are. 30 hours in and just about level 5). You don't get stat points to add in. It just sort of automatically raises various stats and you get maybe 1 or 2 choices on your level up. You get a new spell slot so you can pick which one from a static selection that you saw last level up. Or some small perk choice. There's really not a lot you can pick and you don't really know what you're getting as a choice on the level up ahead of time. It's not like you're getting stat points and a perk that you can count on each time to develop your character. It's like maybe you get to chose another cantrip or spell. Maybe you can swap a spell out..etc. Just very bland, no choice of progression. If you want to multi-class it's a bit tedious and puts you at a serious disadvantage because you'll be getting level 1 stuff for that other class rather then whatever the higher level stuff you would be getting for your class...etc.  

There's a lot more issues with this game that I won't even go into detail here (loot, camera, save scumming, critical success/failure, mind-worm skill tree...etc) that I think people overlook with rose tinted goggles of the Baldurs Gate series or being a D&D fan. While the graphics are good, the game is pretty well programmed. Story seems decent - though a little ostentatious with some of the side stories of characters. But... the combat is pretty lame. Yes, maybe it's very close to D&D and when you're dealing with pen and paper that may be fine but in a computer game it feels pretty limited and dull. Compared to other titles that are tactical combat RPG style such as a Divinity 2 or Wasteland 3, this combat feels like a massive step backwards for the genre. I don't care that I can stack crates and jump on them mid-battle when I can't even take cover behind one. I would say people should try either of those 2 games over BG3 if they haven't played them yet.

If you're huge fan of D&D or Baldurs Gate for the sake of the name "Baldurs Gate". You'll probably love this game. But if you're coming from playing something like Divinity 2 hoping for something even better - this isn't it. Definitely do your research and watch videos specifically showing the combat in this game and if it's something you're going to enjoy for over 100 hours. Because that is the vast majority of what you'll be doing in this game.

I've debated with myself a lot if I should give this game a good or bad review, because in many ways it's a really great game, but the issues I have with the game is so core to the experience that I simply can't justify a good review.

The bad:
 - When you do an attack it attacks in the direction of your last movement input. I believe it should attack in the direction of where you're looking.

 - Poisen/rot/etc. swamps seems to only make you stand in a corner and wait and waste your IRL time mostly.
 - Hotbar and menus in general just seem so badly designed. Hotbar/weapon swaps require you as a mouse user to let go of your mouse to do the swaps.
 - Many bosses 2nd stage seems to use *spam particles on players screen so he can't see* as a difficulty mechanic.
 - Area denial attacks from many bosses seems to have very bad hurt boxes.

The good:
 - Stunning game.

 - Insane amount of hours of content (granted 75% of that is dying fighting bosses).

Overall:
I really enjoyed the game in general, but because the attack/movement mechanics is just such a core part of the game, the frustration with the bad control design in the end means I'll be giving the game a negative review.

Overall it's recommended, but it isn't recommended because these developers need to learn a lesson, that they refuse to learn. It truly has the worst camera you can imagine in gaming. Fromsoftware just thinks it's the best thing ever, and it's never going to change. It's angle is such that you cannot accurately judge how far your weapon is going to hit, or how far the enemy is away from you. It's not high enough to see forward past your character, and it isn't zoomed out enough to keep track of what is going on. It also isn't reliable for actually locking on to the enemy. Sometimes they'll be in view, but you cannot lock onto the enemy, because some invisible hitbox is making them untrackable. You'll hit the camera lock key, and then the camera faces whichever direction your character is facing, which could very well be the opposite direction from the enemy. Add to this the enemy becoming aware of your presence, and you'll be getting attacked with no knowledge of the attack incoming.

The circling of enemies is a place where the camera should be zoomed back, so the camera isn't as disorienting, especially when the enemies are mobile and jumping around. I honestly feel like what makes this game difficult at all, is because of the camera.

In addition to this, multiple enemies are extraordinarily difficult to take on, because the camera locks on to one, and all your weapon strikes go in that direction. You have to keep changing the lock on to deal with enemies as they come at you, but naturally with such a close camera, you really can't keep track of what's going on. The difficulty should be in facing multiple opponents, but the camera plays the biggest opponent of all.

Then there are hitboxes that lock you in place. So many objects, and obstacles to make sure you can't move freely. Some terrain is easy to go over, and some just stops you in place. However you can always move freely when a large drop is nearby. It's like they designed this stuff to be artificially difficult. You get trapped in these hitboxes, and combined with the awful camera, you have no escape available. It feels awful and terribly designed. Maybe you wouldn't fall off cliffs as often during combat if the camera zoomed out more, but they refuse to do this.

Enemies have tracking attacks that you cannot get away from. You must dodge at the exact perfect moment, or you have zero chance. Enemies chain together attacks where if you dodge one, you get hit by the second strike before you can dodge again. They also have defenses, so if you ever attack the guy, before he attacks you and opens themselves up, they can counter your attack, and return with a follow up strike that you cannot dodge out of. This is a pain when opening up the enemy requires dealing with numerous tracking strikes. You'll have to get dodging down to a tenth of a second accuracy.

Then there are the ambushes that are set up to make sure if you are new at all, you will die a lot. Given the death mechanic of dropping all your money/experience, you'll have to put yourself back in the ambush to get your money back. I feel like a better designer wouldn't need to add cheap ambushes and what are essentially jump scares to add difficulty.

Keyboard and Mouse controls are absolutely awful, and this is yet another developer who doesn't care about accessibility for left handed people. Menu controls are hardbound to wasd. You cannot change it to a left handed orientation. This is also yet another Japanese developer that does not allow you to bind all keys on the keyboard. For some reason the Japanese HATE the keys: , . / ; ' [ ] \ - =  as they simply don't allow them to register. Capcom is the same way.
Left handed people are screwed by developers like this. I would prefer to give this a "meh" rather than a flat yes/no, but that isn't an option. I only have 85 minutes on record but that was enough for me as I am a big proponent of first impressions and this game gives a bad one. While it may indeed get better further in, it is unlikely I will ever find out. Had I not got this game for $4 during a mega sale and paid the current $25 they are charging, I would have requested a refund. 
 To start off with, the sounds are ridiculously loud by default and the music is so loud it just covers up everything else that is happening like a thick blanket. After setting the global sound to 70% and the music all the way to 20% the music was *still* a touch too loud in some places if characters weren't talking loud enough. So it is already off to a bad start, but having sounds set to an ear bleeding maximum as default isn't all that unusual to be fair. So lets get into the game.
 The first thing I noticed about the game is the dialogue. It drags on like some terrible novel which, I know, the game is based on. I found myself knowing what was being communicated within the first sentence or two and just jamming skip through the rest of the drivel as it was doled out a few agonizing words at a time as each finished thought or sentence has a lengthy pause before it moves onto the next part. After that came the training. And what a overload of information that was.
 Having played many games of this "style": God of war, Elden ring etc. I found the introduction to the combat of this game jarring to say the least. Everything about the combat just *feels* clunky. The swordplay and the spell casting both feel like an afterthought. Put into the game so there would be an activity to do between lengthy, pause filled dialogues. 
 I played through the initial area of the open world and was not impressed. It was not clear what to do during quests from how things were explained so I ended up just following quest markers or the goals listed on the side of the screen instead of playing the game and looking at the world. The mount controls are bad, mapped in a different way than the character for some reason even though they do the same things. 
 Needs a pass over default sound levels. Needs a look at the long pauses in dialogue. Needs a rework and standardization of controls. 
 But all of this is not why I stopped playing and uninstalled the game. I did that because of a stupid, meaningless side quest I failed because my horse was too far away. Not because of anything I did or didn't do with the information I had available. But because when I hit the button to call my horse, it spawned too far away and by the time I ran backwards to it, mounted up and hit the dash button to get it up to speed, the quest failed.

So this review only concerns the Remastered version and the quirks with it, hence it's a 'not recommended'. Steam's reviews really need an overhaul as they don't allow for any nuance. The game is still really good as it always has been (base game less so, expansions are terrific).

Anyway the new version introduces a whole lot of issues that make you realise "yeah, makes sense they made it free". The graphics overhaul comes at a huge performance increase and the new ray tracing/path tracing makes the game just look off in a lot of areas, while in others it makes it look better. In other words, it's inconsistent and also not worth the performance hit. Worse are the visual glitches that are kinda numerous now which is a shame.

Then there's the updates to combat which... honestly, you barely feel. The devs had a selection of many great mods that tried to do something about this combat system that already felt dated upon release and instead they went for "let's add a few new finishers (that you won't notice in your first hours of playing anyway) and some new sign VFX. done!". The "visual" uplift of the combat isn't even as extensive as it could have been as there are other areas that could have deserved more attention, for example giving you more counterattack animations. The point is, them bragging about "enhanced combat" in this remaster is extremely, extremely generous and far from reality, unfortunately.  It's a shame because there's a lot of great combat mods out there that the devs could have been inspired by.

The new skill tree is... meh? I never liked TW3's character progression as I found the system of slotting skills before they can work to be unnecessarily limiting because you won't take a lot of skills that are just "fun", you'll just take the ones that are the most useful. Adding a lot more skills to the trees just doubles down on this problem and makes it worse, because now there's even more cool looking skills that I can't pick because I don't have the room for them. How can they not realise that a system where you LEVEL UP AND GET A NEW SKILL THAT YOU CAN'T USE BECAUSE YOU DON'T HAVE A SKILL SLOT FOR IT just feels terrible? This needed a Cyberpunk 2.0 esque overhaul, especially with the upcoming expansion it would have been very welcome. The very least they could have done is made it so some of the skills on each tree are "passive" and don't need to be put into a skill slot to work.

But the worst issue is the bugs. After 2 hours in I've already ran into a couple and it's just frustrating to play a 10+ year game and have its new edition feel even more buggy. What is this, a Bethesda game?

There's things that are nice and that I liked about this version though. Some UI changes are nice, the integration of an ingame mod library (and making them available on consoles by effect) is also really nice, though some mods shouldn't be there as they haven't been updated to work with this version.

So yeah, disappointing remaster overall, I should say. It just feels oddly rushed and undercooked which is very questionable since they didn't have to release it now, with the expansion still about a year away. Of course you already have a bunch of idiots on the internet going "iTS fReE wHy aRe yOu cOmPlaInInG" as if doing something for free gives you diplomatic immunity to criticism. But the more important counterargument is that I am pretty sure the new expansion will require you to play on this version, so if you don't like any of the changes but will want to play that, tough luck I guess.

Hopefully it will get patched and improved by then. And I hope that the expansion will get the polish it needs.

The best save-scumming simulator since Pathfinder: Kingmaker.

Baldur's Gate 3 looks fantastic and has all the ingredients of a great RPG: an excellent story, incredible voice acting, cinematic scenes, interesting classes, and plenty of quests. Unfortunately, the dice-based gameplay completely kills the experience for me.

So much of what you do comes down to dice rolls that even characters who are supposed to be good at something can constantly fail at it. What's the point of making a decision or building a character around certain strengths when the game can just decide that your character is suddenly incompetent?

Pros:

- Great story, graphics, and cinematic scenes that make you want to keep playing.
Probably the best voice acting I've ever heard in a game.
- Extensive and interesting class and character building.
- Lots of well-designed and memorable quests.
- The game encourages multiple playthroughs if you want to see everything.
- The amount of choices and possible outcomes is genuinely impressive.

Cons:

-The heavy reliance on dice rolls can make your character choices feel meaningless. Even with a high chance of success, you can still fail at something that should be routine.
-The constant failed rolls can turn serious situations into a comedy show. At some point you could put circus music under almost every encounter and it would fit.
-Some characters and dialogue feel more like edgy teenagers than actual adults, which can really hurt the immersion for me.
-The constant save-scumming becomes almost mandatory if you don't want important situations decided by an unlucky roll. This reminds me a lot of Pathfinder: Kingmaker.
-Loading saves repeatedly gets especially annoying when you already know that a failed roll was the only reason something went wrong.

Overall:

I understand why so many people consider Baldur's Gate 3 one of the best RPGs ever made. The production quality, voice acting, visuals, story, and character building are absolutely top-tier.

But personally, the dice system ruins too much of it for me. I prefer RPGs where character progression actually makes you reliably good at something. If my character has the skills for a task, I want that to matter instead of constantly watching him trip over his own feet because the game rolled a 1.

For me, Dragon Age: Origins and Dragon Age II are still much closer to what I want from an RPG. Baldur's Gate 3 is incredibly well-made, but the core gameplay philosophy simply isn't for me.

This review is NOT how I would rate the game. If it was, I'd give it a 11/10. Great gameplay, story, art, everything! This review is if I would recommend this game to other people who are looking through Elden Ring steam reviews, and If you aren't sure on whether to get this game or not, please listen to what I have to say.

If you are looking for a game with amazing... Everything... get this game. It is allows thousands of different playstyles with thousands of great weapons and armor. Even better with the DLC! HOWEVER... this game does not hold your hand whatsoever, and that is partially why I don't recommend it to newer souls players or people who want to have a laid back time. Before you flame me or tell me I'm wrong, I beat the game with 120 hours with no guide or help whatsoever, so although some things might be wrong, I have a good amount of experience with this game. Regarding this "hand holding" issue, I have two major concerns. 

1. This game is extremely vague with where you are supposed to go.
Sights of Graces are helpful and tell you where to be to some extent, but in some instances, it doesn't help you outright and you are forced to look up where to go or what to do. There is a great example around 1/4-1/3 of the way into the game that I constantly find people looking up where to go.

2. Quest and Items can be extremely hard to find and are locked behind dialogue options, choices, bosses killed etc. Which gets rid of the desire to pursue it in the first place.
This kinda goes with my first reason, but this is such a large issue that it should be mentioned. All of my friends who have played this game struggled to level up or find items, which led them to look up where to go, defeating basically the entire purpose of this game of discovery. I know this game is supposed to be extremely difficult, (I have played other fromsoftware games like sekiro) but for a game as large and expansive as Elden ring, I feel that there should be some sort of way to at least track quests or give you a hint of where to go.

In conclusion, if you skipped everything else, If you are a die hard FromSoftware fan 100% get this game, it is peak. But if you are not familiar with how FromSoftware does it, Elden Ring should not be the first game you play. It overwhelms many beginners and causes them to quit early.

I genuinely tried to like Baldur’s Gate 3. I loved the first two games, and after hearing so much praise for this one, I gave it 27 hours across two separate playthroughs. Unfortunately, I think I am finished with it.

The presentation is excellent. The graphics, music and voice acting are all top quality. Almost everything surrounding the actual experience of playing the game, however, feels unnecessarily awkward.

The user interface is horrendous. I repeatedly clicked on companions or other characters while simply trying to move around, triggering conversations and interactions I never intended to start. The inventory system is cluttered and tedious, and even basic actions, such as entering stealth and positioning a character for a backstab, feel more cumbersome than they should.

Exploration is equally frustrating. Holding the Alt key only reveals interactable objects within a very limited radius, making it easy to overlook important items or routes. On my first playthrough, I reached the Underdark but eventually gave up because I could not work out how to progress through it.

I was not expecting the game to hold my hand, but Baldur’s Gate 3 often seems designed around the assumption that players have endless time to consult online guides, tutorials and walkthroughs. A game should provide enough information for players to understand its systems and make meaningful progress without repeatedly leaving it to search the internet.

The balancing also feels badly uneven. I frequently found my party completely outmatched, and combat rarely felt satisfying enough to justify the preparation, inventory management and repeated reloading surrounding it. Rather than tactical and rewarding, it often felt crude, slow and lacklustre.

There is clearly an impressive amount of work in Baldur’s Gate 3, and I understand why many people love it. For me, though, the beautiful presentation cannot compensate for an interface that constantly fights the player, frustrating navigation and progression that too often feels dependent on outside resources.

Perhaps I am simply no longer the target audience for games like this. Baldur’s Gate 3 was my final attempt to become invested in a widely acclaimed modern PC game, but instead of feeling entertained, I mostly felt exhausted.

I adored this game during my first hundred hours—so much so that I purchased "The World of Cyberpunk 2077," a hardcover book that, now looking back at it, was probably released by Dark Horse as part of the public relations and marketing work of CD Projekt Red to increase hype and sales before launch in 2020. I hadn't been so smitten by a world since discovering Star Wars in early middle school. But somewhere after that 100 hour mark, the story and world began unraveling for me and I finished the game feeling rather hollow.

Cyberpunk appears to be a labor of love for the many involved in making it. Aesthetically, it's gorgeous. There were countless times where I stopped to take in and appreciate the models and textures that were around me. The artists and developers who made this are top tier, no question. Unfortunately, as I continued my time in Night City, I was struck with the feeling of just how massive an endeavor building this city was and just how many assets were reused in monotonous ways. Things began to feel imperfect and rushed, and those moments of awe that happened so frequently turned into me questioning just why the game had to be so big and why certain gigs had to exist. The game feels far too large to the point of feeling incredibly vapid. It made me yearn for smaller, more thoughtful stories and environments that are carefully tailored and handcrafted. You don't have to paint the entire world. Paint a few very interesting locations and allow the viewer to dream about the rest.

The story itself is at its strongest in the early main quests, when the player doesn't quite realize how terribly superficial all the endings will turn out to be. I felt like I had a stronger emotional connection to Jackie for four hours than compared to my 200+ hours with Johnny. I think this shows that CD Projekt Red tried to do far too much without a cohesive overarching narrative or goal. It left me feeling pushed and pulled in many different directions, confused, and frustrated that a game with this much potential could fall so flat. It's a good game and there are there are many things that I experienced while playing that will stick with me for the rest of my life, but I just wish that it was much smaller with more time and care put into crafting the details.

This isn't a good Souls game.

Firstly, let's get this out of the way: Souls fans, this review is not for you. You already bought the game, completed it six times and are busily posting a long rant nobody will read about why whatever weapon is underrated/overpowered. 

For the rest of us, who might dip in and out of Souls games from time to time: this is just a Souls game but worse. The only thing that makes it any different from Dark Souls 1, 2, 3 or any other Fromsoft game is the open world - and the open world makes literally everything worse. 

Don't get me wrong - it was the correct decision to put an open world in. The game isn't for me, it's for the Souls fans who've played every game FromSoft release a dozen times over and just need something new. For those people, the open world is the least harmful breath of fresh air possible. 

If you're not sick of the sight of Souls games, though, the open world is a terrible addition. Pacing is dead and buried, the usually stellar map design is relegated to only existing in dungeons, and you have no idea where you're supposed to go next. If you don't look it up you can guarantee you'll miss a region entirely, then have to choose between never experiencing it or doing it while horribly overlevelled. Speaking of which, if you like to explore and find everything, you'll be overlevelled anyway; I didn't grind once and yet was 30+ levels ahead of where I should be for virtually the entire game simply because I refused to skip content.

The worst thing, though, is the bosses. Bosses are FromSoft's selling point, and they're usually both well-designed encounters and also very visually impressive. In this game, however, thanks to the open world they have to put 300 more of them into the game than there should be - gotta put SOMETHING in the open world after all. They can't design 300+ unique bosses, so that means reprints. A LOT of reprints. By the time I gave up on the game I'd fought an estimated six Crucible Knight versions, dozens of lesser versions thereof, half a dozen gargoyles, seven (I think) Ulcerated Tree Spirits, over a dozen Watchdog Statues... the list goes on. The anticipation and impact Dark Souls usually has with its bosses is entirely eliminated because nine times out of ten you'll see the boss health bar pop up and realise it's the same thing you've already fought before. Repeatedly.

To conclude, if you're NOT someone who plays every Souls game relentlessly, do yourself a favour - buy Dark Souls 3 instead. Hell, buy ANY Dark Souls game. If you already own one, play that instead. They'll have proper gameplay pacing, proper map design, and most of the bosses you fight will be unique and interesting. 

They'll be better than this, in other words. This was legitimately a boring game.

(I will say the one nice thing was that Silence actually did work on the hag. Made the fight a breeze even at level 4. But the fact that I'm celebrating such a basic thing really tells you how poor the rest of the game is.)

Lengthy review because this is one of the very few games of it's genre that has never shown itself to be anything other than mediocre at best and downright awful at worst.

To preface, open world RPGs are my favourite genre. I absolutely adore medieval fantasy and the exploration that comes along with these games. I've played and finished more games in this genre than I can count. I've even seen this game compared to astounding games like RDR2, which is one of my favourite video games ever. Witcher 3 has never, in my approximately 5 times trying to play it, NEVER held my interest for more than a few hours at a time. There is just absolutely nothing to get you through and even on the rare occasion where I have made it a good 10 hours into the game, it never particularly even gets any better. It is just slog after slog after slog. I may force myself to sit through it one day but for now it's impossible.

Story aside, the combat of this game is categorically the most game ruining thing about it. The combat alone is the biggest reason I have decided to put this game aside so many times, remaster "reworked combat" included. It is so shallow and beyond god awful that it's not even like "so bad it's good" it just is the worst thing that CDPR have ever designed. If this game had the same combat that Blood of Dawnwalker, a AA witcher inspired game itself has? It would be probably manageable to actually sit through the snoozefest of a story. But when the main thing you're doing in this game is either story or combat and both of them are terrible? It's the least sustainable thing possible and I wholeheartedly think you are a masochist if you put yourself through it.

Graphics, sound, actual exploration? All fantastic. Please for the love of god for the next game just make everything else as interesting and fun as those 3 things.

It should be telling that half of the positive reviews on the page say absolutely nothing of the game, and more the actions of CDPR making the remaster and DLCs free for anyone who purchased before the fact. I'm aware that they did a really good thing in doing that, however I can't in good faith recommend a terrible game based on that fact alone.

The immersion of the world of Cyberpunk 2077 is the best and greatest aspect of this game. The word of a futuristic dystopia, but not a gray and desolate one - instead a colourful one full of distractions which are there to cover the real rot within. I have a great love for Elden Ring with some caveats.

Having already played through the original Demon's Souls, Dark Souls 1 and 3 multiple times, I believe I have a good enough amount of experience to speak on Elden Ring with some good context.

Elden Ring is simultaneously amazing and yet a little tedious. 

The parts I love are why I have loved all the Souls games before it: great exploration and world building, atmosphere, and a wonderful sense of progression as you slowly build your character. Gameplay is top notch and is as varied as it has ever been in terms of weapons and potential builds.

On the other hand, the shift to an open world has introduced some unfortunate open world tropes, such as a lot of emptiness and open space between all the cool and interesting things to do. The dungeons are all hand crafted with the typical souls level of quality, yet the vast amounts of space between them leaves me wishing it was just more of the densely packed and intertwining level design the souls games are known for.

I haven't quite finished my first playthrough, and even though I'm having a great time, I already don't believe I'll want to play through it again immediately like I did my other Souls games, for the open world reasons I listed above. 

It's a weird feeling because, for me, Dark Souls 3 was the peak of the Souls formula. The level design was top notch, the world was slightly more linear, but the intertwining design of the levels made it so when you unlocked a shortcut to a previous area it immediately felt so gratifying. Some of that magic is lost in a massive open map. There's lots to do, yes, but it's so much more spread out that you get those magic moments much less often.

While I love this game, and I do highly recommend it, enter into it knowing the drawbacks of any open world game. 

Thankfully, this is not the open world formula you may be familiar with in Ubisoft games, where the map is just littered with side quests that pad the run time but leave you feeling empty inside for pursuing. In Elden Ring, there are virtually no markers. You need to go find them for yourself. Exploration is almost always rewarded with some cool item or spell or weapon. But the amount of time spent wandering between these cool moments can sometimes feel quite long, especially if you like to explore every nook and cranny like I tend do to. 

If you go straight for the main quest markers, your time with Elden Ring will likely feel quite different. But for me, I like to take my time and uncover everything. I think my natural tendencies may be why I haven't enjoyed it as much as DS1, or 3. As there is simply so much to explore and so much nothingness between the true points of interest.

If you're a fan of the genre, though, this is a must play. Enjoy it in the way you enjoy playing these games, and be ready for an incredible journey.

PS I have also experienced much of the game on a Steam Deck. While not the ideal way to play, it's well enough if you can tolerate 40fps. Only very occasionally did it dip from this, so it's a decent way to experience the game if you're not able to use your computer or tv for any particular reason.

Would I recommend? yes.
Is it fun? no.

Throws. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ throws. You have to throw a dice if you actually hit the enemy and if your attack has an effect, your target has a saving throw if this effect hits. This leads to situations where you shoot a fireball at an enemy but apparently miss the ground he stands on and the enemy is too intelligent to start burning. A buddy of mine got nearly instantly killed by two enemies, while I survived two turns being surrounded by four of them. From their 12 attacks, only four hit. I got areactive skill that charms (basically useless) enemies that attack me. I only need one hand to count the enemies that [i]failed[/i] the saving throw against being charmed. In a boss fight, a powerful NPC missed all her hits for two turns and the boss wiped as all. Reload, the NPC now hits critical and oneshots the boss. This makes the game feel less tactical and more like entirely RNG depended.
Character progression is very limited. Pick a class, pick a subclass later on, you can pick your skills at level up, that's it. No attribute growth, no trying out builds, no specific ways to play your character. Reaching a new level doesn't feel like something you look out for, but a meaningless thing that just happens.
Very limited loot. Items might give you +1 on rolls or a new skill, nothing more. In act 3, I'm still using some items from act 1, because there simply wasn't anything better.
There is no mana or cooldown to manage, skills are just limited to one use and can only be recharged by resting. This plus the throwing mentioned above made my play almost exclusively with standard attacks as an archer, because why risk wasting a Tier 3 skill that I can only get back with a long rest or a strong scroll when I can simply shoot my bow?
There is other stuff, like seemingly every skill having another status effect or the 10+ effects you can stack on characters or the endless sub-systems, but it should be enough for now.

You either have to pick your companions based on their class or roll with whatever class they are, regardless of party synergy.

Talking about doors, click on the ground behind a door and your characters often wont walk through, but close them. The camera is also oddly level based, making it impossible to move it up or down every now and then

6 years later and on patch 2.31, a lot of people like to say they've "fixed" the game now.
Well, you can patch the bugs, you can rework your god-awful skill tree, inventory and crafting mechanics.
You can add police that actually chase you, quests that actually function and cars that actually handle like cars.
They did all that in an attempt to "make things right", which I'll acknowledge.
But one thing you can't patch is the terrible, TERRIBLE writing.
They don't even give you the ability to skip dialogue until you've gone through the motions of a completely rail-roaded THREE HOUR LONG prologue every time you want to replay the game (or pick a premade character to start at Phantom Liberty, but doing so hamstrings you if you aren't playing a hacker). 
WHY can't you skip dialogue in the prologue? ♥♥♥♥ you, I guess.
The main plotline with the engram is just plain bad. It saps so much player choice out of V's character, and of course there's tolerating Johnny Silverhand.
My God, Johnny Silverhand. With Michael Pondsmith's tabletop character they actually managed to make Keanu Reaves not just unlikable, but insufferable.
You might even find yourself asking just how much of the time CDPR spent consulting with Pondsmith was concerning the game world and how much was spent on faithfully recreating his annoying rockerboy avatar in the video game, complete with a soundtrack that makes you question how this rockerboy ever had a fan base in the first place. Seriously, if SAMURAI were a real band that had to stand on their own merit independent of the game they'd struggle to break 100 views on youtube. "Chippin' In" is one of the worst songs I've ever heard in my life.
And if you thought Silverhand was bad enough they somehow lower the bar further in Phantom Liberty with Songbird, the Mary-Sue the DLC revolves around, who the game treats as a tragic heroine who can do no wrong despite her being another generally awful self-insert and the architect of all her own problems.
Gameplay wise the game is fine.
Combat is engaging with a decent amount of depth once you've gotten yourself a loadout of weapons and cyberware you like, but if you're playing a hacker the gameplay loop is extremely boring and tedious (scan a guy -> dump hacks -> he dies -> scan next guy -> repeat until entire room is dead and you didn't even need to draw any of those guns you went to the trouble of getting).
The voice acting is broadly competent. There are some stand out characters that are well voiced, but again the material they're working with is not ideal. Male V's voice is fine. Competent, unremarkable but not annoying either. Female V's  voice however is just bad. The voice actress they chose for her has two modes: "Make my voice quiver a bit and ham it up" for any scene that is even vaguely dramatic and "sassy girl boss" for anything else. This can get quite annoying given that this is the character your stuck with for the entire game.
Itemization is still all over the place, with certain paths giving objectively superior rewards which further limits replayability (for example siding with Songbird in the DLC gets you the single most overpowered piece of cyberware in the game, while siding with Solomon gets you an ok pistol and a mediocre cyberdeck).
As for role playing, this is not a role playing game.
V is a fixed character, you can choose whether they're male or female and you can make some morality choices here and there but generally your decisions don't have a huge amount of impact on the game.
The stock endings are all quite unsatisfying, Phantom Liberty adds some new ones in what seems to be an attempt to address this, but they're not much better.
I'd give it a 6.5/10 in it's current state, which is unlikely to change as CDPR seem to consider the myriad problems the game still has to be resolved now and they've long since moved on to botching their next game. I shan't be trusting CDPR again, the people who were responsible for the quality of their previous titles are either long gone or simple don't care anymore.

The game has a lot to offer, but in it's current state, 2 years after release, if you want to roleplay as anything but what the intended path is: don't bother.

For multiple hours I've been trying to tolerate many sequence breaks, buggy triggers and wonky fights, but the breaking point is how the game punished me for having the one race that doesn't let me gain an inspiration event... let me explain:

Spoilers for Act 1:
[spoiler]So I'm Dark Urge as a Female Drow, I'm trying to roleplay as an evil character. I'm on the "goblin temple" where Gut is. So I go to the torture chamber to get a Dark Urge inspiration. The goblin tortures see me and I say to step aside and let me handle it. They obey and decide to leave the place... but I have no option to torture the prisoner. I can talk to the prisoner and get information about Halsin and the Nightsong, I can pick up the torture weapons, but I can't attack the prisoner or have a dialogue option that lets me torture him. No option as a drow allows me to torture the prisoner. So the work-around is to use Disguise Self, turn to another race and THEN the option will appear for me to torture... why? Why is this even a thing, considering Drows are basically the more intended-to-be evil aligned races in the entire game and THEY are the ones that miss out on one of the most evil actions on act 1? It's stupid on several ways, and this is a drow-exclusive interaction Larian Studios knowingly programmed without the option to torture.

And if we must point out other issues I have had so far with my playthroughs of this game: NPCs don't react to the bodies of their own kin on ground.... so basically I wanted to slaughter all the druids in the emerald grove, so I, one-by-one, sometimes two at a time, used Performance and Minor Illusion to guide them to some outside area, and repeatedly killed them outside of sight of other druids. And that way I was able to kill all druids with none of them suspecting a thing or reacting to the dead druid bodies.

I accepted to be on a romance with Lae'zel, but with no sex scene yet, it was just the flag to trigger the initial romance. When I went outside of camp, Shadowheart and Laezel were talking about how good we were on bed, even though we never did anything.

Another major issue: at night, Astarion confided to me about his vampiric nature, and I asked about Cazador and his backstory, so on... then, on the same night, the cutscene where Astarion tries to bite me plays out, and my character (and the game) act like this was a huge revelation and they did not know about it. The next morning, the same dialogue options about Cazador and his backstory were there as if I had not triggered them already, so the game got confused with flags.

It also happened that goblins have shot through walls with their arrows to hit my characters in some combat during the blighted village. And it wasn't through a window or crack, it was literal solid wood wall, a goblin was on the other side and Astarion on the other, they shot and hit me, and Astarion couldn't hit back with his bow.

I've also faced many wonky path-finding moments where my characters went through extremely long paths for something that was mere meters away from them, happened at least twice: in the goblin camp and in the dark cave below blighted village.

And there's no search option on the adventurer's chest, which can easily have over 100 items in just a few hours of exploring (which the game heavily encourages)

The game continuously makes several time-restricting scenarios/ideas in the earlygame, which would make you think you shouldn't long rest as that could mean events will happen while you sleep, but the truth is that next to nothing happens if you long rest, in fact you HAVE to if you want to progress character stories. My issue with the long rest system is that it is inversely proportional to the story's narrative and what you would think is going to happen or should happen, and the paranoia that events MIGHT happen if you long rest is completely broken when you realize they won't, such as the hyenas being pregnant with gnolls for several days or karlach being wounded and a few meters aways from her hunters for several long rests, just standing there.[/spoiler]

While I'd love to go on about every inconvenience, some minor and some major, steam has a text limit, so I'll drop here.

So, in summary, the roleplaying game has too many events and scenarios which absolutely break the roleplaying aspect of it, for too many times has my immersion been broken, and basically I can't properly play as an evil character because the game isn't built with that in mind, it's built with you being a helpful hand. Act 1 Druid and Goblin camps are bad areas, If i had not played the areas after I would have deleted the game in the first 4 hours. High miss chances so the fight drags on for no reason. Gameplay rules are poorly telegraphed and explained compared to other CRPGs that I played. Inventory is poorly designed and for some reason trade inventory with merchants has better sorting with tabs,  some special and quest related items are not highlighted as special or items of interest (Frost staff parts, parts needed for forging of special items, quest item in act 2 that removes debuffs related to the area).The game does not inform you that some quests are time sensitive or have time triggers.

The Underdark and Mountain Pass are much better gameplay-wise and the difficulty of the encounters is better paced. Some encounters give you a 'Surprised' debuff even when you ambush the enemy.

Act 2 Gameplay and Story are much better. The area feels like the Asylum from Divinity 2.

Act 3 The game is still good, has some quests that seem like they were cut short or not fully implemented into the game, higher amounts of diversity, has more characters from the previous games.

Sarevok and Viconia are badly implemented; there is no reason why they are even in the game, badly character assassinated. Sarevok feels like he got mind-wiped by the man in black, Viconia could have been replaced by another new character and it would have made no difference. It would have been better if these two characters had only items related to them implemented.

Jaheira had an okay implementation, some parts of the voice acting sounded phoned in. For example, in the first two games she shouts a battle cry “For the Fallen!” and in Baldur's Gate 3 she says it deadpan without emotion as if the voice actor wasn't coached on how to voice it.

With Minsc, they focused on the comedic part of his character. I found his character to be the best implemented. The only problem was his class; he lost his berserk ability and his stats were heavily based on Dex compared to the games before where he was a more STR-based character.

Ending:

The final sections leading to the end boss drag on eternally. There are too many enemies; it feels like they are coming endlessly. If you have a weaker PC like mine, it would be best to take a book and read it while waiting for turns to pass. It got so bad that I forced myself to google a workaround for this part. (There is a shortcut or alternatively you can become invisible and run through it while avoiding the enemies). The choices before the fight feel poorly implemented, forcing you into a binary decision where you must change a character if you choose option A or kill another if you choose option B.

In the end boss fight I had the impression that I would be able to call in the allies that you collect beforehand, but was sadly disappointed (You can only call them in the preceding section).

You can cheese the boss fight by running directly to the portal and ignoring the enemies by teleporting or becoming invisible. After you start fighting the boss on normal difficulty you can kill him in 3 turns. I only got 2 characters through the portal.

In conclusion, the game was in and of itself enjoyable but was not near the Hype that everybody was showering over it.

The complexity of this game is absolutely beautiful. During the first few hours, you feel an enormous sense of freedom and discovery. You do not even know where you should go first, and from the very beginning, even before the first boss, there are so many different paths and alternatives that you can easily spend 20 or more hours exploring before defeating the first boss.

We live in an era where more and more games are released just for the sake of existing, without having much to offer beyond that. Many of them are short or linear, which would not necessarily be a problem if they were done well. But Elden Ring showed me what games can really be when developers put an incredible amount of thought and passion into every part of the experience.

Elden Ring and Hollow Knight completely changed my perspective on games and made me expect more from them.

I have never been an expert Soulslike player, but Elden Ring, even though it can be extremely difficult, does not force you to rush. If you play the game properly, explore, learn from your mistakes and take your time, you will eventually be fine.

Malenia absolutely destroyed me though. She took me over 10 hours to beat, maybe even more, but the satisfaction I felt after finally defeating her was incredible. It is one of those moments that makes all the frustration worth it.

I will recommend this game with all my heart. If you have never played Elden Ring, give it a chance and take your time with it. Explore everything, get lost, make mistakes and enjoy the journey.

It's been 2 years and nobody cares about my opinion, but this is the most overrated game in history. It's fine. It's not a bad game, but I'd recommend Divinity Original Sin 2 instead to anyone who want a good gaming experience. The only reason to play this game (unless you're really into the deeply intertwined settings and can put aside the terrible combat that makes up most of the game, in which case Larian will not disappoint) is if you have absolutely no friends and absolutely NEED to experience Dungeons and Dragons 5e as close as possible to the original RAW. Otherwise skip it. 

This game strikes me as the sort of thing people played because it was hugely popular at the time, and not because people actually want gaming experiences like this. 

It's virtual DnD. Sounds great except they kept all the terrible parts of Dnd that are only there to make mental calculations and in person description faster/more fluid. The combat is slow, like holy hell it is SLOOOOOW. Why is a computer game taking this long? 150 hours for one playthrough? No thanks. It's also really badly done (not Larian's fault). Dnd combat isn't good. It has never been good. It is functional. 
In actual TTRPG play, most of the excitement happens in your imagination and the combat rules are just there to provide tactical decisions. Computer games have been doing better turn based combat than this for decades. Dice are real life random number generators that allow you to quickly add a bit of chance to your game without consulting electronics. Computers have been capable of better deeper RNG since videogames were invented. Why go back to d20?
Because it's d20 based instead of having any actually inventive systems, the lowest percentile you can affect an action by is 5%, which means unless you have a 100% chance of clearing the roll, at least 1 in 20 attempts will fail. In TTRPG play that's fine because your GM can take the content you would have missed and put it behind a different check, but in BG3 you either have to save-scum or accept you don't get that content. (or slog through another playthough). 

Larian is amazing and if Wizards of the Coast wasn't involved, this game probably would have been 10x better and 100x less popular. Hopefully all the money goes to making the next one actually good.

I played finish Cyberpunk 2077 and I found the writing decent but also not outstanding. I feel that the game focuses more on the aesthetic of cyberpunk rather than the philosophical and psychological implications of society being in such a state towards humanity both on an individual and collective scale. The dialogue tends to resort to quoting philosophers in order to appear deep while hiding an inherent lack of depth. The world of Cyberpunk is really existentially empty. Those who are not elite live in extreme poverty and capitalism drains the life out of everyone and yet Cyberpunk ignores this sickening emptiness of existence. Johnny Silverhand is quite interesting at times but all he is is a walking talking ideology such that he appears shallow rather than complex. He appears to be just as dogmatic and narrow minded as those who accept the status quo. I would say the gameplay beats RDR2 but it is definitely has a much weaker story. Each character felt more like a trope, a kind of caricature rather than real. I don't believe anyone can live in the world of Cyberpunk without experiencing severe mental illness. It is a sick society and the game pushes colorful narratives upon us, beckoning us towards an adventure that is ultimately insignificant in the grand scheme of things. It just focuses on hype moment after hype moment rather than delving into the world which they have created which simply put is on the pinnacle of decadence. Disco Elysium is infinitely superior in writing about spiritual decay in relation to political ideology. However, the gameplay is highly addictive and the world is immersive and beautiful.

Witcher 3 is still one of the best games ever made. Simple as that.

I first played it on my PS4, my last ever console, and I'm glad a game like this is on PC. Otherwise I never would have got to experience such a masterpiece. With the remaster out I had to buy it again, and it feels like a whole new game. Sunsets over the hills, fog rolling through the swamps, rain hitting the mud in Velen. Textures are sharper, faces look way better in cutscenes, and the lighting alone makes it hold up next to stuff coming out today.

The world is where it really flexes. Velen is grim and miserable in the best way, with burned villages, hanged men and swamps full of things that want to eat you. Novigrad is a huge packed city that feels lived in, and Skellige has the cliffs, storms and Viking vibe. You'll stop riding just to look at the view.

Even the side quests are better written than the main story of most games. Your choices come back to bite you later, some quests have no good answer, and the love saga hit me harder than I expected. The characters stay with you long after you finish.

The fights feel better too with the reworked animations. Swings look smoother, hits have more weight, and mixing signs, bombs and potions mid-fight feels natural. Monster hunts are still the best part: you read the bestiary, pick the right oil, and it pays off. The remaster also adds some quality of life stuff that makes it smoother to play.

Got all this for 20 euros, which feels like a steal. Hundreds of hours for the price of a pizza night.

If you haven't played it, buy it. If you have, the remaster is a great excuse to go back.

After having played and 100%ed Dark Souls Remastered, instead of going to play Dark Souls 2, I chose to buy Elden Ring at full price while waiting for a discount that never came during this Summer Sale. Regardless, I bought it, played it, and 100%ed it.

At first, the game was amazing. Big map, lots of weapons, and so many things to explore. I wanted to put in as many hours as possible. Up until the end of the early game, I was having a great time. But eventually, the game started feeling very repetitive, and it only became good again at the very end, when I was already bored and underwhelmed.

One of my biggest issues is how often content gets reused. The same bosses appear multiple times under different names, many enemies feel copied from previous Dark Souls games, and the dungeons quickly start blending together. As time went on, it became more and more evident to me that the developers created a huge map without always knowing how to fill it in a meaningful way. At times, I genuinely felt like I was fighting the same boss for the fourth time in a different location.

That isn't to say the world doesn't have great areas. Limgrave is amazing, Caelid is memorable, and several of the endgame locations are excellent. But areas like the Mountaintops of the Giants, Altus Plateau, and much of the underground felt tedious to explore. Also, because the world is so diverse, it doesn't give you one specific vibe. One moment you are in a dark cave and the next in a flower field, it doesn't feel like the world is corrupted and dying, unlike Dark Souls.

The same applies to the bosses. Some are absolutely fantastic. Malenia, Godrick, and the Elden Beast are obvious highlights. The problem is that they're surrounded by so many repeated encounters that they lose some of their impact. The standout bosses are great, but they're buried beneath a mountain of recycled content.

To be fair, the world is packed with locations and things to discover. The map rarely feels empty. My issue is that much of that content follows the same formula: enter a dungeon, loot a corpse, get ambushed by a group of enemies, fight a familiar boss, and move on. After dozens of hours, it became very tedious.

Another problem I had was the difficulty balance. Groups of small enemies were more dangerous than the actual bosses most of the time. Most bosses that were supposed to be major challenges got destroyed within seconds by my max-level Mimic Tear and Bloodhound's Fang. What's funny is that I wasn't even trying to make an overpowered build. A friend simply told me Bloodhound's Fang was a great beginner weapon, and I liked the concept of the Mimic Tear. Apparently that was enough to beat Malenia, supposedly the hardest boss in the game, on my first try, as well as a lot of other bosses. The only challenges I had were Starscourge Radahn, Valiant Gargoyles, Elden Beast and Dragonlord Placidusax.

I never wanted to avoid using the Mimic Tear because it's part of the game. The developers put it there. But that's exactly why I think Spirit Ashes hurt the balance. It feels like they were added to make sure bad players could finish the game without quitting, but in the process they ruined many boss encounters.

Also, fall damage was my true nemesis. I probably died to it at least ten times more than I died to actual enemies, and I'm not exaggerating. It's not funny, it's just annoying.

Beyond gameplay, I think Elden Ring exposes some of FromSoftware's outdated design philosophies. Back in 2011, when the PS3 era was at its peak, those design choices felt innovative because the games achieved so much within relatively small worlds. The map of Dark Souls 1 remains my favorite map in any video game. Not because it's massive or packed with content, but because it's so cleverly interconnected and thoughtfully designed.

The storytelling is another area where I think Dark Souls 1 handled things better, the characters too. I still miss Siegmeyer and Solaire... And you would always come across them because there was only one or two ways to go. Here the NPCs (if you manage to locate them), feel passive-aggressive towards you, and they are not even memorable (bar Alexander). 

DS1's lore complemented the atmosphere and world design, while in Elden Ring it often feels like important story details are hidden inside item descriptions simply for the sake of being hidden. The story itself is actually very interesting, but I had to Google large parts of it to understand what was happening.

Personally, I think the game would have benefited from clearer storytelling: more cutscenes, more meaningful dialogue, more explanations, and NPCs who play a larger role throughout the adventure. I wish they wouldn't just spawn outside the boss gate to help you, but actually followed you or something, or made an actual epic entrance. It feels so outdated and 2010-coded. The storytelling actually got even worse for me with all the similarities between names... Godfrey, Godrick, Godwyn and other examples, some of which are fought more than once under different aliases or forms. This is not lore or worldbuilding, it just makes the player discombobulated, like reading a Dostoyevsky novel.

Furthermore, all questlines and even major bosses feel intentionally hidden to the point where a guide becomes absolutely necessary. To me, that doesn't feel rewarding but pretentious. And yes, I absolutely hate Ubisoft games and dislike Bethesda's too, but this is the other far end of the spectrum, which is almost as bad...

That's what frustrates me most about Elden Ring. Beneath all of my criticisms, it is a game I kinda enjoyed. The gameplay is excellent, many locations are memorable, and several bosses are very well designed too. The story is also surprisingly good once you actually understand it.

But despite all of that, I don't understand why so many people call it the greatest game ever made. It's a good game, but I don't think it deserves that level of praise. If the world had been smaller and more tightly designed, if the storytelling had been more direct, and if the enemy variety had been more original, I honestly think the game would have been far better than what we got.

And yeah I didn't even mention the poor performance, locked 60fps with no DLSS, bad camera, and subpar hitboxes.

Pros: Beautiful art design, particularly character and monster design. Architectural design can be a bit generic and repetitive but it fits the setting. Incredible world design. 

Cons: Combat is, at its heart, a knife fight simulator. Not a true RPG and would not recommend to other RPG gamers. The magic system is shallow and underbaked and fundamentally doesn't fit a combat system that wants to be a rhythm game. If you like casters, stay away.

The game occasionally stops being an RPG and confiscates your build. As an egregious example: Rykard gives my pure-Intelligence sorcerer a twelve-weight Strength weapon that ignores Intelligence entirely, then balances two enormous health bars around using a weapon you'll never touch again. 

Other complaints: 

1. The sorcerer's principal progression region, Raya Lucaria, heavily resists magic. If you rely purely on exploration and refuse to metagame and explore Caelid early to get Rock Sling you will suffer. 

2. Casting speed is governed by Dexterity, making magic the playstyle with the most awkward stat distribution and imposing an archetypally incoherent stat tax.

3. The already lackluster spell variety collapses under the FP economy. The first spells you get will likely remain among the most efficient throughout the game. Many of the spells are situational, redundant or boring, larger version of a previous one.  

4.  Weapon skills and Ashes of War frequently deliver the feel and look of 'magic' with far fewer downsides. Moonveil and Dark Moon Greatsword as the obvious examples here. 

5. The summoning system is heavily restricted by geography but is also the only broadly reliable way for casters to create the uninterrupted openings required by the game's longer and more elaborate spells. Where summoning is disabled, the caster is pushed back toward quick, close-range attacks like Carian Slicer. In practice you'll often spend a good chunk of your game outside boss arenas as a spellblade by necessity, whether that was your intended playstyle or not. 

6. Summoning is also so poorly balanced that roughly 90% of its enormous roster is not worth upgrading. A handful of durable generalists and exceptional group ashes are almost never the wrong choice, reducing most specialized summons to self-imposed novelty picks. 

7. Damage-type adaptation is locked behind obscure spell acquisition, hybrid stat requirements, or entirely different casting traditions. To “adapt” here often means abandoning the mage you built. Even respec is gated by play-time and a somewhat rare consumable so it's not an encounter-level solution here either. 

8. Bosses frequently erase the strategic advantage of range. There's no real magic, in an RPG sense, without it. 

The standard Souls player rebuttal “but mages can melt bosses” doesn’t counter any of this. Sorcery has enormous optimized peaks when the enemy stays still and the player stacks Terra Magica, a Physick, specialized headgear, talismans and a summon. But that does not show that it consistently supports experiencing the world as a caster. 

Given that I had to ask an AI model to heavily rewrite the magic system into something resembling an actual RPG, I can't in good conscience recommend this game to other RPG players in spite of hundreds of hours of playtime.
