As other reviews note: BG3 is excellent... mostly. But it's so fundamentally broken in critical areas that I cannot recommend it — especially not to players who want to roleplay beyond the devs' intended path.

Three years after release, this game still has game-breaking bugs. But this isn't a random glitch — this is quest design failure.

Here's what happened: To progress through the Shadow-Cursed Lands, you need a working Moonlantern. I made two valid story choices the game explicitly offers:

The game provides zero working lanterns through this combination of legitimate choices. No warning. No alternative path. Just: your save is worthless now.

I didn't cheat. I didn't exploit. I didn't do anything "wrong." I played the game exactly as designed, made roleplay choices the quest system clearly didn't account for, and the game simply... broke.

This isn't a soft-lock. This is a hard lock. Game over. The end. Hours of gameplay gone unless you install third-party mods to fix the developer's mistake.

A €70 AAA title should not require third-party mods to fix progression bugs that shouldn't exist. A €70 AAA title should definitely not hard-lock players for making valid story choices.

If you like linear, heavily railroaded RPGs where every decision is pre-approved: you'll probably love this.

If you want actual roleplaying freedom: be warned. The game punishes you for stepping outside the intended path."

[h1]UPDATE[/h1] after more hours playing

[b]I now have 3 broken Moonlanterns and one that works. The working one I found deep into the area that can only be reached with a working Moonlantern.[/b] This is like selling concert tickets in front of the stage — a virtual game over. [b]Must be fixed with mods.[/b]


[h2]The Good[/h2]

The battles are genuinely fun and motivating. Losing a fight makes me want to retry, not quit. That's rare and well done.

[h2]The Bad[/h2]

[b]Zero tutorial.[/b] You either know D&D 5e like the inside of your nose, or you'll spend hours googling what your spells actually do. For a 70 euro AAA game? Unacceptable.

[b]Inventory management is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ PITA.[/b] Sorting, moving, identifying — all unnecessarily clunky.

[b]Bugs and annoyances.[/b] Party members suddenly stop following because they randomly didn't make a jump they've done 100 times without issues. Clicking through doors (on the ground behind them) to walk through them closes them 80% of the time. The whole interaction with the game feels extremely clunky. The camera often makes you wanna pull you hair out. I've had fights that took forever because it was so extremely hard to even find the enemies because the cam just doesn't work properly (especially true for enemies on higher ground). I could make this review at least 10 times as long as it already is by just writing about all the bugs that Larian obviously didn't care to fix in those 3 years since release.... WTF?

[b]Open world is marketing fiction.[/b] As one player perfectly put it: Somehow this game deluded everyone into thinking it was open world when it has more obvious rails than Railroad Tycoon.

[h2]The Game-Breaking[/h2]

[b]Gale's explosion mechanic is catastrophically opaque.[/b] The game can end with zero warning and zero explanation. You load your last save, camp again, same explosion. No clue what triggered it. No way to fix it.

[b]Shadowheart's pivotal story moment[/b] has essentially ONE continuing branch. Knock her out instead of killing her? She becomes a lawn ornament forever. No story, no consequence, nothing.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
It's not Baldur's Gate 3. It's [b]Baldur's Rail 3[/b]. No open gates to be seen.

Still fun despite itself. But the your choices matter marketing should come with an asterisk: as long as they match the flowchart.

I'd say... if turn-based combat is what you're here for... you will enjoy this (if you can live with the bugs, some of them extremely annoying!). If you're after good roleplaying with lots of open branches... look somewhere else.

I'm a new gamer, only played DOS2 and now BG3, so this is not from a seasoned gamer's perspective. While I have some grasp of turn-based combat, I don't know DnD rules -- but BG3 assumed that I did, and that made it hard to understand many mechanics for which there were no tutorials. I just wanted to jump in and have fun, not spend hours Googling tutorials and guide books or stumbling about clueless. It was not a great introduction to the game, especially since I'd set it to Explorer Mode and was hoping for a beginner-friendly start.

I enjoy it when if I plan my combat well, I get rewarded with a win. With the primarily chance-based combat model of BG3, best-laid plans too frequently meet catastrophic failure. I felt really limited in what I could do with each character per turn, especially i.t.o. crowd control, and there was nothing to be done to mitigate the effects of chance. I ended up doing my best to avoid combat because I just found it so tedious and unrewarding.

Out of combat, everything was also random, and I ended up only taking actions at which my characters had the best chances of succeeding, so I couldn't do the things I actually wanted to do. You don't get to see how high a number you have to roll before you commit to an option, so that was also frustrating. Failing just one of the many random rolls throughout the game often meant ending up in yet another impossible fight or walking into an insta-death trap, meaning I was spending as much time reloading the game as playing.

The high risk low reward setup just had me so on edge the whole time that I didn't want to move further in the game. Uninstall. Not for me.

I went into Baldur’s Gate 3 with absolutely no D&D experience, so I really didn’t know what to expect. It ended up being a great introduction to that world and style of gameplay, and I never felt like I needed to already know D&D to enjoy it.

The characters were probably my favorite part. I actually cared about them and wanted to see how their stories played out. There are so many different choices, relationships, and storylines that I ended up doing multiple playthroughs just to experience different romances and see how making different decisions changed things.

I even did an evil playthrough, which is usually really hard for me because I always end up feeling bad and making the “good” choice in games. 😂 The fact that Baldur’s Gate 3 actually got me to commit to an evil character says a lot about how much freedom the game gives you to play a completely different story.

After more than 230 hours, I still feel like there are things I could have done differently or storylines I could have missed. Definitely recommend it, even if you’ve never played D&D before.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a story rich RPG featuring a beautiful open world, with the best character writing I've seen. The game covers themes such as freedom, identity, greed, and social inequality. It's an unforgettable experience worth playing. Jackie Welles & Johnny Silverhand are [b] GOATED [/b] support characters!

Story: You play as V, a lone merc in Night City, a futuristic violent dystopia dictated by greedy capitalist mega-corporations. You take on the most dangerous jobs trying to stay alive and make a name for yourself. There are 3 life paths to choose from: Nomad, Streetkid, and Corpo. They don't make much of a difference gameplay-wise, aside from unique dialogue options and shaping V's perspective on the world. After your biggest high stakes job goes FUBAR, the story truly begins as you race against time for your life! 

Gameplay: This game feels like a mixture of GTA and Borderlands because of the interactivity, stores, looting, class building, and the leeway to play however you like. Unfortunately, some elements are not well polished, but its not that bad because they can be fixed with mods. Majority of the cars handle terribly! I got around the map 90% of the time using motorcycles because they're really fast and consistently handle well. Another thing I did not enjoy too much was the early game. Enemies scale heavily to your level at all times, so the beginning is kind of rough because your guns aren't strong and targets feel tanky. Shotguns, revolvers, and snipers became my go to weapons. You'll be fine if your aim and positioning is really good. Mid to late game is when you can really start going crazy. 

Environment: Along with the story, this is another great aspect because of its visual storytelling. It shows you how bad things are, instead of telling you. The city is plagued with advertisements, some even reaching the sky! Gangs rule certain city districts, crime thrives more often in some places, and you can really see the poverty and flourishment of areas. What I truly did love were the small mentions of the 2076 Edgerunners crew. You can find iconic items left behind by a few members which is very cool, it makes the city's history feel more connected on a deeper level.

Side Quests: There are many to do and they give you really good rewards, but they aren't special because they follow a repetitive format. The only good quests are the character story missions, these deepen your bond with key characters, allowing you to learn their history and help them out with personal troubles. 

TL;DR Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best story rich RPG games you can ever play. It has some issues gameplay wise, but they're relatively minor and won't hurt your overall experience. Never stop fighting, my chooms!

First off, Cyberpunk 2077 is a genuinely enjoyable game. The atmosphere, visuals, combat, and overall design of Night City are impressive. However, the longer I play, the more I notice just how many opportunities were missed.

On the technical side, I've experienced some rendering issues that may or may not be related to my PC. I've lowered my graphics settings considerably, but the problems persist. I've also encountered a handful of bugs that required me to save, completely close the game, and restart it. Annoying, but nothing that has ruined the experience.

My biggest complaint, however, is Night City itself.

For a city that looks so alive, it feels surprisingly dead.

There's an incredible amount of detail throughout the world, but very little of it actually responds to your existence. You can spend hours completing side activities, fighting gangs, and building your street cred, but it rarely feels like any of it carries meaningful weight in the world around you.

Take the gangs, for example. If I spend my time hunting down members of a particular gang, eventually they should recognize me as an enemy and attack me on sight. On the other hand, if I've consistently avoided conflict with another gang, maybe their members should acknowledge that. Even something as simple as different dialogue, attitudes, or reactions based on your history with a faction would make the world feel significantly more immersive.

Street cred could have been so much more than a number. Imagine having separate reputations with different gangs, where your actions determine whether you're respected, feared, tolerated, or hated. That alone would give side activities a much greater sense of purpose.

Cyberware customization is another missed opportunity. For a game centered around a society obsessed with body modification, installing cyberware has surprisingly little impact on your physical appearance. Being able to customize the color, style, or design of your implants would have added another layer of immersion and personal expression.

But all of that ties into my biggest issue with the game:

You never really feel like you're part of Night City.

At times, it almost feels like The Truman Show, except nobody is actually watching you. Nobody seems to care who you are, what you've accomplished, or what you've done to the people around them. You can be an absolute menace to a particular gang, and the next group you encounter acts like they've never heard of you.

The city is beautiful, flashy, detailed, and full of people, yet somehow manages to feel strangely lifeless. It's almost like exploring an incredibly elaborate movie set rather than living in a functioning world.

And that's what frustrates me the most. The foundation for something truly incredible is already there.

Despite all of this, I still recommend Cyberpunk 2077. I've had a lot of fun with it, and there's plenty the developers got right. I just can't shake the feeling that Night City could have been so much more.

I don't want to be that annoying guy or downplay the great work CD Projekt Red did in giving us some free improvements. I played the Witcher for a long time, and it was always great to revisit the landscapes, the unique experiences, and that feeling only TW3 can deliver. Sometimes I’d just ride aimlessly with the HUD turned off, simply to enjoy the journey. It’s no wonder some scenes in The Witcher rival those in Red Dead 2.

That said, I wanted to start a fresh playthrough on "Death March" difficulty to get the last three Steam achievements I was missing. Right from the start, I noticed quite a few things, specifically:

Cons

#1 Missing textures: one instance occurred at Vizima Castle after speaking with Emhyr the chessboard and the wall were invisible.
#2 The colors have definitely changed, they look a bit more washed out, almost pastel. I noticed that nights with a full moon are practically as bright as day. I can see distant trees illuminated by the moonlight.
#3 I have to talk a bit about the new interface, I think they tried to modernize the UI to make it more intuitive but... seeing 30 separate notifications for every piece of silver or iron I crafted doesn't exactly keep the interface clean.
#4 Honestly I don't see a huge difference in gameplay between the previous version and this one. The things I noticed that actually helped were dynamic combat camera and new target-locking options (which made combat easier, I’d say)
#5 I’ve run into the occasional bug here and there while playing like seeing Geralt in a Tpose while in inventory.
#6 This is just my personal opinion but the updates to graphics, lighting, and color reminded me of Crimson Desert. Nothing against it but I vastly preferred the colors in the previous version.
#7 Having played with mods for a long time I was happy that CD decided to add official mod support, including for consoles. But I really missed basic features that should have been implemented already, like using a torch while riding Roach
#8 Well, basically now if you dive underwater you can see absolutely everything.
#9 Character cutscenes look almost pitch black, you can only see the lifeless glint in their eyes, haha. 
But seriously, it looks scary now.

Pros:
#1 It supports mods now. Apparently, there are already some working, hehe
#2 I was eager to see the skill trees! Honestly, I’ll keep playing just to see how I can craft my Witcher builds.
#3 It’s easier to notice certain skill tree "powers" in action now like the perfectly timed dodge that makes the sword glow blue.

There are plenty of side quests to keep you busy, and some of them are genuinely great. That said, I still found myself wishing there were more. Apparently, I have developed an unhealthy appetite for wandering around Night City doing increasingly ridiculous jobs for complete strangers.

The biggest problem, however, is the main story. It's simply too short. If you focus mostly on the main quests, the game ends before it really feels like you've gotten your money's worth. You spend all this time building your character, exploring Night City and becoming murder machine, only for the main story to basically end too soon.

Thankfully, Cyberpunk 2077 has some solid replay value. You can approach the game with completely different builds, whether you want to be a stealthy hacker, a heavily armed psychopath, a katana-wielding lunatic, or some other combination of questionable life choices. Changing your stats and playstyle can make another playthrough feel surpprisingly different.

Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a fantastic-looking and incredibly smooth game with a huge amount of potential content, but I can't help feeling that the main story should have been significantly longer.

My biggest issue with Baldur's Gate 3 is that the gameplay is simply weak. Substantially inferior to Larian's previous games.

The writing, voice acting, and "world building" (lore, interactions, etc) are excellent, but the actual combat and progression systems feel like a significant step backward from Divinity: Original Sin 2. The root of the problem is its commitment to Dungeons and Dragons. What works at a tabletop doesn't automatically work in a video game.

DnD's rules are designed to support a group of players and a human Dungeon Master who can improvise, interpret edge cases, and ignore bad rules when they get in the way of fun. In Baldur's Gate 3, those same rules become rigid restrictions. Combat is slower, more random (to the point of being frustrating), and far less expressive, constantly held back by arbitrary action limits and dice-roll dependency. I wanted to experience the whole thing. The characters are really nice and I really wanted to know them better, but honestly... The gameplay is unbearable. I would describe [b]Baldur’s Gate 3[/b] as “bootleg D&D”.

It’s a “popcorn” game, which is to say it’s fun and good but ultimately artistically insignificant, just barely a step above other popular generic fantasy games, and I’m giving it a thumbs down ONLY because I don’t think it deserves the 720.000 “overwhelmingly positive” score.
(However, I’ll change it into a thumbs up if the score ever dips below it)

[h1]X-Factor[/h1]
Locales are good looking and have variety in them, physical and voice acting are on point, music does the job but sprinkles in some banger tracks, and the changes to the original D&D rules are mostly great and well implemented.
Also, it’s offline D&D, so if you ever missed a session or want to see how a build works you can always fire up this game and just do it.

Despite being a series of rigamarole fetch quests, most setpieces are very cool.

Importantly for replayability, even more than multiple classes with multiple abilities granting no end to how you can build your character, is the modding scene, adding just about everything to freshen the game up for a second and third go-around.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
It’s D&D fifth edition.
If you don’t know what that is: You choose how good a character is at something by slotting a certain number of points in six scores that define who you’re playing as.
On top of this you choose a “class” or what kind of things you’d want your character to be centered around, each class providing different mechanics to achieve this, both inside and outside combat, along with different equipment to give you that extra edge to succeed.
There’s a lot of nuance but that’s pretty much it.

[h1]Story[/h1]
You find yourself aboard an alien ship and infected with a brain parasite that threatens to turn you into a monster, so partner up with an unlikely cast of characters in your quest to seek a cure for this shared burden.

A good hook that gives an excuse to be joined by anyone, no matter how good or evil they are, as you need eachother’s expertise to find a solution to this problem.

The story progresses mostly through dialogue, simply walk up to someone to talk and be either given quests or advance them.

The game also features LOTS of side stories and especially questlines for the ones that either want to explore more of this world or to satisfy their inner completionist.

[h1]Downsides[/h1]
An interesting and focused story that could’ve been told in a couple of hours was instead overfilled with generic writing and other filler content stretching it to about a 100 hours where the game keeps bumping into weird pacing, losing momentum, reiterating over already-made points, and sending you off onto yet another wild goose chase when it doesn’t want you to get to the point, again, all of this isn’t necessarily a bad thing depending of the level of writing required for your enjoyment.

In D&D players can say and do anything they want whenever they want and the DM reacts to it.
In BG3 you’re stunted in your roleplay choices, because of course you can’t have a simple system that accounts for every possibility, but even then, I don’t exactly like how most dialogue choices are: Yes, Yes, Snarky Remark, *attack*.
Also, unfortunately outside a few quips almost no companions interact with eachother, only with the situation at hand which makes them feel more like reactionary robots than the alive characters that should’ve been.

From a purely aesthetic aspect I don’t think anyone will argue about how bad the camera system, the overcrowded UI, the million magical effects overlapping, and other constant immersion breaking aspects of it are, although there are community-made mods that thankfully partially fix some of those issues.

It’s very generic.
That itself isn’t a bad thing but if you want anything more than what the term “fantasy game” conjures in your head, this is not it.
A lot of characters are set up to be interesting in the themes they could explore, but then the writing team ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed and makes them say the same generic trite lines over and over again.

This game is singleplayer at heart while all TTRPGs are to be played with friends.
It has a hard focus on story but without having good writing to justify it, nor trying to capture the insanity and/or silliness that is player agency.

An even better description for it would be “Singleplayer MMO from the 2000s” but with better graphics that’s only related to TTRPGs due to its D&D playrules.
If that’s sounds like your cup of tea, I’d suggest it, even at full price as there’s a lot of content for those who have the right appetite for it.

I don’t like the D&D system; I love roleplaying, but the mechanics D&D uses to simulate roleplay and combat make it actively less fun than just roleplaying with no rules at all. If I thought about it for even a moment, I would have realized this wasn’t going to be a game for me. But I didn’t. I had two playthroughs, the first I quit after completing Act 1, and the second I managed to finish the game  On the surface this game has all the things you’d want from an RPG, exploring areas, filling out your map, beating enemies, collecting items, completing quests; lots of little hits of dopamine that make it easy to keep going. But when I really think of the quality of each of these aspects, they aren’t very good. First, and the only one I don’t mind, exploring the world is enjoyable. There are lots of hidden items to find and areas to explore. My only complaint would be that it got a bit overwhelming at times with how much exploring and options I was given. Next, beating enemies, my second least favorite part of the game. As stated, I don’t like the D&D’s combat system. I feel it does a bad job of simulating real time combat and the combat isn’t very fun. BG3 is a video game though, so turn-based combat is normal. However, I personally don’t like the initiative order system; initiative is easily the biggest determiner of how well you’ll do in a fight, so it’s annoying that something that important is random. There’s a reason why most RPGs either have you and the enemy alternating attacks, or have everyone’s attacks refresh on timers, it makes the combat much more strategy based, which is what you want for turn based combat. In general though, BG3’s combat is way too random, with how likely you are to hit and how much damage you do. You could replay the same fight with the same strategy over and over again and get vastly different results. Yes, you do want some randomness in a combat system so that it isn’t a solved game, but BG3 has just way too much randomness for my liking. In general, enemies don’t really have weaknesses or special attacks; most combats feel very similar to each other, boiling every fight down to just draining the collective HP pool, and once you figure out the best ways to do that, you’ve basically trivialized the whole combat system. I have more gripes with the combat system, but I don’t want this review to run too long, just know it is easily the worst RPG combat system I’ve experienced and is not fun. As for my least favorite part about the game, it’s collecting items, which might just be a thing only I care about. Typically, RPGs do one of two things. Either they have a bunch of basic loot scattered about, or have lots of unique loot across the map with in-game ways of helping you find it, both are completely valid ways of doing loot. BG3 on the other hand had a crap ton of unique loot all over the place with no built-in way of helping you find it. I am a loot goblin, and I enjoy picking up everything, but there is no good way of tracking loot you’ve gotten and finding loot that you’ve missed. You either have to heavily explore every area when you enter it or use a guide, otherwise you will miss a lot of stuff and have no way of knowing what you missed. For example, I was doing a thrower build for Karlach, and there was a weapon that I wanted to get. I ended up having to reload a save because the guy who sells that weapon leaves if Shadowheart is your party, which she was. Like, I didn’t even know that guy was a vendor. It’s way too easy to miss loot in this game. Also, I hate how so much of the best loot are from shopkeepers; I want to find the really cool loot, I don’t want to just buy it off some guy. BG3 is clearly made for people to only find some of the loot, which sucks for people who enjoy collecting loot like me. I mean, so many games feature collectathons for a reason. Anywho, BG3’s lack of care for loot goblins like me made exploring feel like a real chore. And finally there are the quests, which I personally wasn’t a big fan of, but I can see why people are. I was never able to get invested in the world, and while I enjoyed the characters well enough, the slight joy I got from these characters was vastly offset by how little I enjoyed the gameplay. Whenever I dislike the gameplay in a game, it makes it hard for me to care about the game’s other aspects, and BG3 is no exception. Although, I do have a couple of actual complaints about the quests. First is that in Act 1 nothing you did really progressed the story at all, heck you can just walk up to the mountains and pretty much skip the whole thing, it made the first few dozens hours of the game feel like it had little momentum. Second is that Act 3 has way too many quests, like I only got through half of Baldur’s Gate and I already have like 20 side quests, some of which would require me to go into the second half of the city and pick up even more side quests, I just got way too overwhelmed. I feel like they could’ve paced the quests better so that you’re finishing some as you get new ones. Overall, I don’t have much to say about the quests, I’ve experienced far better and far worse. And finally, in terms of the story, which everyone seems to adore, I don’t really see what’s so great about it. It’s overall a pretty simple story, with you just travelling from place to place, helping random people, killing bad guys, until you eventually get to the ending. It was a pretty standard RPG story. And in terms of choices you can make, there almost always two options, one good one and one evil one. Sometimes the choices you are given are more morally ambiguous, but for the most part if you are doing a good or evil playthrough, you only really have one choice. And of course, the majority of the game is exploring, fighting, side quests, etc. So even if you did a second playthrough of the game, the vast majority of the game would be identical, with only minor things changing. Of course, this isn’t a problem, most RPGs don’t have branching stories, but with how much emphasis this game puts on roleplaying, I expected a bit more options to make the character feel like my own. So overall, the exploration was enjoyable, but collecting loot wasn’t fun, the combat is boring and has way too much randomness, the quests and characters are alright but nothing to right home about, and the story is pretty standard. As always with games critically acclaimed for their story, I fail to see the hype. 6.5/10

TLDR I basically can't run the remastered game. It replaced my og copy and I had no say in it, only could revert it with issues, so remastered gets thumbs down.

1) They changed the game to "remastered" instead of making the remaster a standalone installation. My potato could run the OG on ultra just fine, but the remastered can't keep 20fps on low while standing still and not moving the camera. You have to switch the game version to "classic" in Steam settings if you want to play the original.

2) When I switched back to "classic," the RED launcher couldn't initialize the game. File verification (which the launcher asks you to do) didn't help. You have to go to \\bin\\x64\\ in the game folder and run witcher3.exe directly.

3) Saves made on the Next-Gen/Remastered build got converted to the new format on update, instead of doing it when you load the save, or ideally only making new saves use the new format. My 1.32 saves were untouched, but my NG+ saves (made on 4.0) got converted to 4.04 and won't load in classic which is 1.32. To fix this, hex-edit the save file (located in Documents on your system drive. Make a backup first tho). Find the line at offset 00000C10 — don't get confused by the bunch of 00 entries before you find the right line. In the 6th or 7th column of that line, you'll see 1B. Change that entry to 13, don't touch anything else, save the file, and the save will load in classic just fine. Credit to Maxizera's guide.

Regarding prevailing evaluations, I contend that BG3 is an exceptionally well-crafted game, yet ultimately constrained by excessive structural rigidity.

While the game offers substantial exposure to the practical mechanics of DnD, it falls short of delivering the degree of agency typically associated with the genre. Although such restriction may be justified as a compromise to accommodate novice players or to streamline development, the resulting experience is overly prescriptive and limits genuine player autonomy.

The narrative architecture is predominantly linear and unidirectional. Consequently, players are confronted with a dilemma: either compromise immersion—an essential expectation in CRPGs—by exhaustively completing side content despite the urgent narrative premise of a mind flayer parasite, or engage in repeated playthroughs with alternative characters. In the latter case, players are compelled to enact decisions that may contradict prior moral alignments or emotional investments, thereby undermining narrative coherence and experiential continuity.

The core design deficiency lies in the absence of a meaningful post-narrative state. Unlike The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, which permits continued exploration in a decompressed, post-resolution environment, or Red Dead Redemption 2, where narrative succession is achieved through a character such as John Marston, BG3 terminates the player’s progression abruptly upon completion of the main storyline. This design choice is neither sufficiently foreshadowed nor mitigated.

As a result, the relational bonds formed with companions, along with the accumulated value of equipment and progression systems, are rendered functionally obsolete. The player’s sustained investment—both affective and strategic—is effectively nullified at the moment of narrative closure. What remains is a diminished incentive structure, wherein the only recourse is to re-engage with previously unexperienced content through repetition rather than organic continuation.

This structural limitation significantly attenuates the game’s long-term experiential depth and undermines the durability of player engagement.

My three general complaints are: 
1. You level up way to fast to the point where it feels punishing to play the hacker playstyle. Every mission you can kill everybody no matter what by only clicking a few buttons. I do think this is a general game issue because the game feels very easy even on the highest difficulty. The only real challenge is when I tell myself "I will only use [x] weapon for this mission." Some enemies have "resistances" to certain forms of combat, but attaching that to the ram system negates it due to the many ways to regen ram or overcharge mode, which allows you to sacrifice hp to hack increasing your ram pool near infinitely. 
2. I don't know if this is just me, but the main story fails to entertain me. This is okay because the side missions are honestly more fun than the busywork the main missions provide. Too much dialogue, too much following frustratingly slow NPCs, and too many tasks and decisions that feel unimportant. 
3. Lastly I know its hard to make games look good while flying; but having flying cars around, millions of dollars in the bank, and being unable to buy one feels kinda bad for a futuristic game. 

All that being said: The world has amazing atmosphere. Driving around, especially in the rain or at night, feels just amazing. The music, the views, and just something I cant explain gives me a amazing feeling of being small... of peace. I do wish there were driving sounds though. 

Here is a list of bugs I have experienced so far. 
1. Picking up items or opening a chest frequently causes things to go flying.
2. NPCs t-posing while driving their cars.
3. Story NPCs get hit by cars during cutscenes causing their dead bodies to drag on the floor while talking to me until they start a different animation and get revived.
4. Enemies glitching into walls and floors.
5. Enemies seeing you through walls and floors.
6. Once a enemy I killed glitched so hard his body was shot into the sky while his head was stuck on a railing causing his entire model to be a massive tapestry spanning over a block and crashing my FPS till it unloaded.
7. Cyberpsycho missions, while being some of the most fun, are also insanely buggy with their triggers. Three times I have had to fast travel, skip 48 hours in time, and then go back just to have things spawn or trigger.
8. Constant floating items, occasional floating NPCs, and briefly floating cars before they crash down. 

The bugs are the main reason I just cannot recommend this game. They break immersion more than anything else.

I really wanted to like this game. Spent so long with my friends trying to get a campaign going. We tried with 4 people and after months and months of aligning schedules and starting multiple campaigns I decided it just is not meant to be played with more than 2 people on your first run.

So I tried it solo and for the first couple hours it was so much better. I tried tactical difficulty and after dying a few times it felt like my decisions in character specs and party config actually mattered. But after failing repeatedly in a couple fights against higher-level opponents I realized a lot of the time, winning and losing was less about skill and more about going back and gaining experience to buff your crew.

It's an RPG and some grind to beef up your characters is totally expected. The problem is that for me, the story elements were so slow and not rewarding. The little amount of strategy sprinkled in was too few and far between bland dialogue trees. So many story beat payoffs felt like just edgy sex jokes involving fantasy creatures.

The conversation around this game is so positive and I've never heard anyone talk about the downsides of multiplayer in this game so I'm very disappointed with it. We wanted an online D&D-type experience, and it just fundamentally fails counts of 3 or more new players. Even solo I got only a few hours of entertaining game play, but I believe the right people would enjoy it solo. I imagine for those who play it solo, you could then have fun playing with others who have already beaten the game. But starting fresh with multiple people ruins the experience. If players wander to different places, they start and end quests independently, and trying to enforce your party staying together is extremely difficult because listening to every conversation and waiting for the speaker to choose their dialogue is tedious. So you either have sessions where almost nothing happened and everyone sat around or you have sessions where you feel like things have happened randomly and you don't know what's going on.

Upgraded visuals, Enhanced combat, Improved traversal & movement, New Witcher signs FX, Revamped mount handling, Enhanced monster behaviors, Skill tree revamp, Transmogrification and the list supposedly goes on and on and on...

0% difference. All the Remaster does is just reshade the game slightly and add some pretty skyboxes.

Combat is still clunky, slow, boring, and unimaginative. Dialouge is still tedious and lengthy - requiring you to slam the spacebar key over and over just to get through dialouge you've already heard before. Nothing's changed in the story. Picking up loot is still a pain in the a$$. Enemies still only spawn in set, non-random locations and don't respawn unless you leave the area. There aren't any new quests. No new spells. Levelling up is still as slow as ever. Geralt still dies after stubbing his toe or falling 50cm. Roach still handles like threading a sock through a needle. The skill tree still sucks fat butt and takes 4eva to get through.

 ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ I guess they really wanted those some 10,000 fans to really get keen again for the series and to buy their completely random new DLC early next year for a game that's a now decade old.

Look, I know it's an amazing game. But it's not without its faults. If I'm playing an RPG, what I care about is the narrative. This game has a stellar narrative, but the game design actively resists showing it to you. The narrative allows some choice, but it's mostly built on allowing failure and presenting consequences for failure. Sometimes it's off of a failed dice roll and very often it's based on conversation tree options that vague and don't communicate the weight attached to them. I'm not opposed to meaningful choices or hard choices, but... the way the game allows and punishes failure often leads to worse gameplay and a lower quality narrative than what the game has to offer.

This can be related to small things, like a combat encounter that becomes impossibly hard and frustrating because you missed a character's side conversation, failed a persuasion roll, or didn't realize that it'd be easier if you LET yourself be ambushed. This can be annoying but it's not a dealbreaker.

The dealbreaker is allowing failure on major plot points (losing characters, or even losing companions), then doing nothing to transition the story or character dynamics in response. I'm having to Google if certain things are bugged. The negative consequences often come on suddenly and they aren't followed up with conversations or narrator cues to unpack what happened and what comes next; nothing fills the void of what you missed or lost. I've had to repeatedly save scum and force the "good outcome" just to feel in touch with the narrative. I'll still dump a ton of hours into BG3, but I'll be frustrated for far too many of them.

A 10,000-line review will not fit in one response. I can write it in numbered parts, keeping the review overwhelmingly positive and avoiding repetition.

Elden Ring: A Monumental Triumph of Open-World Design

Elden Ring is not merely a successful action role-playing game. It is a vast, mysterious, and deeply rewarding adventure that demonstrates what an open world can achieve when discovery matters more than checklists. FromSoftware takes the demanding combat, intricate environments, and cryptic storytelling associated with its earlier games and expands them across the Lands Between without sacrificing their identity.

The opening hours establish the game's confidence immediately. After a brief introduction, the player emerges into Limgrave and sees a landscape filled with ruins, forests, cliffs, castles, and distant landmarks. The game does not overwhelm the screen with icons or insist upon a rigid itinerary. Instead, it invites curiosity. A ruined church may contain a merchant. A forest might conceal an underground elevator. A distant tower could become the beginning of an adventure lasting several hours.

This approach makes exploration feel personal. Players are not simply clearing activities selected from a menu; they are constructing their own journeys. One person may travel directly toward Stormveil Castle, while another spends hours investigating caves, fighting optional bosses, gathering equipment, and discovering characters in unexpected locations. Both experiences feel valid because the world accommodates different priorities without losing its carefully designed structure.

The Lands Between is enormous, but its scale is supported by remarkable environmental variety. Limgrave's green plains create a welcoming yet melancholy beginning. Liurnia of the Lakes surrounds the player with mist, flooded ruins, and magical institutions. Caelid presents a diseased landscape whose crimson skies and grotesque creatures communicate danger before a single enemy attacks. Later territories continue to introduce distinctive architecture, weather, terrain, and atmosphere.

These regions are visually memorable because they do more than change the scenery. Each area produces a different emotional response. Limgrave encourages adventurous confidence. Caelid inspires dread. Leyndell creates awe through its immense golden architecture and layered streets. The Mountaintops of the Giants convey isolation through snow, wind, and tremendous empty spaces. The environments serve as storytelling devices, shaping the player's understanding of a fractured world.

Torrent, the player's spectral steed, makes this immense landscape pleasurable to traverse. Torrent moves quickly, can double-jump, and gives exploration a sense of freedom. The mount allows players to leap over obstacles, climb unconventional routes, and escape dangerous encounters. Mounted combat adds another dimension, particularly when fighting dragons or groups of enemies across open fields.

The absence of excessive guidance is one of the game's greatest strengths. Elden Ring trusts players to observe their surroundings. Statues can point toward hidden catacombs. Unusual rock formations may indicate concealed paths. A distant structure can become a navigational reference. Even the fragments required to reveal each portion of the map must be found in the world, turning cartography into part of the adventure.

The map itself is beautifully designed. Rather than functioning as a sterile interface, it resembles an illustrated artifact filled with geographical clues. Drawn ruins, mines, forests, and unusual formations encourage investigation. A careful player can often predict where something interesting might be located without the game explicitly identifying it. This preserves mystery while rewarding attention.

Combat remains the foundation of the experience. Every encounter asks the player to consider distance, timing, stamina, positioning, and enemy behaviour. Attacks have weight, shields provide meaningful protection, and dodges demand judgment. Victory rarely comes from pressing buttons thoughtlessly. Even ordinary opponents can punish carelessness, which makes successful encounters satisfying.

The game's difficulty is demanding, but it is unusually flexible. Players can improve their attributes, upgrade weapons, summon spirits, use cooperative multiplayer, exploit elemental weaknesses, or leave a difficult area and return later. These options do not trivialise the adventure. They create multiple ways to overcome its challenges and allow a broader range of players to find a workable strategy.

Build diversity is exceptional. A character can become a heavily armoured knight, a swift duelist, a destructive sorcerer, a faithful healer, an archer, or a warrior who combines several disciplines. The enormous selection of weapons, spells, shields, talismans, armour sets, and consumable items encourages experimentation. Discovering a new piece of equipment can inspire an entirely different style of play.

Weapons feel distinct rather than interchangeable. Colossal swords strike slowly but deliver tremendous impact. Spears control space and allow cautious attacks. Curved swords reward aggression and mobility. Bows offer ranged utility, while magical staffs and sacred seals open extensive spell systems. Even weapons within the same category may possess different attack patterns, scaling properties, or special abilities.

The Ashes of War system deepens this variety. These abilities can grant weapons dramatic techniques, from powerful leaps and spinning attacks to magical projectiles and defensive manoeuvres. Many Ashes of War also allow players to modify a weapon's affinity, helping it complement a chosen distribution of attributes. The system makes ordinary equipment adaptable and gives experimentation practical value.

Magic is particularly impressive. Sorceries and incantations are not limited to variations of basic projectiles. Players can summon spectral weapons, manipulate gravity, breathe like dragons, hurl lightning, conjure flames, cure ailments, strengthen allies, and unleash enormous beams of magical energy. The visual spectacle supports a system with genuine tactical breadth.

Spirit Ashes are another valuable addition. These summonable companions range from packs of wolves to powerful individual warriors. They can distract bosses, apply status effects, or contribute substantial damage. More importantly, they let players shape the rhythm of difficult battles. A fight that feels overwhelming alone can become manageable when a spirit divides the enemy's attention.

The bosses are among the game's defining achievements. Major opponents combine imaginative visual design, memorable music, elaborate arenas, and complex attack patterns. Their movements often communicate personality: some fight with disciplined precision, others with animalistic violence, and others with supernatural grandeur. Learning these encounters can initially feel intimidating, but improvement is tangible.

Margit provides an excellent early lesson. His delayed attacks punish panic, his quick follow-ups test positioning, and his aggression forces players to engage with the combat system. Defeating him feels meaningful because the battle teaches patience rather than merely checking numerical strength. It establishes that observation and adaptation will be essential throughout the journey.

Godrick is equally memorable for different reasons. His grotesque appearance embodies the game's themes of ambition, decay, and stolen power. The encounter escalates spectacularly, combining brutal axe attacks with a transformation that is both horrifying and absurdly magnificent. It is a perfect example of FromSoftware's ability to unite mechanical challenge with unforgettable imagery.

Rennala's battle demonstrates the game's theatrical range. Its dreamlike staging, magical effects, and haunting atmosphere distinguish it from conventional duels.

While playing any of the Infinity/Aurora engine games, did you ever caught yourself thinking: 

- Damn, wish this game had platforming! 
- Maybe you would like to spend hours opening barrels and crates to find no loot? 
- How about spending a LOT of time in inventory management, due to small and generic icons, and a LOT of crappy loot?
- Do you want a really clunky UI, that not only doesn't improve on the genre games that preceded this one, but it also makes some things worse?
- You think that highlighting interactable items is too easy, and you want to pixel hunt for items?


If you answer yes to any of the questions, maybe this game is for you...

On a more serious note, this is one of those times that I wish I could leave a neutral review, but Steam doesn't have the option. THE GAME ISN'T BAD, but it doesn't feel like a Baldur's Gate game. Heck, sometimes it doesn't even feel like a Forgotten Realms game. The are a lot of generic places, places that doesn't feel like their lore accurate counterparts, etc...IWD for example got a lot of the ambiance right, and more than 20 years later, BG3 failed to stand on it's predecessors shoulders.


There are also other problems, like some minor bugs, but I find baffling that more than 2 and a half years after release, Larian still manages to introduce new, major bugs with new patches, like with the most current one. Other downsides if I'm being nitpicky: No LVL 20 (the cap is at 12), a party of only four characters, lack of nuance with party relationships, very low variety of armor/weapons, mechanics info (like crit range or calculating base dmg+elemental dmg from weapons is missing), some staple items, like the Bag of Holding and the Holy Avenger are completely absent and the loading screen drives me nuts, loading to 100% and then staying at 100% for a long time, to actually load (the game is on a nvme SSD, so I don't think this is a me problem).

As a last complaint, after seeing the longevity that NWN1 and 2 got by having amazing toolkits, you'd think Larian would give us something comparable, maybe even better after two decades, but, no...There's nothing.


On a brighter side, the game looks good, most of the voice acting is decent to really good (and there's a LOT of voiced lines), The music is good when it is present, some of the small tidbits and sidequests are very well written and the game is long (that can be a plus or a minus...) and very replayable. 

With all that said, I'd say I've played 3/4 of the game, and it keeps growing on me. I might change the review to positive after I end my first run.

It's not just one city like in GTA 4. So if you're not a fan of Los Santos, you can find plenty of areas that will suit you. 

Character and vehicle customization make a return at a grand scale with the options to change your haircut, facial hair, add tattoos, even piercing. Clothing tattoos range from cheap street wear to expensive suits and tuxedos. 
Vehicle customization is so much fun by itself - you can add spoilers, bumpers, change entire bodyworsk, add custom paint jobs, change wheel colors. I've easily spent hours just customizing vehicles. Add to that hundreds of hours driving them around.

The combat is also really good, but I would argue not as fun as in GTA IV. You have waaaay more weapons, which can also be customized, but the ragdoll physics are not as impressive anymore.
The story and characters are memorable, but not as impactful, as the tone is lighter and I would describe it as an action-comedy flick. 

Missions are more chaotic and really want to make you replay them over and over again. With the exception of the missions where you have to do yoga or slowly walk around the port doing mundane tasks.

The radio is once again amazing - nothing will top West Coast Classics, Radio Los Santos, Non-Stop-Pop FM, FlyLo FM and Radio Mirror Park.

The writing is good, the environments are nice, and the soundtrack is great. However, I've ran into so many gameplay issues and bugs in the game that I've completely lost interest in playing. The main issues:

- Useless autosave system. A major portion of my playtime is just redoing hours of lost progress because I forgot to quicksave enough. Why couldn't they at least make it so that it autosaves after major conversations/events or after leveling up, for example?! The most annoying part is having to redo all of the inventory management. It has to be the worst autosave system I've ever seen in a game.

- Amount of bugs. I've encountered a high amount of bugs during my playthroughs. I've had to redo progress way too many times due to annoying things like enemies teleporting to where they shouldn't be, getting stuck out of bounds, visual bugs, aural bugs, or various other annoying issues.

- Other issues include enemy vision going through terrain or solid objects when sneaking, being forced to stop sneaking and/or enter combat when you are in the vision cone of a non-hostile NPC that is not involved in combat in any way, and accidentally interacting with something while trying to just move your character. What a great idea to make every single interaction use the left mouse button! Trying to move to a specific spot for a sneak attack? Nope, you pickpocket your ally and get spotted. Trying to read a book on a shelf? Nope, you steal an item and the whole town wants to kill you.

- Misleading conversation options with irreversible outcomes. I've noticed that there are a lot of conversation options that seem completely neutral/non-hostile, but unexpectedly lead to the other party becoming hostile towards you. Even if you never attack them and only help them fight the other enemies, they will remain permanently hostile towards you, and there is no way to talk to them or pacify them. If you manage to knock them out with non-lethal attacks, the narrator says that they died, even though they didn't, and they remain hostile, which means you can't help them. It's just so lame that the only options are to take the very obvious "good" path, or to fight them to the death, nothing in between.

- Co-op conversations. It's very disappointing that only one player can participate in a conversation. NPCs can interject, but players can't? Not even when it's a non-verbal conversation, like a skill check. A lot of the time I end up just feeling like an NPC during conversations because I can't interact in them in any way, even though my character is standing right there next to the player leading the conversation. To utilize your characters properly, you have to already know what options the conversation will have beforehand.

My tips for any new player are to hammer the quicksave button all the time, avoid stealth builds, and choose only the most obvious conversation options. For co-op, turn on the "eavesdrop" option in the settings, so you don't miss important moments, and try to keep your characters balanced enough to be able to succeed in most skill checks by themselves, since you can't pass the check to another player.
If your not playing this game you might want to rethink your life choices.

This abomination has almost nothing in common with the original Baldur’s Gate titles and should never have been seriously considered for Game of the Year.

Black Isle Studios was an American company that understood what made Baldur’s Gate special. This modern entry comes out of Belgium, and it shows. It feels completely disconnected from the traditional spirit and tone of the series.

The deliberately debilitating camera limitations are a perfect example. You can’t even properly look up. In a modern RPG? Seriously? It feels less like a design decision and more like an artificial restriction that constantly reminds you that you’re fighting the interface instead of exploring the world.

Item and spell descriptions are vague and poorly explained, forcing players into endless trial-and-error loops. Instead of the satisfaction of figuring something out, you’re left repeating the same failures simply because the game couldn’t be bothered to communicate clearly.

And then there’s the lore. Goblins speaking perfect English? Really? Do the developers even know what a goblin is supposed to be in the Baldur’s Gate universe? The world feels like it was stitched together by people who skimmed a wiki instead of actually understanding the setting.

Where are the Gibberlings? Where’s the mad necromancer and his deranged halfling thief? Xzar and Montaron were iconic companions that gave the original games their strange charm. Instead we get characters that are forgettable at best and bizarre at worst.

And what exactly is a Githyanki doing here? It all feels less like faithful Forgotten Realms world-building and more like creative licensing run amok.

This feels less like Baldur’s Gate and more like some unrelated RPG wearing its name like a costume. It’s the equivalent of releasing a Gothic remake with no Shadowbeasts—technically you can do it, but you’ve completely missed the point.

What a waste of time and money.

One of the most disappointing big-budget games I've ever played. The main missions are 90% dialogue and 10% gameplay. Almost every mission consists of traveling to a location, talking to a character, then traveling somewhere else to talk some more. That wouldn't necessarily be a problem if the story stayed engaging after Act 1, but it quickly loses its momentum.

Almost the entire plot revolves around figuring out how to safely remove the biochip that's slowly killing V, yet there's never any real sense of urgency. The story falls into the same repetitive structure for dozens of hours with V doing mercenary favors for a handful of characters, who then promise to give him a lead on removing the chip. You simply follow these breadcrumb trails from one character to the next, with every mission padded by lengthy conversations that have no real meaning. The game constantly pauses to let you choose how to respond, but outside of the ending, very few dialogue choices have any impact and most conversations play out the exact same. For a game that prides itself on player choice, the RPG mechanics are incredibly shallow.

I've played dialogue-heavy games like visual novels and JRPGs, so Cyberpunk simply having a lot of dialogue isn't the issue. The presentation and writing are just so boring and bland that it's difficult to sit through. Every conversation is just you looking at the other character speak in first person, making them all feel the same and drawn out. There are no traditional cutscenes, no cinematic camera angles, and very little physical character animation when talking. The dialogue itself also starts to feel repetitive because almost every character talks the same way. Everyone constantly throws around the same handful of phrases like "preem," "delta," "zero," "choom," and "gonk." The game leans so heavily on its slang that many characters end up sounding interchangeable. A few stand out, but most of the cast feels surprisingly one-dimensional. 

For a game that's so heavily driven by dialogue, the English voice acting is also a letdown. Male V constantly delivers lines in that stereotypical gruff AAA protagonist voice - "gotta find a way to jack in," "maybe there's another way through"... Once you notice it, it becomes hard to ignore. I found Gavin Drea's performance terribly flat, especially considering how much dialogue V has throughout the game. Keanu Reeves doesn't fare much better. His performance often sounds overly restrained, like he's trying to channel John Wick in every scene by speaking in an exaggerated rasp. It's unfortunate that the two voices heard in nearly every conversation are among the weakest performances in the game.

Now, during the 10% of the main missions where you're actually playing a game instead of talking or driving between checkpoints, Cyberpunk is genuinely fun. The gunplay and stealth mechanics are solid, and there's a good variety of weapons and playstyles to experiment with. The stealth gameplay reminded me a lot of the PAYDAY series, with mechanics like marking cameras, distracting enemies, and silently taking guards out one by one. I just wish the game rewarded stealth more often, since carefully clearing an entire area usually takes twice as long as simply shooting everyone for the same outcome. Outside of combat, though, you're mostly walking, waiting for elevators, or searching for power boxes to open doors so you can continue walking.

If you want more gameplay, you're expected to spend time doing side gigs. They're enjoyable at first, but after a handful you've essentially seen everything they have to offer. The same goes for the cyberpsychosis encounters, which amount to fighting dozens of bullet sponge enemies with a large health pool and very little mechanical variety. None of the side content ever becomes particularly challenging or memorable.

Cyberpunk 2077 is an extremely disappointing and repetitive game that loses its appeal shortly after the first act. Its amazing premise and story is buried beneath dozens of hours of repetitive dialogue, terrible voice performances, and excessive padding. While the combat is enjoyable enough, there simply isn't enough of it to carry the experience and it feels like watching a TV show packed with filler.

Good luck with things like Action, Bonus Action, Opportunity Attack and Disengage. And that was just the tutorial.

I really like that all your Actions and Bonus Actions for each character are laid out to you during combat. It’s given me a whole new appreciation of what classes can do in a turn. Especially since it took me about six months of regular sessions of the tabletop version to understand the terms.

Controlling your character to move and interact with the world is really complicated. There are so many buttons to push, interaction options and wheels to pick from. And that’s outside of combat with one character. Things can get really overwhelming.

In my fourth hour of playing, I got my whole party killed. I’m not sure why the combat-difficulty spiked so suddenly, but it did. Every combat encounter in that area was suddenly four times harder. I guess Bethesda isn’t the only company that have no idea what game balance is. It’s the first area of the open world. Calm down.

Combat can be really annoying with how difficult the camera is to use. If there are walls or multiple levels in the area, the camera doesn’t know what to do. And the movement cursor can get very confused when there are multiple objects you can interact with next to the spot you want to move to.

I am sick of how badly ranged attacks work in this game. You try to target an enemy and “sometimes” the game will suggest moving to a good position. Unfortunately, sometimes it suggests “run to the target and fire at point-blank”. When just moving a little closer does the same job. And sometimes the game can’t figure out a clear shot, when manually moving to a good position is easy. I cannot stress enough how irritating the targeting can be and hoping you don’t run out of movement while you reposition.

I didn’t expect almost all of my party members to talk about jumping my bones so quickly in this game. Like, wow. There was the option to accept advances for almost all of them. That was sudden. Even weirder when it felt like they were getting jealous of each other after I accepted with one of them. My goodness, I’ve known you people for three days and we’ve hardly conversed.

This game makes everything feel long. Bloating simple things like moving from place to place. It took me about 30 minutes to find the door to a building with a stupid number of floors, balconies and rooftops. With lots of little containers and items all over it. I’m just looking for the door. It’s so slow-paced that it felt like I barely did anything after an hour.

And that was just Act 1. “The good part” that received “a lot of polish”, according to the community.

Be aware that sometimes set-pieces will break themselves. I’ve had that many scenes that were supposed to start with dialogue, but instead started with combat. I know this because I talk to my friend about this game and he’s informed me about a lot of scenes I’ve accidentally sequence-broke.

Anytime a really cool character is temporarily fighting on your side, you should assume they aren’t good at fighting. This is a reoccurring thing. Oops, the cool character forgot how to fight. Oops, they ran from the boss for random enemies on the opposite side. Oops, they’re down. Oops, they did it all over again every time you attempt the fight. Useless! This game is confusing.

The writing is, well, not the worst thing ever. At least it’s better than what you might see in a more recent Bethesda game. But there has been a lot of “What is even going on?”, “You guys are really stupid” and “Oh, who saw that coming? Everyone” moments.

There is a serious problem with the combat in the late-game. You see, you should be leveling-up to become stronger, gain new combat powers and keep up with enemies. Problem. To keep the game challenging, the devs had the genius idea to make the stronger abilities not reliable against the harder enemies and you’ll end up relying on the weaker attacks. This is really dumb. I feel like I’m playing the game backwards. What’s the point of all these cool abilities if the really hard enemies have very small hit-chances or immunity? I’m either garbage at this game (which I am) or these devs figured this was good enough.

I think I’m starting to understand the weirdness of Balanced (standard) difficulty. I often share stories of my playthrough to because the reactions are humorous and I learn what I missed. I’ve heard just how easy it can be to cheese the heck out of this game. In fact, another friend has also told me similar things. Problem. I don’t know how to do any of those. It’s my first playthrough and I don’t know any overpowered exploits. I can’t do 1000 damage by launching an owlbear or filling a room with grease to burn everything. I guess the default difficulty is so high because the devs expected you to exploit it. Um, hi, regular player, here. I don’t know how to cheat everything! This game is harsh to new players. That is my current understanding of why the difficulty feels so hard.

I made it to the final part of the game. I would say with my sanity, but that wasn’t be for long. It is...awful. It’s awful. It’s the bad combat on steroids. Wow. I am so mentally fatigued from this game that I went to a guide pretty quickly. When will it end? End the game already, please. They forgot to put the game in Cyberpunk.

I've been playing through the story for about six hours now, and I think I've seen half an hour of actual gameplay.
The rest of the time has been spent on the intro, endless dialogues, tutorials, driving sequences (which can run on autopilot — no interaction required), and a “Braindance” — which basically means dragging sliders until the game tells you you've done it right.

At times, it feels like you’re playing a one-button game where you’re constantly pressing the “Next” button. This is often the highlighted dialogue option, opening a menu, walking into a trigger, or buying an item. Considering that you’re basically just pressing “Next” the whole time, the key bindings are absolutely bonkers. For example, there are three different buttons for drawing/holstering your weapon on foot and in a vehicle. Why this isn’t just a simple toggle key is beyond me.

You’re constantly forced to wait: Wait for dialogue, wait for the scanner, wait for a cutscene, wait for an elevator, wait until the NPC has walked somewhere. Think I’m exaggerating? Pay attention to how often the current task says something like “wait for … to happen” or how often you’re presented with a progress bar. The only progress bar I expect to see in games Is the loading screen and that should be as quick as possible.

Combat feels both overloaded and one-dimensional at the same time: You’re shown all kinds of stealth and melee mechanics, but you don’t need them at all — you just end up shooting everyone in the face. If you’re playing stealth, the loop goes: Kill, quicksave, kill, quicksave, quickload if you’re spotted, repeat. And then there’s this thing where the game teases you in the intro that you could perform a simultaneous takedown with your companion. Turns out it’s not part of the missions — it only happens when it’s scripted.

The gunplay is somewhat reminiscent of loot shooters like Borderlands, where enemies are bullet sponges and headshots aren’t lethal. Instead, you end up grinding just to get that one upgrade that lets you reload 20% faster—something you should have from the start, so the gameplay isn’t so terribly sluggish. If you can’t take out an enemy from a distance, you just run right up to them and blast them in the face with the shotgun. In any serious shooter, you’d be dead in seconds. But not in Cyberpunk. And this is on Hard. It’s topped off with a bit of hacking, which means you can make enemies explode or stun them just by clicking on them.

Unfortunately, the story hasn't really grabbed me so far either. There are a lot of people who want to hurt you. You die twice. There's a heist, and they implant some stuff in your brain. That's mainly because of the uninteresting characters. We've got Hispano B.J. Blazkovicz and a handful of other plastic buddies, all of whom are way to talkative and never get to the point. If the dialogue options have serious consequences, the game doesn’t convey that very well.
I experienced a bunch of soft locks already where a npc just would not enter his trigger and the mission would not continue.
[Edit ~20h] In the mission "Never Fade Away" I experienced frequent crashes.

It’s all a real shame, because I thought The Witcher 3 was absolutely fantastic.
The lighting is nice, though. Just like the sound design. It can get a little busy at times. But overall, the technical aspects are pretty good.

I’ll keep on playing. If people say the story is good, there must be something to it. Maybe I’ll find the fun at some point. Maybe John Wick will cheer me up. But then again why does it take a game like this 6 hours to present something interesting? I could have played an entire other game with actual interaction at that time.

[Edit at 10 hours]
I found a scene that’s symptomatic of cyberpunk:
In a brothel, you have a conversation with a prostitute. The goal is to get some information. During this conversation, you’re bombarded with calendar quotes:
“You’re scared because you have given up on your dreams.”
“Not a single thing in this world isn’t in the process of becoming something else.”
“Fear is our weapon in the fight against death.”
"But everything has its end."
The conversation is so generic: if you replace V with $Name and Night City with $Location, you could insert it into any series or game. I suspect you’re supposed to learn something about V’s character, but you don’t. What makes this even more absurd is that you can bypass the scene from the very beginning by saying the safeword (even though you are not in an extreme situation). 
What some might call “building atmosphere,” I consider a waste of time. There are so many games that manage to portray deep characters and atmosphere without trapping you in hours of fluff dialogue.
This scene lasts 5 or 6 minutes. After that, you have to move on to the next cutscene.

[Edit at 32 hours]
The final mission does not have any gameplay either. [spoiler] You can just decide to kill yourself. V probably should have done that right at the start, That would have been a lot less painful. [/spoiler]

When you see the negative reviews from people like me with hundreds and thousands of hours of playtime, that's your signal that something happened. Something went wrong. 
Elden Ring is a masterpiece of a game with excellent story telling and visuals. It's a piece of art that I intend to continue to share with as many people as I can because good art deserves to be seen. So why the negative. 
FromSoftwares parent company recently had a shift in power via a stock buy from a company who has shown anticonsumer interests in the past. Now I'm not going to lie to you about the contents of the 5$ addon. It's something like 5 sets of armor, 2 npc encounters, and 3 cosmetic skins for your steed. These may not be the exact details, and in any other game this would be not the most egregious addon on offer. But this is the first of it's kind in a fromsoft title. It's a canary so to speak. What is more important to me is the history of the addon itself. The addon was a way to move copies for the switch 2. This extra content was exclusive to the switch 2 for a period and is now being allowed to branch out to the other versions. Which is fine, that's how business works. The problem, however, is that the switch 2 copy of elden ring is the exact same price as the shadow of the erdtree bundle. Meaning switch 2 has the new addon content, the dlc, and the base game for 79.99. Everyone else is the ONLY ONES footing the "bill" for this addon content. 
Recently a "community quest" went live. It doesn't matter what the challenges are, the rewards are artwork and twitch badges which irrelevant to the game. This is a blatant bid to boost player count. The company that bought the controlling interest is a hedge fund, more players means higher share price. I'm not fooled and neither should you be. Participate in the quests, there's no harm in playing the game you love. But don't buy the horse armor. It's a trap, a crack in the ice, the first of many needles.

This is hardly the greatest form of activism, but we are all called to do what we can where we are. Elden Ring, along with just about everything else FromSoftware has created, is a solid entry in the canon. There is no denying this. This review has nothing to do with the base game. Yes, I think you know what this is actually about. The ugly little elephant which consistently plagues the gaming industry as well as the many aspects of modern life, I'm afraid. Consolidation of power, income inequality, the end of individual ownership. You see these phenomena play out in all walks of life. And yes, it's infected even the most beloved studios of our day. Perhaps this is inevitable, but this is no reason to give in to mediocrity and extortion.

The implications of "horse armor" need no introduction. Once implemented, they tend to signal a decline in the equitable partnership between player and developer. Bethesda, Ubisoft, EA, Activision, to name the obvious ones. Oh microtransactions. Oh gated content. Oh Pre-order bonuses. "They are totally optional. They are purely cosmetic." "Content" of this kind is completely overwhelming in the space today, so commonplace that few even seem to notice or remember a time before their coercive ubiquity, but those of us who do remember, we are still out here, and we still care. I know whoever decides to read this cares too. And you can do something about it.

As a very simple and free form of activism, I implore you not to buy the new Elden Ring "DLC," or any DLC like this. As others have said, this very well could have been a free update. I hope it goes without saying that no one who loves FromSoft would begrudge giving them money for genuine add-on content to their games. However, we all know this is not coming from the hardworking developers. No, this is yet another push from shareholders to extract what little money you have to spare. It really isn't about $5. It's about the intrinsic and ever diminishing supply of one's own time. It is long overdue that we all reckon deeply with this fact. You're getting older. You don't have as much freedom to do the things you want to do anymore, and as more of life gets behind you, the equation will never pencil out in your favor again. So for all that is good in the Universe, please stop wasting your life.

Wow...where do I even begin?

I want to start by saying that I have nothing but love and respect for Larian.  Divinity: Original Sin 2 is one of my favorite video games of all time, easily top 10 and maybe even top 5, and every time traces of that game shine through in BG3, a genuine smile appears on my face.  Then a moment later I get reminded that this is a D&D game, based on D&D rules, and the smile vanishes, because I realize I could be playing DOSE2 for the 30th time instead and having much, much more fun.

Baldur's Gate 3 sucks, but not because BG3 itself sucks.  Rather, it sucks because only getting to cast 5 fireballs per long rest sucks.  It sucks because having 28 STR and still failing a STR check in act 1 on normal difficulty because the dice decided to f**k you sucks.  It sucks because utility spells like teleports still consume limited per-rest slots even when you cast them outside combat, which limits exploration hard.  BG3 sucks because it's a D&D game with D&D rules, and D&D rules absolutely, completely, and totally suck.  They suck all the fun out of what could have been, and should have been, the greatest game ever made.

And I know this because DOSE2 shows what happens when Larian doesn't have to stick to a D&D rulebook.  DOSE2 is an unequivocally better video game.  In DOSE2, cooldowns are turn-based, which translates to 1 second per turn outside combat.  Thus, when you want to teleport outside combat, then do it again, you just have to wait 8 seconds.  This is long enough to get caught by patrolling enemies, if you plan poorly or just get unlucky, but you can still do it.  Character stats are also made in a way that actually makes sense - if your character has 28 STR and the check only requires 20, you pass the check, period, full stop.  You only have a dice roll when you don't surpass the threshold - so if the check requires 30 STR, THEN you have a chance of failure, but EVEN THEN that chance is based on the difference between your stat and the check.  So in this example, your 28 STR would still give you a 93% chance of success.  In BG3, your odds would either be completely random or a 100% chance of failure, but in DOSE2, you can spend stat points such that even if you can't guarantee success, you can directly dictate what your odds are.

I know a lot of people have said "trust the dice."  Well, I don't.  I tried to.  I've completed Act 1 of this game 3 times now, including every single side quest.  And no less than seven times, my character with 30 in every core stat and advantage in several areas still somehow managed to fail a dice roll.  I'm sorry, but I cheated myself a god character and the game STILL found a way to f**k me over.  Any ruleset that allows a character with maximum stats to fail ANYTHING is an inherently flawed ruleset, whether I trust it or not.

So I'm done with this thing.  I don't regret buying it and won't ask for a refund, but only because I love Larian and I am confident that the next Divinity game will be absolutely, positively amazing.  But I will never play this again.  Never.  Why would I, when I could just play DOSE2 again and have a better experience all around?
Not for me.

And the way her chest bounces as she walks.
And the way you’d absolutely do her in until her infernal engine combusts.
