• Queen Marika – the vessel for the Elden Ring, a goddess elevated by a cosmic deity (the Greater Will). Over time, she began to doubt the established world order and rebelled against her creators.

• Radagon – a red-haired, powerful warrior and champion. Unlike Marika, he was blindly loyal to the Golden Order and the Greater Will.

1. Marriage to Rennala: Radagon goes to war and subsequently marries Queen Rennala, with whom he has children (Ranni, Radahn, Rykard). At the same time, Marika rules from the capital and has children with Godfrey (e.g., Godwyn).

2. Radagon’s Return: After Marika exiles Godfrey, she suddenly summons Radagon back. Radagon abandons Rennala, returns to the capital, and... becomes Marika’s second husband and the new Elden Lord. People in the game world were shocked that a "mere champion" had received such an honor—for they were unaware of his true identity.

3. Divine Incest: The union of Marika and Radagon produces twins—Malenia and Miquella. Born of one and the same god, both have been afflicted by powerful curses since birth (Miquella’s eternal childhood and Malenia’s scarlet rot).

• Marika seeks to destroy the system: She takes up the hammer and shatters the Elden Ring, aiming to free the world from the influence of the Greater Will.

• Radagon seeks to save the system: He seizes control of the same body, grasps the same hammer, and attempts to repair the fractured Ring.

George R.R. Martin—this world is beautiful.

Mohg, Lord of Blood, serves the Formless Mother, for her power manifests through blood. When the Formless Mother’s body is wounded or pierced, "Bloodflame" spurts forth—a burning blood that Mohg wields in combat.

As the son of Queen Marika and Lord Godfrey, Mohg (along with his twin, Morgott) was born an Omen—a being covered in horns, deemed cursed by the ruling Golden Order. Consequently, both brothers were taken from their mother, bound in holy shackles, and cast into the sewers beneath the capital—the Subterranean Shunning-Grounds—to be forgotten forever.

The Formless Mother communicates with the world through blood, and the blood of the Omen serves as an exceptionally potent and appealing conduit for her. The goddess sensed the suffering, the pain, and the powerful blood—amassed in the darkness—of the imprisoned demigod.

The Finger-Eater is responsible for rot, while the Frenzied Flame represents chaos.

All Fingers in the Lands Between were born of a being named Metyr, the Mother of Fingers. Metyr was the first star-born entity sent to the world by the Greater Will, serving as a colossal antenna for receiving divine signals. It was she who gave birth to the Two Fingers, so that they might convey instructions to mortals.

Metyr descended upon the Lands Between in prehistoric times—long before the rise of the Erdtree and the birth of Queen Marika. This was the absolute first epoch in the world's history, often referred to as the pre-Elden era.

World building and exploration: 4/5
Few games have locales and lore as evocative as this game, but the From formula for half-baked lore might be beginning to wear thin. The world is often also too large, and the level design of the open world is... lacking.
Visuals and art direction: 5/5
Every frame a painting. The DLC especially is amazing, visually.
Build variety: 5/5
Never has a From game offered such variety, and it's hard to think of many other games that offer this much, either. Tens of weapon classes, spell schools, lots of armor and talismans, different buffs and synergies to build on - it's great. It's too bad that so much isn't viable in the late game without cheese, but it's difficult to balance so many options.
Dungeons: 3/5
Some legacy dungeons are very good, like Stormveil and Leyndell. But many are incredibly linear, like Farum Azula, and devolve into straight lines.
Enemy variety and quality: 3/5
Enemies are recycled ad-nauseum to fill out the large world, and enemies are often poorly balanced and the over-use of delayed attacks where an enemy (misbegotten, I'm looking at you) will hold their weapons up for 6-7 seconds before finally attacking is just comical, the only way to know what to anticipate is to be subjected to it a few times first. Game design in general is very akin to arcades, where you would have to memorize a pattern, not hone your pattern recoginition and reactions, so that you would die as much as possible and put another coin in. More on this on the bosses.
Bosses: 2/5
Most bosses are bad. Margit, Morgot, Mohg, Godrick, Rellana, Messmer are examples of good bosses that are worth your time to learn, but in a roster with 100+ that's a very poor crop. Input reading is rampant, delayed attacks and 10-hit combos that can only be avoided by failing over and over until you memorize them (or looking up guides) feature in every boss, bosses in general do massive damage, especially towards the end of the game, and their health pools balloon. The end result is that you will spend 90% of the boss fights just watching the boss have fun, before you might be able to get a hit or two in, rinse and repeat. A boss like Malenia is actually really well designed besides two moves, but the moves are telegraphed really poorly and can come out at any time, and if the player's positioning isn't optimal when she decides to do it a non-streamer without 1k hours learning the fight will die and have to try again. But she could also just never do those attacks, you could be lucky. Then you'll beat her since the rest of the toolset is very fair and managable. And Malenia is not alone in this. Radagon is not a particularly fun fight, Elden Beast outright sucks, Fire Giant is absolute bottom tier of From's bosses ever, PCR phase 1 is too basic and phase 2 turns your screen into a white smear where you can't see what he does, Malekith phase 2 spends 80% of his time airborne and untouchable, Metyr is garbage tier, bosses are recycled again and again - even remembrance bosses like the Ancient Spirit, Godrick and Astel. In short it's difficult to say much positive about the bosses as a whole. In previous games, like Bloodborne and DS3, bosses were difficult but fair. There were few gotcha mechanics. The developers did not try to waste your time. Here you should probably look up boss guides before you touch the golden walls since that's a much better use of your time. There's gigantic crutches that a player can whip out to avoid all of the above, like strong spirit ashes or the mimic tear, but they trivialize the boss encounters so much that saying that it is intended to fight them that way just can't be true.

Overall, a good game brought down very low by what has been the highlight of From's previous work: The bosses. They are mostly very bad. Considering how much of the game is centred around overcoming bosses and how much time you will spend fighting them, it's difficult to recommend the game on its merits as a whole. Many players will build their character around a fun use of weaponry and spells they discover as they explore, only to find their build useless against a big chunk of bosses, demanding either a respec or the use of spirit ashes.

Most likely, a new player going in with the viewpoint of bosses as necessary speed bumps filled with visual spectacle that should be overcome with spirit ashes, rather than the absolute highlights of their journey, will have a much better time than most.

Okay so I'm rewriting this review after having played several more hours, and beaten the first 3 main boss fights. Of course, all opinions are my own, and it's very subjective as to what a "good" playstyle is. 

     My biggest problem with the game is the combat, which obviously significantly hinders my experience with such a combat-focused game/genre. It feels generally "clunky" to me, not smooth and intuitive. Not to say that the motions aren't smooth, they are, it's more so that you can't adapt as frequently as I think you should be able to during a battle. 

     So for example, in the first main boss battle with a guy named Margit, I would like to run in when there's an opening, get a few strikes in, and then dodge out of the way when he's about to strike. However, one thing that this game doesn't do that I think it really should is give command priority. So I might strike 3 times, but right after I try to strike for the 3rd time, I realize Margit is about to strike and my hit won't land, so I need to doge early and cancel my strike. But because you already pressed the attack button, you can't doge until the game finishes that strike. So what happened is I ended up playing very conservatively, only risking a maximum of two hits before running away. Having to play that reserved makes the fight drag on and isn't necessarily overly difficult, it just feels boring to me. 

     Another thing I found very infuriating, especially with Margit, is the insane amount of variability in the time between the start and execution of an attack. Sometimes Margit raises his weapon and strikes immediately, the next try he raises it and strikes 3 seconds after holding in the air doing nothing, the next attempt he does it for 5 seconds. Again this contributes to only getting one or two hits in when sometimes you could get 5 or 6 in, but because you don't know, you have to play conservatively instead. 

     Now the second boss's attack pattern was actually much more intuitive for me. He had the right amount of variability. Not the exact same script, which would be too easy, but not the insane range of variance that Margit had. Sadly, the third boss, felt exactly like Margit all over again. Just a frick ton of attacks, then a short window to get a few hits in, then back to dodge city. 

     Which leads me to my next point: repetitiveness. See, all three of these bosses have felt extremely similar, just each one having subsequently faster attacks. Godrick's (the second boss) pattern differed, for the better, but it still followed the same principal of needed to overuse dodge's a bunch, be very conservative, and keep doing the same thing for 5 minutes. I found it boring. Essentially, up to the third boss anyways, the game's battles felt very "same-y". 

     Now, the last big thing I'll point out is the game's exploration. It doesn't make me want to go explore the world at all, and when I have gone exploring, the world feels very "empty" to me, to say the least. Most of the people you encounter are either enemies (which are trivially easy and repetitive), and the NPCs you encounter, at least by 10 hours into the game still, are few and far between. Plus they're just not very interesting. 

     I also think the entire UI, specifically the Inventory and Equipment menus etc., are overly complicated but that's a nitpick, once you get used to them they aren't that bad. 

     Overall, I just think the game's combat is too repetitive, clunky, and the exploration is very lackluster. Even if the game gets a lot more interesting as it progresses, I still feel confident leaving this review now, as a game shouldn't need more than 10 hours to hook you. Steam's refund policy even suggests that Valve believes hours should be plenty of time to understand if a game is good or not, but at the same time, I do understand the appeal, after all I've played for 10 hours now.

All is forgiven, Polish devs. But is it? As much as there is about Cyberpunk 2077 that I like and as much as I respect the support CD Projekt Red continued to put into it. We need to talk about the massive elephant in the room that never actually left. Borrowed time.

Majora's Mask is probably one of the most famous examples of making time itself part of the gameplay. Even though its three day loop, that doomsday clock is always ticking. The player constantly understands that time has value. For more modern examples, look at games like The Blood of Dawnwalker or Kingdom Come Deliverance II. Neither necessarily hangs one giant doomsday clock over the player in the same way. Instead, time becomes part of the player's agency. Dawnwalker gives you a limited amount of time before the endgame, with quests and major actions advancing that clock. Deliverance II takes a more situational approach, where certain quests and events will move forward without you if you wait too long. Personally, I think Deliverance II takes this idea a little too literally. Persona 5 is another great example. You have a limited calendar and have to decide how to spend it. Do you improve a relationship? Work on yourself? Explore the palace? Prepare for the next major confrontation? All of these systems are asking the player some variation of the same question. What are you going to do with the time you have? And Cyberpunk presents one of the strongest possible versions of that question. When you're dying, what do you do with your time?

Apparently nothing. Get up samurai, we're going drag racing. Get up samurai, we're clearing every gig and side mission on the entire map. Get up samurai, we're going bowling. This is the massive elephant that I don't think gets criticized nearly enough. The story presents V with a very simple and horrifying problem. You are dying. Your life is disintegrating in front of you. The writing becomes emotional. Relationships start forming. People begin attaching themselves to V. Johnny is slowly taking over. Every lead toward a possible cure should feel increasingly desperate. Your entire story is supposedly happening on borrowed time. And then Cyberpunk almost immediately throws that idea out the window. The clock doesn't actually exist. Take as long as you want. Do every gig. Help every fixer. Buy every car. Make every friend. Finish every companion storyline. Explore every corner of Night City. Eventually, whenever you finally feel like it, go choose your ending.

That's not meaningful agency. That's a story telling you that your time is valuable while the game design simultaneously tells you that your time is infinite. And that creates a massive disconnect. Your relationships with people begin to lose weight. Desperately taking gigs because you need money to upgrade your cyberware stops meaning anything because... why not just do everything? Eventually you'll be swimming in money anyway. The writing constantly asks for an emotional response from the people around V. Meanwhile, V suppresses the biggest problem in their life, another identity is literally eating away at their mind, their body, and eventually their entire existence. That should hang over everything. Every relationship. Every choice. Every job. Every conversation with Johnny. Instead, the uncertainty loses its weight. The confrontations with Johnny lose some of their urgency because, at the end of the day, who cares? Johnny, you and me are going bowling, again.

Once again, modders enter the scene. Modders add an actual doomsday clock, progressing V's deterioration according to the in-game passage of time. Other mods add life sim elements like eating, drinking, sleeping and generally maintaining yourself. The most baffling thing about all of this is that the foundations for these systems are already sitting inside the game. There are food vendors everywhere. Vending machines everywhere. You have a bed. You have showers. You can buy multiple apartments and living spaces. These places are presented like somewhere V can return to, decompress, sleep, shower, eat, and temporarily escape Night City. But for what? The game has all these little pieces suggesting that V is supposed to be living in Night City while simultaneously dying inside it, yet almost none of them carry any real mechanical consequence. And that becomes even stranger when you consider how heavily the writing emphasizes borrowed time. Every new person V grows attached to is potentially someone they're going to lose. Every relationship V builds is happening under the shadow of an approaching death. Every lead toward a cure should matter because another day wasted is another day gone. But without any meaningful passage of time, that shadow never really moves. And that's why, even after all the updates, all the fixes, Phantom Liberty, and everything CD Projekt Red poured into this game, part of Cyberpunk 2077 still feels half cooked to this day.

One of the biggest contradictions is still sitting there at the heart of V's story. Untouched. Unfixed. They wrote about a person discovering that their life suddenly has an expiration date, but never implemented the one element that could have made that premise truly meaningful. Your life is supposed to be on borrowed time. The grim story of a dystopian hell where one person is desperately trying to find some meaning in the trash heap around them loses much of its weight when the game refuses to make time matter. For all the work CD Projekt Red has done rebuilding Cyberpunk 2077, this contradiction has been sitting there since the beginning.

Recommended | 70 hours

Geralt of Rivia has two swords, one facial expression, and somehow more emotional range than most RPG protagonists with a full dialogue wheel.

Who is it for? Everyone. If you've never played an RPG, this is a good place to start. If you've played fifty, you'll still find something here.

Story and quests. This is where the game earns its reputation. The main story is strong, but the side quests are the real show. A contract to kill some random monster turns into a family tragedy, a village feud, and a moral dilemma where every option feels slightly wrong. Other games give you "collect 10 wolf pelts." The Witcher gives you "collect 10 wolf pelts, discover the wolves were a cursed family, reconsider your life choices."

Worldbuilding. Velen, Novigrad and Skellige feel lived in. Peasants complain, soldiers are bastards, and everyone has a reason to be miserable. It's bleak in a way that's oddly charming.

Graphics and sound. With the next-gen update it still looks great. The soundtrack is excellent, especially in Skellige, where the music does half the storytelling.

Gameplay and combat. Exploration and questing are excellent. Combat is the weak link. It's mostly roll, hit twice, roll again, cast Quen, repeat until the drowner dies or you do. Progression is underwhelming too. Most level-ups give you small percentage boosts that you won't notice, and gear is level-locked enough that you'll carry a legendary sword around for ten hours before you're allowed to use it.

Performance. Ran smoothly for me, no notable issues.

Value. Worth full price, and the DLCs are worth buying too. Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine aren't filler; they're some of the best content in the game. Whatever you think of CD Projekt Red's other launches, they got this one right.

Pros

Outstanding side quests
Strong main story
Rich, believable world
DLCs are excellent value

Cons

Repetitive combat
Flat, unrewarding progression
Gwent will consume more of your time than the actual war

Bottom line: Come for the monster hunting, stay for the side quest about a baron's family that ruins your evening. Ten silver out of ten.

Rockstar's most refined skinner box. GTA Online has interesting aspects but is ultimately dragged down by greed and spaghetti code. Recent events may come to mind, but the reality is that the writing has been on the wall. Shark cards were always around, servers were peer-to-peer, shareholders had their meetings. It was only a question of "How" Rockstar will try to screw over players, not "If" or even "When". 

As a skinner box, GTA Online acts somewhat like an idle game: Spend time to build up your resources, and use those to get more resources. Higher rank means more weapons and health, higher stats give small but useful benefits, more money lets you buy more content to play as well as more methods to make money. It contrasts from traditional idle games by... being GTA, so to speak.

Of course, the fundamental flaw here is that Rockstar doesn't respect your time. No, it might be better to say that GTA Online is designed to waste as much of your time as possible while you try to make progress. The various businesses players can purchase will take several hours to fill up to capacity, but can easily have all product turned to dust with raids or by encouraging the entire lobby to sabotage sell missions. 

The heists are the best and worst part of Online. The most interesting content by far, self-sabotaged by legacy code, greed, and plain old bad game design. Enemies randomly firing off their entire magazine in one short burst, limited healing that can only be refilled in free roam, challenges that can't be retried from checkpoint, damage reducing payout and said reductions carrying over between checkpoint restarts, and full restarts only being possible by exiting the heist entirely and going back to free roam. 

Not to mention the jury-rigged stealth mechanics that never get fully explained AND have variable rules every time they appear. Some stealth encounters require you to stay pacifist (and don't tell you), and others have guards with a 0 second delay before they alert everyone. Even in the new Kortz Center Heist, the stun gun is silent for the entire heist until you exit the building, where it's so loud that even using a melee takedown will alert guards halfway across the map. 

The two most recent heists, Cayo Perico and the Kortz Center, have severe tonal dissonance. Even ignoring the numbers, they fail to live up to the fantasy of looting of a large island or museum. You can put in the time and effort to do every prep mission, clear every guard and avoid every camera, but in the end each person can only carry a handful of loot. It silently begs the question: Is it really a heist if you leave so much behind?

Rockstar is never going to fix that dissonance, nor do they care to. With the recent patch that came with the Kortz Center Heist, it's clear that Rockstar does not want players to experience GTA Online in any way they please. They want sessions to be weekly, they want players to wait on timers before playing, and they do not want people to experience everything too fast without putting real cash in. 

Considering this is the Legacy version's review, it's worth noting how horribly unstable the netcode is. Infinite loading screens make it nearly impossible to play for half an hour without needing to restart after entering/exiting an interior, moving to a new session, or entering/exiting any mission. Even years ago it wasn't great, but trying to play this recently felt like all the exaggerations you could make about bad netcode coming true.

Even before this patch, I wouldn't recommend getting into GTA Online. It asks for a lot of time and effort from you without giving nearly as much in return. If you really have to play it, find a way to bypass the grind (not with shark cards) and only do whatever catches your eye.

If you're crazy about idle games that hate you but love your wallet, maybe play it. Otherwise, find another game.

I don't hate Grand Theft Auto V. I had fun with it, but after 239.4 hours, I eventually realized how repetitive the experience had become. GTA V was once something I could easily spend hours playing, but over time, the appeal faded & the game started feeling less like entertainment and more like an endless checklist.

GTA Online has an enormous amount of content, but that doesn't necessarily make all of it meaningful. You earn money, buy something, use it to earn more money, unlock another item, complete another activity, then repeat the same process. There is always another vehicle, property, business, outfit, weapon, cosmetic, event, achievement, or collectible waiting for you.

Eventually, I started asking myself: what am I actually working toward?

The biggest problem is the pursuit of exclusive & rare content. GTA Online has accumulated years of limited-time items, event rewards, promotional content, rare vehicles, clothing, liveries, tattoos, collectibles & other items. Some can still be obtained through specific requirements or returning events, while others have been removed or are no longer normally obtainable.

That creates a strange situation where someone can spend hundreds of hours trying to build the "perfect" collection, only to discover that something they wanted was tied to an event from years ago.

If the item is no longer obtainable, there is no amount of grinding that can get it back.

That's what makes the completionist mentality particularly frustrating. You're not simply trying to finish a game. You're trying to keep up with an ecosystem that has been evolving for years, while some of its history is permanently locked behind time-limited availability.

And even the items that remain obtainable can require an enormous investment of time.

For example, GTA Online's money-making activities often involve cooldowns, preparation missions, travel, matchmaking, setup, completion, & repetition. Even one of the game's major solo money-making activities has a cooldown between finales. Multiply that type of waiting & repetition across the countless things a player might want to purchase, unlock, or collect, and the hours add up very quickly.

My 239.4 hours alone equal roughly 9.98 full days of continuous time.

That's almost ten entire 24-hour days of my life spent inside Los Santos.

And that's only the recorded gameplay time.

It doesn't include time spent researching how to obtain items, watching guides, waiting for events, comparing prices, sitting through loading screens, or deciding what to do next.

That's where the opportunity cost becomes impossible for me to ignore.

I'm not saying video games need to be productive. They're entertainment, and entertainment has value. But once a game stops being entertaining & you're continuing only because you've already invested so much time, it becomes worth asking whether that time is better spent elsewhere.

GTA Online can make that especially difficult because there is always something else to obtain.

You can never quite be finished.

Another update arrives.

Another vehicle is released.

Another business becomes available.

Another event begins.

Another exclusive item appears.

Another achievement becomes something to chase.

Then the cycle starts again.

One sequence of the game eventually replaces another.

And eventually, Grand Theft Auto VI will replace this generation's attention with a new world, new characters, new gameplay systems, new content & potentially another online ecosystem to explore. Rockstar currently lists GTA VI for November 19, 2026.

That's not a criticism of GTA VI. It's simply the natural progression of the franchise.

My concern is how much time people can spend trying to completely exhaust an older game before moving on.

You could spend hundreds of hours collecting vehicles, grinding money, unlocking cosmetics & pursuing exclusives, only for the next Grand Theft Auto to arrive & give everyone another massive world full of things to collect.

The sequence never really ends.

That's why I'm no longer interested in chasing every GTA V exclusive simply because I don't have it.

If an item is available, great.

If I miss it, I'm not going to let a virtual item dictate how I spend my time.

Some people genuinely enjoy collecting everything, and that's perfectly fine. But for me, the collection itself eventually became more burdensome than rewarding.

I also don't think GTA V deserves to be treated as a bad game because of this criticism. It has had an enormous impact on gaming, GTA V's single-player campaign remains memorable, & GTA Online has maintained an extraordinary amount of content for years.

My criticism is much simpler:

There is such a thing as having too much of a good thing.

After 239.4 hours, the repetition became difficult to overlook.

The game went from:

"What should I do today?"

to:

"What else do I still need to unlock?"

That distinction matters.

At some point, you're no longer playing because you genuinely want to. You're playing because there's another box left unchecked.

And I don't want a game to become a second job.

My last session was December 2, 2024, and I'm comfortable leaving it there.

I don't regret every hour I spent in GTA V. I had fun, experienced the world, played with other people & made memories. But I also recognize that my time has value, and I don't want to spend hundreds more hours chasing increasingly obscure items simply because the game provides an endless list of things to obtain.

Grand Theft Auto V was fun, but it became repetitive.

GTA Online has more content than most players could reasonably exhaust, yet that abundance can also become the problem.

With GTA VI arriving, I'm choosing not to spend more of my time trying to complete an ecosystem that was never designed to truly end.

Let me get this straight. This is definitely not a game for a broad audience. This game is for D&D lovers. If you've never played D&D, just skip it. Now, let's go through some specific points.

**1. The game is slow**

And when I say it's slow, I'm not talking about the kind of slow that builds atmosphere, like in *Red Dead Redemption 2*, where you're riding your horse and actually feel like a real cowboy. No. *Baldur's Gate 3* is slow in a negative sense.

Every time you fight, you have to move from point A to point B, then wait while all the AI on the map does the same thing, and then you press the "Attack" button only for your opponent to dodge. These fights are long, and they're not interesting at all.

When you finish a fight, you start looting bodies and containers, and believe me, you'll spend HOURS of your playthrough managing your inventory. In most RPGs, you often find valuable loot that helps your progression, but in BG3 you can spend hours without finding a single useful weapon for your main character (or you find the same weapon with +1 damage).

Progression and combat are not rewarding at all.

But the biggest source of "slowness" is the D&D dice system. Believe me, you'll reload your save file a lot. Like... A LOT. You'll spend hours staring at loading screens.

This brings me to my second point. Also, whenever you want to do anything in combat, you need to press a button and then click on a target. Sometimes I click a skill, miss the target by a little bit, and hit empty space instead. That can literally cost me the fight. Guess what you have to do then? Reload your save.

The game has a lot of randomness because of the D&D mechanics. You have 10 Intelligence, need to pass an Intelligence check, and the required roll is 12. You roll a 1. Nice. Guess what? Reload your save. And you do it hundreds, if not thousands, of times.

**2. The game is overwhelming**

You don't have one character who progresses through the game and upgrades their gear. You have an entire party.

Unlike *Clair Obscur*, for example, where you start with one character and gradually recruit others, BG3 fills your four party slots very quickly.

And if you have at least one mage or cleric—good luck. These classes have tons of skills. You need to spend so much time reading and remembering everything that it starts to feel like a second job.

You also have four separate inventories to manage. Inventory management is a huge pain. You find an item, read its description, transfer it to the right character, equip it, and then sometimes realize you can't even use it.

**3. The writing and style are just mid**

I'm talking about two things here: the writing and the world design.

I'm not talking about the story because I dropped the game during Act 1, so I can't really judge it. But from what I saw, it felt like very basic fantasy without anything special. The dialogue is on the same level as Marvel movies—simple writing with occasional jokes.

As for the style, the game doesn't really have one. If you look at *Disco Elysium*, for example, you can immediately tell there's nothing else quite like it. If you look at other top-tier fantasy franchises, they usually have a unique visual identity and a distinctive world.

*Baldur's Gate 3* just feels generic to me.

I don't have much else to say about that.

The Witcher 3 was my favourite game when I first played it on PS4. It remained my favourite game when I played it again and again with mods on Steam. Eventually, I branched out into other Witcher media, from the earlier Witcher 1 and 2 to the spin-off Thronebreaker, and eventually, the books. What began as my favourite game had developed into my favourite fantasy series.

It has its problems, for sure, particularly with bugs, texture and lighting pop-ins that persist even with mods and hotfixes. Some of these issues are addressed in the remastered edition, while others are exacerbated. But beneath all those technical quirks lies a once-in-a-lifetime gaming experience that will suck you into a universe that is uniquely dark, yet profoundly human.

The story, obviously, remains the highlight of the game. The unbelievable amount of freedom the devs give players to interact with their stories remains jaw-dropping even today (some would argue especially today). This approach applies not only to the main quest but also to the hundreds of small, 30-second-to-two-minute interactions you can stumble upon at every turn of the road, each capable of either singeing your conscience or tugging at your heartstrings. This is where I personally feel The Witcher 3's greatest strength lies, and it's something that, in my opinion, isn't talked about nearly enough.

A typical game might focus on a specific tone or a predefined moral spectrum that guides and restrains its characters' actions. This often works in service of the story or gameplay, but it can also make the experience forgettable, largely because of a lack of emotional fluctuation when most characters are predictable and seemingly operate on the same wavelength. What The Witcher 3 has effectively done, however, is create a striking contrast between its characters—a chiaroscuro of storytelling, if you may.

The game repeatedly reinforces that the Witcher world is a dark and grim one, where only evil and something worse exist. It is through the lens of this chaos that even a small spark of humanity can feel like salvation, reigniting your hope in this world. From a granny who takes in war orphans to the genuine gratitude of farmers who thank you for your services, the game does a wonderful job of reminding you why Geralt would uphold a standard of personal integrity, why he cares for the people he's defending, and why he, again and again, inserts himself into someone else's troubles, often at great personal cost. All this despite the nasty name-calling, the prejudice, and the vile acts he witnesses.

A spark of light is only as bright as the darkness around it, and this game is a perfect encapsulation of that. This is why I recommend the game.

I wish I could give a neutral review, but as i cannot and because most reviews are positive, I'm selecting a thumbs down. I won't get into the positives as other reviews expound on those aplenty. I do not think it is a bad game, just not a very good one either.

First of all and most importantly, this game is often described as being open world and having a heavy emphasis on freedom and choice. This left me very disappointed. I've played through most of the game (did not finish it, more on why later) over 200+ hours,  and it's actually very linear. Unlike in BG1-2 especially 2 where you can explore anywhere, constant cliffs, walls, gorges and roadblocks that box you in. Sure, there's a couple of alternate paths with small new areas, but not much. And this gets only worse over time - Act 1 is the most open but really still isn't, and 2 in particular is very locked down.

Linearity aside, Act 2 started to pull a good story together but it fell off hard in Act 3, which takes place almost entirely in Baldur's Gate. It should have been the high point of the game, but the city is boring, samey, little of interest to do, and the story gets a lot more boring. It was so jarring, that I left Act 2 hopeful and excited for the story but stopped playing not long after. I played through Raphael's house and got too bored with the story to continue much more. I don't know what the ending is and don't care tbh. Act 3 also performs badly, even with the native build update for Steam Deck it performs well under 30 fps. That was disappointing.

The characters were also mostly medicore. Gale and Wyll are boring, Gale even being insufferable. Shadowheart has a cool story arc in Act 2 but she consistently remains unlikeable despite being the "I can fix her". Karlach feels very unserious, like an irl person playing in a dnd session rather than a real character (though this does make her a great choice as an origin character), and it's a bit immersion breaking. Very OOC. Lae'zel is another "I can fix her" but she is very abrasive, nasty and constantly racist which put me off hard. Halsin's entire appeal is him being a literal bear, he's hot but uninteresting. Jaheira and Minsc i can't say much about as I never got them in my party.

However, the drow (wont say the name for spoilers) has a really interesting hidden arc on a good playthrough and is well-done as a character. And I have nothing but praise for Astarion and his questline, which went places I didn't expect and revealed a lot of his character depth and who he is and made me really like him and want to care for him.

Overall, the game isn't bad but also isn't that great and is very overrated and overhyped. It's unfortunately linear, with a very disappointing Baldur's Gate itself (the city). The companions are mostly uninteresting and overpraised. Sleeping with Raphael's incubus was really hot though

10/10 - A must play for all gamers

GAMEPLAY
--------------

As close to perfect RPG gameplay as we have ever seen. Every single situation can be resolved in what feels like thousands of ways. Whether it's ridiculous cheese or clever party tactics. The roleplay potential is incredible, with every race, class, and then subclass having unique dialogue/in-dialogue action options in many conversations. The build variety is amazing, especially with multi-classing. You can go the traditional Warlock/Wizard caster or Barbarian Bruiser route; or whip out the excel sheet and create a multi-class demon that excels at your ultra-specific playstyle. Considering you can have 3 other party members, this adds so much gameplay/combat potential that it'll make your head spin if you try to consider all the possibilities. You can approach encounters in pretty much anyway you want; whether that's teleporting targets in-between your damage dealers, going invis for stealth, shapeshifting, sending someone to talk to the target while you attack their allies, dropping 50 fire barrels from your inventory on their head, spamming arrows from the high ground, cheesing them with CC, the list goes on forever. There is definitely a learning curve if you have never played D&D or the like, but starting the game on "Easy" and watching a YT video is really all you need. I recommend playing a little first, then watching a video, as the terms and info dump are hard to contextualize without exp in-game.

STORY
--------------

But a massive RPG is dependent on it's story and companions. BG3 has excellent female companions, with Lae'zel and Shadowheart being the most interesting and with the best questlines. The other recruitable female companions are good too, with interesting backstories and dialogue options. And this is all without their romance questlines, which are all quite well-done. But the male companions are where the game kind of suffers. Gale, Astarion, and Wyll especially, are just kind of annoying. Their questlines are all pretty interesting so it is worth completing them, but I found myself leaving them in camp in further runs. They come on to you pretty quickly as well, even if you are already progressing another party members romance. These companions never really hinder the game, but I definitely would have preferred a few more stoic, less quippy type male characters. There is a companion you can recruit who is a bit more serious, but that is late into the game. Regardless, completing your parties questlines and hearing their interactions with you and others were some of my favorite moments in the narrative. There is a very immersive element to hearing your party members talk to each other and mention their surroundings or past events without your input. 

The main story is great, with the voice acting and character models being stellar. I would have preferred a slower or more grounded start to the game and overall story, but that is just personal preference and others might enjoy a more epic fantasy tale which the game has. The ending cutscenes feel a little rushed and it would have been great to have more options when it comes to who you have to fight, but these are pretty excusable considering the rest of the games story. 


OVERALL
------------

After more than 350 hours in Baldur’s Gate 3, I can confidently say: this game is phenomenal.

What makes it so special is the freedom it gives you. You can talk your way through trouble, sneak past it, fight it head-on, or try something ridiculous and discover that the game actually allows it. Exploring different approaches is part of the fun, and the world’s reactions make your decisions feel meaningful.

The writing and performances deserve enormous praise. Characters have personality, conflicting motivations, and enough depth to make conversations worth paying attention to. Even smaller encounters can turn into memorable stories. There is so much care in the dialogue, environments, and little details that exploration feels rewarding beyond simply finding better equipment.

The combat is another highlight. Positioning, terrain, preparation, and the interaction between abilities give battles plenty of tactical depth. A clever plan can completely change an encounter, while a terrible plan can lead to something hilariously memorable. Experimenting with classes and builds adds another layer of enjoyment—and another reason to start a new character.

The replayability is incredible. Different choices, party compositions, and approaches give you reasons to revisit the adventure. This is a huge game, but its appeal goes beyond its size: it gives you room to make the experience your own.

It does ask for some patience. There are systems to learn, plenty of dialogue, and decisions that can keep you staring at the screen while you consider the possibilities. For me, that is a big part of the appeal. It is a game worth taking your time with.

More than 350 hours is probably the strongest recommendation I can give. Baldur’s Gate 3 combines tactical combat, fantastic storytelling, and an extraordinary amount of player freedom into something truly special.

Overall, one of my favorite games of all time. 

Source Material: I love the Witcher books and comics, and this game is a very good adaptation that respects the source material. There will be some "uhm-acktually" redditors that will tell you how this game does things differently than the books, but no one likes those people. Compared to the TV show, this is an AMAZING adaptation. There are plenty of references to the source material that attempt to expand on what has been planted. For example, all the different Witcher schools, the progression of the Nilfgard v North Realms war, the development of Ciri as a person. So many interpretations that I feel did the source material great justice.

Story: The main plot is okay, but that is because the real emotion and depth of this game lies in the side missions/quests and exploration. So many of the side quests are extremely interesting, emotional, and fun. Something you learn from this game, that is brought up a lot in the books, is that there is rarely one correct answer. Or in other words, most situations are not black and white. The moral-dilemmas this game puts you through are things I wish I could mimic in my own writing.

Combat: Probably the most contraversial topic for this game. I personally like the combat. Yes, like all RPGs, if you min/max and grind all the side content, you will be over-powered regardless of what difficulty setting you are on. I recommend you try to implement, swords, signs, potions, and bombs equally into your combat style. This is what makes you feel like a true Witcher. Of course if you make a 100% Sign build with maxed out armor and skills, then of course you're gunna mow people down with Signs. Read the beastiary for additional hidden tips for fighting monsters and try them out! 

Finally, I highly encourage you to treat this game like a savory steak that you take at your own pace. Don't just sweep through every region going to all the points of interest. This makes it more of a chore than a game. Take your time and do what interests you.

[h2][u] Regarding the remaster [/u][/h2]

I'm mostly going to address the things I find most critical (good or bad) in the remaster, and I'll start with the most glaring thing; Visuals: Yes. They are very well touched up, color-wise especially, everything seems to 'pop' a bit more. And if what you were looking for out of a remaster was a visual boost, I think it will scratch that itch.

As for gameplay; to be honest, I was underwhelmed by the changes. The movement is the highlight, as jumping no longer has that some-milliseconds delay that plagued it before, and it legitimately feels easier to move around... but that's it. A large chunk of changes are in camera angles, and I found myself reverting to their original counterparts within an hour of play--they feel too zoomed in and offset. It feels distinctly '[i]different[/i]' but that's where it begins and ends, it's not meaningful, and feels FoV limiting. Otherwise, the combat aspect is only really altered by a reworked skill tree system, which still unfortunately uses the vanilla 'slot' system that limits you to a 3x3x3x3 system (pre-DLC) 12 perk total system. So how is it different? A large number of the skills are altered or brand new, Mostly meaning that their effects are from the original game's perks that are combined, or they have all-new effects, including but not limited to: stacking instant-kill percentages; sign intensity increases after light or heavy attacks; increased crossbow damage (which finally feels viable). Apart from the crossbow bit, it largely feels like a mix/match and combination of old skills to make having the same skill amount feel more in-depth, which works to an extent but still, to me, feels lackluster as it didn't address the core issue of feeling limited by a lack of overall slots.

I also have to say that more than a few of the control changes don't feel 'improved'. Horse controls feel less responsive than they did originally. And additionally, the 'modern' lock-on controls feel poorly executed -- to detail, they tried to improve group combat by creating a 'soft lock-on' when you don't use the full lock-on control that sticks the camera to one enemy, but it practice, it has a habit of being too sticky, and many times I found myself swinging at an enemy in the opposite direction that I was intending, regardless of stick direction (yes I play this with a controller, scold me all you like).

Thankfully, many of the 'modern' control and camera changes can be reverted to their original designs, in the event they don't mesh well with you, so that at least is not an overt issue.

Ultimately I would consider this a good remaster. However, it still feels like a [u]heavily[/u] outdated game that was arguably outdated in some major aspects at the time it was originally launched. But, it's a CD:PR game, if the visuals and gameplay don't keep you around, the story probably will. And for me, it does.

I have to preface this and say that this is my first soulslike experience. Elden ring videos and players promise hard gameplay, great story, and cinematic experience. In reality? It's [b]unmeasurable disappointment[/b] on several fronts.

My first issue is that this game was supposed to be made for controllers. You'd think with controllers your movement would be optimized with omnidirectional movement, variable speed, etc. No. No it is not. Too simple of concepts for these simple devs. In order to sprint in this game you have to hold the same button you dodge with (B as I'm on Xbox controller). So if you were to do something as simple as dodge while running, you have to hold the direction and quickly release and tap your dodge button again. This is already awkard of a movement and you'd think it'd be fixed in early builds of the game. Nada. On top of this awkward movement, your dodge actually only starts once the dodge button is released. This wonderfully stupid idea of a mechanic makes reactive playstyles (what'd you'd expect to play as a game centered around boss fights) useless. The amount of time it takes for you to actually do what you inputed is elongated by dumb design. This leads to another problem later on. [i]I'm just gonna forego the horrible auto-lock and let other players tell you about that dumpster fire.[/i]

My second issue is FPS being locked. 60hz is stone age. People have to spend $60 to get this game (crazy ik). When you can get a 60+fps monitor for $80. Let's think here, are your customers going to say "God I hope this cinematic game is locked at 60fps". Seriously unless you're a foot in the grave you can see the slop that is 60 fps. Did you buy a actual monitor? Something beyond 60fps? Yikes you're going to see some stuttering if your hz isn't divisible by 60 f*cking fps or has freesync. Now in the defense of this game, I understand that the game is based around the 60fps for engine reasons and for console players. Yet, WHY is it 60 fps when ported to PC. I'm writing this review 4 years later and there is still no support for higher framerates. Dollar per frame game.

My third issue, difficulty. This game isn't "hard", it's tedious. I started playing this game in hopes of dodging bosses last second, paying attention to a flurry of attacks as they came out, and getting bested because I lacked the mechanical skill to beat a boss. Reality? This game has THE MOST BORING BOSS FIGHTS. Let me explain. Every boss has movepools.  Which when learned make the boss easier, but Elden Ring makes it BORING. However, the fun should lie in going against new bosses right? Maybe getting lucky and beating them first try? Well unless it's one of the billion copy print dungeons with bosses that might as well be 2D for the lack of depth to them, you're going to die (probably in those dungeons too). You'll be hit with a move you can't properly dodge because well you've never seen it before.Or even worse, you have yet the timing is slightly different, with extensions of range or attack(s). Some people may not have a problem with this whole "see a new move, die and come back pattern". And to those people I say, "Keep flipping those burgers." The allure in bossfighting games is making yourself a betterplayer. One able to become better in any situation as you progress. Not dying 2-3, 4 times before you get the boss to a next phase where you'll have to repeat the same steps. This loop? It's not skillful dodges, parrying, or anything cool like that. It's just dying, learning, and coming back. That is profoundly boring. If all your bosses can just simply be put into a youtube video devolving strategies to counter every situation, you didn't make a skillfull game, you made a knowledge gap. [u]Seriously the bosses might as well be a quizlet looking at each boss's attacks like flashcards and memorizing.[/u]

And you'd know I'd take it all back if the story was redeeming. Stories can carry bad gameplay after all. But truth be told you won't really even learn the story in this game. You have to go OUT of your way to find what this game is about. Other RPGs I've played such as Fallout 4, Cyberpunk 2077, Pokémon, all find ways to sprinkle in story if you just go a little bit off the game's main course. This game? You pretty much need a guide to get a inkling of it at all. You will have many questions when the game starts and as it progresses, you'll just have more and more. It's hard to find motivation to do quests with characters you know nothing about. This game doesn't motivate you to do anything, you pop in the world, you look around a bit, and you're confused. I understand that it is a game for adults, so make the story a bit complex. However at the start of the game, you as a protagonist get the sole goal of becoming the Elden Lord from a good cutscene. Now it may just be me, but [u]why does it sound like we're setting up a tv show?[/u] Could it be that it just said a bunch of characters nobody knows, gave the tiniest amount of backstory that you don't really understand, and had a vague direction? Maybe...maybe. But surely this is a good story. It will tell you a bit more as you start the game... Yeah no, this game has bad storytelling. Not necessarily a bad story I hear if you have thousands of hours to waste reading every item, replaying for minute things you missed because the game [b] Doesn't Have Story Direction [/b]. My advice F-Soft, narrow the guage just a little bit more so people can know why they should give a crap. Then the whole discover the lore thing works. 

But hey, if all that sounds appealing to you, go ahead and pay your $60 for 60fps. Have fun wasting your time memorizing an interactive textbook everyone else has already read, memorized, condensed, and posted the results of online.

470 hours, every achievement, Honour Mode included, and I'm still not convinced I've seen everything.

Baldur's Gate 3 is the most reactive game I've ever played. Almost every problem has four solutions, and whatever weird fifth idea you try, the game usually saw it coming. Talk your way out, sneak past, shove them off a ledge, or skip the fight entirely. Your choices stick, and people remember them.

The writing and voice acting carry it. Astarion, Karlach, Shadowheart and Lae'zel are some of the best companions in any RPG, and Dark Urge is worth playing at least once because it's the strongest version of the story. My Durge run was a Lolth-sworn drow necromancer (Death Cleric / Necromancy Wizard / Spores Druid) with a small undead army in tow, and the game rolled with all of it.

Combat is 5e done right. Height, surfaces and positioning all matter, and multiclassing goes deep enough that I was still theorycrafting builds hundreds of hours in. The Patch 8 subclasses only made that worse, in the best way.

Honour Mode is the final exam. One save, no reloads, and bosses with legendary actions that punish lazy play. It forces you to actually learn the systems instead of save-scumming past them, and every dialogue roll gets tense when you can't undo it. Those golden dice were earned.

It's not perfect. Act 3 is massive but can still chug in the Lower City, inventory management is a chore, and a few companion arcs and quest threads wrap up more abruptly than the rest of the game deserves. None of that comes close to outweighing what Larian pulled off.

This is the new bar for RPGs. See you in hour 471.

Elden Ring has mountains of potential but it is simply held back by some very clearly rushed and lazy development choices. this game suffers from a similar fate to dark souls 1, in that the second half of the game is awful. The difference here is, not only was the first half of ds1 good, but the seconds half (while not great) didn't take terribly long. Elden Ring is a half-baked game.  Ill stop ranting and ill just go beat by beat. To start off, this game is only half open world. The first half is open. The second half 100% is not. This sucks even more because the open world is very very good in this game. Seriously the open world is some of the best I have seen. if you don't like souls but like rpg's you will like Elden Ring. Anyways the bosses and their awful balancing is where this game falls short. To start off we have Margitt as the very first boss. Margitt isn't great and he foreshadows certain awful trends you see later in the game.  He has very delayed attacks, which in a vacuum is fine, but as someone who knows how much this mechanic gets spammed later on, it simply seems like a way to unfairly increase difficulty. Margitt also has very long combos that make it unclear when they end, which is another trend we see later on. Finally, Margitt has a small dagger that he uses if you get to close after he attacks. The problem here is, it is unclear when this dagger will come out, so you can punish what you think is an opening, and then take damage to no fault of your own. 4/10 boss. next is Godrick. Godrick is better but still not great. I don't havve a ton to complain about with him, he is a  fairly solid fight 7/10. The next boss you will probably fight is Renalla. Renalla is a gimmick fight packaged with the souls classic: boss that constantly runs away from you and spams op projectiles. That pretty much is the entire fight. First phase is a gimmick waste of time. Second is just chasing her around trying not to get hit by her annoying projectiles and summons. 2/10 boss, chasing a boss isn't fun. The next boss you will most likely fight is Loretta, and boy is this a nice change of pace. Loretta is a fantastic fight and really shows you fromsoft still has the ability to make really solid fun and fair experiences. My only minor complaint is her second phase projectiles can be a bit much at times, but that isn't really a big deal. 8.5/10 has that Fromsoft touch. Next up we have Draconic Tree Sentinel, or DTS. DTS brings us back to the awful bosses. DTS features spammy AOE projectiles, and attacks that have a delayed massive shockwave that will hit you even if you dodge the initial swing. Not much to say here, this boss abuses delayed attacks slightly less than the others but thee big problem is the awful AEO shockwaves produced by many of his attacks. these waves come out slightly later after DTS's weapon hits the ground which feels weirdly unnatural even though that is more reallisiticaly how it works. Point is it feels bad and to make it even worse it does a ♥♥♥♥ ton of damage. (I forgot to mention this earlier but it is worth noting how inflated these bosses AP and HP is). Dts gets a 3/10 not the worse but Fromsoft can do way way better. Next up is, technically a miniboss, but it is just the first phase of a later boss so ill just talk about it there. Anyways next is Morgott (Margitt is weaker kind of fake shade of Morgott). Morgott is one of the biggest offenders of the stupid long combo. morgott spends so much time just comboing it is awful. Not to mention he is way way faster than you to a point where it is unfair. This fight basically consists of Morgott aura-farming doing crazy flips and combos while you wait for the single attack you can get a hit off of. this boss really demonstrates how so many Elden Ring fights are just two sets of attacks: all the attacks it's impossible to get a hit on, and the about one or two you can get a hit on. this system just leads to a lot of waiting and waiting for getting the corrects attacks. Anyways Morgott still has all the usual, delayed attacks, too much HP, too much AP, way to damn fast, etc... just with more combos to really waste your time, 5/10 better than Margitt because he looks a bit cooler and instead of waiting while he does nothing, you wait while he flips around comboing the air. Our next  boss is really where the quality goes from bad to borderline unprofessional garbage. The bosses from here on out are so bad it is crazy to think this same company made Sekiro and DS3. These bosses are all some of the absolute worst in souls (I would seriously rather fight bed of chaos than most of these). Started off we have a contender for worse souls boss,  the First Giant. Fire Giant features and even more inflated Hp pool, with tons of one-shots, awful terrain, annoying projectiles, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ camera, and to top it all off he constantly runs away form you making you get on and off your horse to try and keep up with him. 
This fight is a slog, it is awful. One of the most boring terrible fights ever. I could go over all of the bad stuff about the second phase but I do not want to talk about this awful fight any longer. 0/10 remove from the game. Next on the list we have the God Skin Duo. This boss is just Ornstein and Smough, but awful. instead of having opposite attack styles and kind of attacking one at a time. They attack in fairly similar ways and they don't let up meaning most of this fight is spent running them around the terrain trying to separate them so you even have a chance. 1/10 really undercooked gank fight. Now this next boss, this next boss is actually very very good. I'd even say the best boss in the game by far. Next up we have Maliketh. Now ill admit his first phase is kind of mid, but once Maliketh comes out it is such a fun fight. first of all, all of his attacks are telegraphed in a way that is predictable and makes sense. Second, you can respond to all of his melee attacks with a counter attack (especially by strafing which I really like). Third and finally of all, his health is fairly low. The only thing here is his massive AP, but I think that is fine because he is ALSO pretty flimsy so he is more of a speedy glass cannon type. 9.5/10 FromSoftware you dog. Next is a mini boss. Sir Gideon Ofnir. Ill keep it short and sweeet. He just spams verry OP projectiels and runs away from you. 0/10 bad unless you get good RNG and he doesn't spam his really OP spells. Our next boss would be Godfrey and Hourah Loux and ill, be rating these two seperatley even though they are the same fight. For Godfrey I basically no comments, an overall really reallly good fight, 8/10. For Hourah Loux, he is way too fast and has too many grab attacks making it really hard to even take a breath in the fight. 2/10 feels like the speed of a Sekiro boss. Now for the final boss and this one is also two bosses. Radagon, and Elden Beast. radagon is an extremely unremarkable mid filler fight. Nothing super interesting about him, he is just a basic souls boss, 6/10. Now for Elden beast, Elden Beast sucks. Elden Beast commits so many dark souls sins. he runs from you all the time, he spams projectiles most of the fight, his health bar is massive, the camera can be a little weird, his arena is huge giving him ample room to run away from you, and finally, he is just an ugly looking boss. For a final boss he is very underwhelming 3/10. 

I hope you enjoyed my rant about this game, If you are wondering why I have so many hours, it is because the bosses in this game take ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ages to kill!

I understand why a lot of people love Baldur’s Gate 3. The writing, voice acting, world reactivity, companion interactions, and freedom of choice are impressive. There is clearly a massive amount of work in this game.

That said, I do not enjoy playing it.

The game feels painfully slow. Movement feels like power walking everywhere, combat encounters take way too long, and the pacing constantly drags. I like turn-based games and JRPGs, so the issue is not simply that it is turn-based. The issue is that this feels more like a slow tabletop rules simulator than a smooth video game.

The dice rolls are also constantly in your face. Everything feels like a roll: dialogue, combat, perception, traps, attacks, checks, saving throws, and more. I understand that this is based on Dungeons & Dragons, but as a video game experience, it makes too many moments feel like RNG rather than satisfying player skill. In JRPGs, RNG exists in the background. Here, the game keeps shoving it directly in front of you.

The gear and stat systems are also not explained clearly enough. It is often hard to tell whether one weapon or armor piece is actually better than another because the bonuses, conditions, and mechanics are not intuitive. The game gives you a lot of options, but not enough clarity.

For hardcore D&D fans or players who love slow, tactical CRPGs, this may be a masterpiece. For me, it feels clunky, overcomplicated, slow, and frustrating. I respect the ambition, but (well I realize I am in the minority here,) I do not think it is fun to actually play.

EDIT: Steam currently shows that I have only played this game for around three hours, but that is not accurate. I usually play offline, and Steam does not appear to be counting all of that time correctly. I have put at least 20+ hours into the game because I genuinely tried to give it a fair chance and understand why so many people love it. This review is not based on a quick first impression.

Balders gate 3 is a game I very much want to like... but I can't no matter how much I try. It's a very strange meld of larian studios doing an excellent and terrible job at the same time.

The gameplay is excellent, while not a 1:1 of the tabletop experience its about as close as you can get without just playing tabletop simulator. Combat is fun, the world is interactable, and you can approach things differently. It all well made.However this all gets bogged down by the characters, story, and mechanics. 

Starting with mechanics; There is one that absolutely bogs the game's pace down. If you've played other crpgs you'll be no stranger to dice rolls for dialog, interactions, etc. One thing youll notice however is that they do this automatically. I select the dialog, the computer will run the rng with the modifiers, get the number, compare it to the dc, and give the success or failure, plus give the rolls information in the log, all in the span of about .03 seconds. Balders gate 3 does away with the working formula, that their previos titles also used, so that you can sit there and watch digital dice roll (that doesnt matter because the animation is just there for you it still just uses a rng) At first this isn't so bad, some might even find it charming, but after a while it gets old. Ive played 40-50hrs of this game and probably a good 5 hours is just watching dice roll. And you cant even disable it, you can skip the animation but it still wastes more time than the game simply running it immediately. It honestly is just infuriating to me, it takes me out of the game so much and just wastes my time. 

If it was just that then I'd be irritated but fine I'd still play it. Unfortunately there's more: The characters. I'm not really sure how they messed this up so bad, though I have a theory, in their previous games theyve had little trouble making, mostly, well written and  interesting characters. While I wouldn't say every main character from divinity 2 is my favorite, they are all interesting. I don't find any of the main characters interesting in bg3. Honestly it feels like they made them "sex appeal" first (twink, goth girl, muscle mommy, etc) then gave a half assed story to them. I had zero interest in progressing almost any of their stories, let alone even recruiting them. (The hirelings from withers are usually more interesting...) About the only one that larian gets a pass on is the githyankee simply because their lore has always been trash so she was doomed from the start. Their dialog is ok and sometimes its cool that theyll have something unique to say about stuff but they pale in comparison to larians previous works. I could write a master's thesis on each character and why they suck/are not great. But I don't feel like doing that much writing, and it wouldn't help the review anymore than if I just said the characters are boring.

However the single most terrible design choice they made was the main story itself. I would say that from an objective stand point the main story's writing is lackluster. The clinical term being that its simply "eh". From a subjective standpoint however I find it to be incredibly boring. Mind flayers are probably one of the most boring/lame/uninteresting monsters in the dnd universe. (Honestly I'd rather die to a pack of goblins than have to admit I died to a mind flayer.) This is further compounded by the fact that they say the word "tadpole' so damn much that simply hearing the word in a normal conversation irritates me. If you played a drinking game where you took a half shot every time someone said tadpole you would be dead and in late stage liver failure before the 3 hr mark. Out of all the monsters/gods/driving forces for a campaign mindflayers are a terrible choice (and the other half to the mind flayers isn't great eirther but given the series I understand why they're there) Liches, vampires, celestials, demons, devils, etc. Would have made for a far more interesting story. 
Back to being more objective, the story carries little weight because if how its presented. The game constantly says "oh my god you have to hurry and rush to get the thing out of your head" But you can just wander around and do whatever with no consequences. Everyone you meet who shares your affliction is also doing fine whether they're looking for a cure or not. (unless they're dead I guess) so the main hook of "you need to hurry otherwise you'll die" seems more like a suggestion rather than something I really need to work on. The issue is only further exacerbated by the fact that you can't actually do anything about it even if you try. You can go talk to everyone under the sun about needing a cure or you can seek no help at all and it makes no difference till the story gets to a certain point and you're actually allowed to do something about it. Meaning that I am literally only talking to people for loot and xp instead of actually being invested in the story and learning. which at that point I could just play actual dnd witha mediocre dm.

Also the game has weird level limit... despite trying to be tabletop accurate where the level limit is higher, But more strangely while most things are very accurate to the tabletop they just gutted warlocks for some reason? I'm not even a big warlock fan who's like upset about that. I'm just confused. My friend who dm's says its likely because warlocks are stronger in the early levels so they'd be strong all game due to the level cap, to which I have to say ok...? thats just how a similarly leveled campaign would work out on the tabletop. 
Also I do want to clarify while I do mention larians other games, mainly divinity 2, Im not a giant divinity 2 fan. I think it was a good/alright game overall just in comparison it had a lot more thought, care, and general work put into the *important* parts of the game. (story, characters, etc.) instead of focusing on graphics and making me watch virtual dice as a selling point to make it feel more like the actual game. (if they wanted that they should've just made the enemy/allied ai take super long turns and give me virtual dice to stack/roll/play with while I wait for my turn) 

My point is that if you want to play a crpg called balders gate just go play 1 or 2, its crunchy and oldbut theres a reason people still play it to this day. This game is a waste of time and money (and sanity and tadpole will become a trigger word)

Before I start, I would like to say that this it not a negative review. I have very complicated feelings towards this game. Feelings that could not be measured by a simple like or dislike. 

Let's start with the positives. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LOVE the art direction of this game. Each region feels distinct and full of detail, conveying a beautifully tragic war-torn world so well, albeit one that feels as though it can be saved and its not all hopeless, and yet despair lurks around every corner.

I loved a lot of the NPCs, they feel considerably more fleshed out than some of the previous Souls games, not to say they didn't have any, but a lot of them made me really question the choices I was making along the way, in particular Varre, who I found intriguingly creepy as hell. It has some of my favorite character designs as well! Blaaid, Alexander, Godrick, Mohg, Malenia, I could go on! The voice acting is top notch as well, some of the best I've heard in a game. 

The music was pretty nice too, unfortunately I'm usually too distracted by my mission or fighting a tough boss to really appreciate it for what it is. 


What made me leave a "negative" review, however, was the difficulty. Not that it was HARD, this genre is known for its relatively high difficulty. It was brutally hard, moreso than every other Souls game I have played, (1 and 3, 3 I have the most experience with) but it's not even that!

The difficulty of this game is....is just....all OVER the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ place!!!

Like...ok. You start out in Limgrave. You have barely any health to speak of, so you need to start leveling Vigor. My advice to you all, get that ♥♥♥♥ to 40 IMMEDIATELY. And then towards the mid-late game, get it to 60. I have gripes with this, more on that later. Liurnia, a bit more difficult, but not a huge step up.
Every region after that has a rather large jump in difficulty. ESPECIALLY Caelid. ♥♥♥♥ Caelid! But wait!! It gets even WORSE!!

When you get to the late game areas, (Leyndell, Mountaintops of the Giants, Crumbling Farum Azula) the game just throws as much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at you as it possibly can, and doesn't ever hold back. JESUS. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. CHRIST. I have NEVER seen such a horrific difficulty spike in any game up until this point! 

The Fire Giant was the first boss to really question my sanity. It is INSANELY tanky, and while largely telegraphable, it will destroy you in 3-4 hits. With 60 VIGOR. 

60 Vigor is practically MANADATORY at this stage of the game. Everyone and everyONE will ♥♥♥♥ you up in 3-4 hits. I say 60 because it's the second softcap. After that you get barely anything from Vigor. Which ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SUCKS BECAUSE YOU DON'T EVER GET ENOUGH HP TO WORK WITH!!!

As are summons. The PC version is the definitive version because the online is free. You NEED co-op to beat most of these bosses. Especially towards the end. Spirit Ashes can work too, but here's the thing I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate about this. NOT. EVERY. BOSS. WILL LET YOU. SUMMON. SPIRITS!!!! WHY?!!! This is a HORRIBLE design choice!! They're not even as good as a player can be! Just let me USE them for Christ's sake!!


But THEN....Maliketh.

Maliketh, and the boss you fight at phase 1, the Beast Clergyman, might just be the worst boss I've ever dealt with. And right before, in my mind it was the Fire Giant. 

Imagine a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as tanky as the Fire Giant. Now make him INSANELY mobile, have multiple AOE projectiles, and make much of his attacks go through the pillars that LOOK like they're safe, but oftentimes won't protect you from ♥♥♥♥. I mean this to BOTH bosses by the way.

Maliketh, is even worse. Now give him a sword that can DRAIN YOUR HEALTH OVER TIME, AND! Reduce your Max HP, Make him even MORE mobile, and make him tanky too. 

I am stuck on this boss right now. You need two summons. Not one, TWO. One is not enough. And many times for some godforsaken reason I hardly get anyone online to help! 


There's another aspect of Elden Ring I really don't like, unrelated to difficulty.

It is, by far, the most walkthroughiest game, I have ever played. You NEED a walkthrough for most of this game. After a while I just gave up playing it blind. There's no shame in using one either, especially for games like this. Dark Souls 3 could be like this too, but I used it more for building my character rather than much of the game itself!

NPCs have the most obtuse questlines in the world. They practically DEMAND a guide. How are you supposed to know what to do next, what items to get to progress a questline, without using a guide?! It's ridiculous!!

Pages upon pages, videos upon videos, all just to be able to play this game without losing my mind. And I'm still losing my mind. 


Dark Souls 3 could be like this at times, I remember Irithyll being absolute HELL in regards to difficulty. But in regards to difficulty CURVE, that is the big ass difficulty spike of the game, but a lot of lategame areas tend to generally be more fair relative to the area. The final boss of the game was notably easier than Irithyll's own. And, ♥♥♥♥, Margit the Fell is harder than most Dark Souls 3 bosses, and is the FIRST major story boss! That tells you everything about this game. 

Speaking of which, I have yet to beat the final bosses, (yes there are TWO of them in a row, and if you die at the second one, you have to start from the first one all over again, ♥♥♥♥ THAT.) But I CAN tell you that both of them have twice as much health as the final boss of Dark Souls 3. BOTH. OF. THEM.


It all combines into the most unaccessible, harder than hardcore, not for the faint of heart or the short of temper Souls game, I have ever played. For their first attempt at an open world Souls game, I'd say FromSoft did a pretty good job, but its also meandered with questionable design choices that ultimately lessen what I would've otherwise called the best Souls game! It shows a lot of promise!!....but holy ♥♥♥♥, are the lows some of the lowest I've seen in a game. 

I wouldn't give it a flat out thumbs down because I DO like a lot of this game. I ultimately did have fun most of the way through, and if a video game is fun, that's great! I would give it a more, thumbs sideways, I guess???

I say "not recommended" not in the sense that the game sucks, it doesn't, I know I sound like I think it sucks, but its moreso certain aspects that really get under my skin, enough to make me not recommend it for most people. I would just start out playing either Dark Souls Remastered, or Dark Souls 3, if you want to get into these games. Elden Ring is for the most hardcore ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the planet, clearly. 

And from what I heard the DLC gets even worse due to certain mechanics, and DLC of Souls games generally being even more brutal than the main game, but that is standard at this point. The late game is brutal enough for me, and honestly I'd say it's too much. I'm not ever getting the DLC.

Quest design in a 9th gen game this obtuse is beyond stupid. That is not to say show markers pointing every step of the way, just make it so we don't need a guide. There's a lot FromSoft can do in regards to making a game like this so much more accessible without really "dumbing down" the difficulty.
