A Legendary Franchise Reduced to Shock Value

Let’s be honest: this game is obsessed with sex to a point that feels embarrassing.

Instead of delivering a mature, lore-driven Dungeons & Dragons epic, it constantly drags the player through intrusive sexual tension, unsolicited advances, and dialogue trees that feel engineered to funnel toward sexual outcomes. You can barely interact with companions without conversations bending toward flirtation or outright propositions. It doesn’t feel natural. It feels compulsive.

And when one of the first defining choices in character creation is genital size, that tells you exactly where the priorities were. In a universe built on decades of rich lore, layered politics, divine conflict, philosophical depth, and complex moral choices, this is what they decided to emphasize? It’s juvenile. It’s unnecessary. It cheapens what should feel epic.

The problem isn’t that sexuality exists. The problem is how intrusive and persistent it is. Dialogues corner you. Emotional beats derail into awkward intimacy. Instead of earning connection through storytelling, the game repeatedly defaults to sexual provocation as if that’s the most compelling form of character writing available.

What makes it worse is the generational disconnect.

I started my Dungeons & Dragons journey at 12 years old with Baldur’s Gate I. That game sparked imagination, strategy, moral dilemmas, and a lifelong appreciation for RPGs. Now my own son is 12 — the same age I was when I fell in love with this universe — and I would genuinely feel uncomfortable introducing him to this as his entry point into role-playing games.

Not because fantasy should be sanitized. But because this feels excessive and unfocused. It feels like shock value over substance. Instead of welcoming a new generation into a vast and intelligent fantasy world, the game risks pushing them away with its constant emphasis on genitals and sexual encounters.

And that’s the real wasted potential. This could have been the bridge between generations of players. Instead, it feels like it slammed the door shut.

To be clear: the technical achievement is undeniable. The combat is deep and satisfying. The production quality is extraordinary. The voice acting and cinematic presentation are top-tier. There are moments of brilliance throughout.

Which only makes it more frustrating.

The talent was there. The budget was there. The lore was there.

Restraint wasn’t.

It had a rough beginning, no doubt about it. However, since then, this game has become an absolute masterpiece. There is no game on this Earth that has ever made me feel what this game has. It is a masterclass example of what exceptional story writing should be. There are no happy endings in Night City, and no game has ever made me, as the main character, feel so powerless. 

When Phantom Liberty was released, I was expecting a simple DLC that added a few extra hours of gameplay, but man was I wrong and I couldn't be happier about that. This DLC alone is better than 99% of the full-fledged games I have played throughout my entire life.

Aside from the story and the writing, the characters are exceptional by themselves, especially Johnny, the other main story characters, the romance options, and honestly, all the character of Phantom Liberty. No matter what you do in this game, whether it be focusing on the main story, doing side quests or gigs, or simply exploring, you will find gems hidden away at every corner of this map.

The combat is phenomenal. It is highly responsive, bloody, and gritty. There are dozens upon dozens of builds you can do, focusing on melee, snipers, blades, netrunning, drugs, spray and pray, stealth, and on and on. There are various types of weapons such as the basic ballistic firearms, but also power firearms that pack a greater punch and can be increased via certain builds, smart weapons whose ammunition locks onto targets and can be more effective with a netrunning build, explosives, burning, poison, blades, dildos (yes, I'm serious, you can beat people to death with dildos), hammers, etc. You can also forgo weapons altogether and focus purely on netrunning hacks which permit you to do various things such as spread viruses, knock enemies out, force them to commit suicide, and so on and so forth.

You could replay this game a dozen times and have a different build each time. How many games offer that much freedom?

Vehicles in this game are also quite beautiful and fun to use. Some of them are a little too slippery on the road for my liking, but those are the minority. There are at least 40 cars from my count that you can either buy or find throughout the world and use, a good chunk of them being original/unique vehicles such as Johnny's Porsche 911 that you can find through a quest.

And lastly, the music? I have to say, without a doubt, the Official Soundtrack of Cyberpunk 2077 is the BEST soundtrack of any game out there, hands down. Samurai? Phantom Liberty (the song)? And atmospheric music like Killing Moon? Absolutely out of this world. Its very rare that I listen to music in videos games outside of said video games, but I see myself coming back to the OST very often.

There is nothing more I can say. Get this game, it is a masterpiece, the greatest game of the last three decades, and I have no doubt it'll remain on that pedestal for me for many years to come.

I played GTAV for the first time upon its original release on my PS3, wondering how on Earth that old console was able to process a game like this. And now, as I am writing this review in autumn 2026, GTAVI is coming out next month. Considering that GTAV has sold around 220 million copies by this point, along with all of its re-releases, it has obviously proven itself to be an enormous success in virtually every regard, whether we're talking about critics' reviews or fans' opinions. GTA games have always been a cultural phenomenon and a major force in pushing the boundaries of gameplay, immersion and, especially, vast open worlds. And I think most people would agree that GTAV became the series' highest point in all of these areas. I should note, however, that before GTAIV I personally wasn't a fan of the series for some reason. But GTAIV changed that completely. Its new engine and more realistic approach to almost everything, combined with a serious story and a huge leap in terms of immersion, finally sold me on the series. So, when GTAV was about to be released, I decided to buy a PS3 Super Slim primarily to experience it at launch, as I had previously been a PC gamer. It's crazy to think that this was 13 years ago. So I guess now is the perfect moment to draw some conclusions about GTAV and decide how we will remember this game. Personally, I would say that in many ways this game still holds up remarkably well, despite its dated movement and shooting mechanics, which feel rather clunky by today's standards. But when talking about GTAV, we cannot ignore the elephant in the room: GTA Online. And this is where two completely opposite opinions about GTAV can coexist. There is GTAV's single-player mode: a crime comedy set in a huge and immersive open world that also serves as one of the best portrayals of Los Angeles in a video game, as well as an amazing time capsule of the early 2010s. And then there is GTA Online, a rather controversial multiplayer mode, which was arguably one of the main reasons Rockstar ended up taking 13 years to release GTAVI. Back in 2013, when GTA Online first launched, I genuinely enjoyed it. It felt revolutionary for its time in terms of multiplayer and what could be achieved in an open-world game. But I think many people will agree with me that its monetization eventually ruined a large part of the experience. Not to mention how much Rockstar changed the tone of the game itself through all those updates. A good example would be the heists. The original heists were quite innovative and worked surprisingly well for their time, both in terms of gameplay and immersion. But then Rockstar added the Doomsday Heist, which turned GTA into some kind of absurd spy-drama parody of itself. And, of course, much of the later content was also tied to increasingly aggressive grinding and monetization. To put it simply, today's GTA Online is a bizarre and incredibly grindy experience, filled with flying futuristic cars, flying bikes, Batmobile-like vehicles, and an enormous amount of content locked behind some of the most monotonous grinding imaginable. So, as entertaining and enjoyable as the single-player experience is, the online mode has become almost the complete opposite for me: bloated, bizarre and, ultimately, rather boring. So, this is my final take on GTAV after all these years. And because of me actually playing to get 100% achievement completition, I think it's indeed valid. If you agree with me, feel free to rate this review positively.

Baldur's Gate 3 is basically an F5 / F8 simulator disguised as an RPG. The dice system dictates the outcome of major decisions, and a ridiculous number of those outcomes lead directly to instant failure, unfair fights, or outright game over screens. The game literally rolls dice to decide whether you’re allowed to continue without reloading... that’s not depth, that’s bad design dressed up as innovation.

A huge portion of the so-called “choices” are fake. Pick the wrong dialogue, fail one arbitrary roll, and suddenly you’re trapped in an unwinnable encounter or punished with a game over. That’s not player freedom... that’s trial-and-error with extra steps.

They sold this game as some gigantic RPG with unmatched scope, but that claim falls apart the moment you actually play it. Most quests are effectively mandatory, either because the game artificially locks progression or because stepping outside the intended route gets you instantly destroyed by enemies far above your level. The result is constant paranoia: spam quicksave every few minutes because the game loves punishing exploration with cheap deaths.

And if you want proof of what this game’s audience actually values, just look at Nexus Mods. The most downloaded mods tell the whole story: most are adult mods expanding romance and sex options, and another big chunk are cheats.

A huge part of the praise comes from people who don’t care much about CRPG systems at all, they just wanted a polished fantasy dating simulator with cinematic dialogue and party members to sleep with.

Same one tree sentinel. Same one tree spirit.

With enemies scattered all over with nothing to gain from killing them, the game heavily encourages you to not fight, and just explore in the open world. What's that? John Knight patroling a random road drops a unique item, but you ignored him as he's literally a generic enemy found all over elsewhere? Oh well, thats unfortunate. Better luck next time. 

Souls games inherently will never be possible to mostly complete on a first run without some sort of guide, and quest chains even more so as they're intended to be done over multiple playthroughs, but the insane amount of NOTHING in this game that is just recycled over and over and over that you CANNOT skip without a guide because guess what, that one dungeon you chose to skip, missed or forgot was the one dungeon that didnt just have useless ashes in them. That one hill over there might have a key item for your build or quest chain, so you better go explore it thoroughly, but wait... there was nothing. Again.

As I started with, the game isnt bad. The game is mostly enjoyable. The difference is that Elden Ring gives you more freedom with builds, weapons and strategies, but that feeling of finally beating something that seemed impossible is the same.

101 hours. Cyberpunk finally defeated me.

I got a lot out of this game, and when Cyberpunk is good, it can be really fun. The combat is great, building out your character and cyberware is addictive, and a lot of the gigs and side missions were easily my favorite parts of the game. They were quick, gave you an objective, let you approach it your way, and then got the hell out of your way.

Unfortunately, once I started focusing on the main story, I hit a wall.

The pacing is absolutely exhausting. Walk with somebody. Listen to them talk. Get in a car. Listen to them talk. Follow somebody. Listen to them talk. Sit down. Listen to them talk. Repeat.

Some of these sequences feel like they go on for 20–30 minutes, and because the game is committed to first person, so much of the storytelling is literally just standing there staring at another character while they dump dialogue on you. There aren't interesting camera angles or cinematic cuts to keep scenes visually engaging. You're just trapped in V's head waiting for people to finish talking.

The braindance sequences were especially miserable for me, and I hated how often the game takes control and momentum away from you for scripted rides, conversations, slow walks, scanning, following characters, and other sequences where you're technically "playing" but barely doing anything.

That's what makes it frustrating, because underneath all of that is a game I actually enjoyed. I loved sneaking into buildings, hacking cameras, throwing knives, using suppressed pistols, upgrading cyberware, experimenting with quickhacks, buying ridiculous cars, and figuring out different ways to clear an objective. When Cyberpunk lets me play Cyberpunk, I like Cyberpunk.

But eventually I realized I was spending too much of my time waiting to get back to the parts I enjoyed.

I even tried Phantom Liberty, unlocked the Relic tree, entered Dogtown, and almost immediately found myself thinking, oh God, more walking and talking.

I wanted to finish the main story. I really did. After 101 hours, I figured I had to. But gaming shouldn't feel like homework, and eventually I realized I was forcing myself to finish something I wasn't enjoying anymore.

So I'm calling it.

Great world. Great combat. Great character-building. Some genuinely fun side content. Terrible pacing, overly long dialogue sequences, too many moments where control is taken away from the player, and storytelling that I found incredibly stale.

After 101 hours, Cyberpunk didn't beat V.

It beat me.

4/10 — Not Recommended.

J’ai vraiment bien aimé Cyberpunk 2077. Au début, j’étais pas forcément à fond dans le jeu, mais plus j’avançais, plus j’ai accroché à l’histoire et aux personnages.

Le truc que j’ai le plus aimé, c’est clairement Night City. La ville est énorme et il y a toujours quelque chose à faire. Même quand on ne fait pas l’histoire principale, on peut faire des quêtes secondaires, des contrats, se balader ou juste découvrir la ville. Je trouve que l’ambiance est vraiment réussie, surtout la nuit avec tous les néons et les bâtiments.

L’histoire principale est aussi un gros point fort. J’ai bien aimé suivre V et surtout la relation avec Johnny Silverhand. Il y a pas mal de moments qui restent en tête et certaines missions sont vraiment excellentes. Les personnages secondaires sont aussi assez intéressants et certaines quêtes sont presque aussi bien que les missions principales.

Au niveau du gameplay, j’ai bien aimé avoir plusieurs façons de jouer. On peut utiliser des armes, des armes de corps à corps, le piratage ou jouer plus discrètement. Le système de cyberware permet aussi de rendre son personnage beaucoup plus puissant au fur et à mesure.

Graphiquement, je trouve le jeu encore très beau. Night City est vraiment impressionnante et certains endroits sont magnifiques. Avec de bons réglages graphiques, le jeu peut vraiment être incroyable.

J’ai aussi beaucoup aimé les quêtes secondaires parce qu’elles ne servent pas juste à gagner de l’argent ou de l’expérience. Certaines racontent vraiment des histoires intéressantes et permettent de mieux connaître les personnages.

Pour la durée de vie, je trouve qu’il y a largement de quoi faire. J’ai passé pas mal de temps dessus et je n’ai même pas terminé tout le contenu. Le jeu peut facilement occuper pendant plusieurs dizaines d’heures si on fait aussi les quêtes secondaires.

Pour Phantom Liberty, je ne peux pas encore donner mon avis complet parce que je ne l’ai pas terminé. Pour l’instant, j’aime beaucoup l’ambiance et les nouvelles missions, mais je préfère attendre d’avoir fini le DLC avant de donner une vraie note définitive.

Au final, je donnerais environ **10/10 à Cyberpunk 2077**. C’est un jeu que j’ai vraiment apprécié et dans lequel j’ai passé beaucoup de temps. Il n’est pas parfait, mais son histoire, son univers, ses personnages et tout ce qu’il y a à faire font que j’ai vraiment aimé l’expérience.

Pour Phantom Liberty, pour l’instant je partirais sur **9/10**, mais cette note pourra changer quand je l’aurai terminé.

This can be noticed as early as chapter one, but it is painfully obvious by the time you reach Baldur's Gate, some characters pretty much have their arc mostly complete and you have to wade through a couple more encounters to actually finish them. They feel like padding more so than organic parts to the it stories. There's also some weird thing with how the game handles events or how characters react that sometimes gives you the impression you unintentionally sequence broke a questline? it's very jarring, it's made me replay entire sections only to be frustrated by the same thing happening.

Lastly, the combat, the main thing that the DnD system cares to have detailed mechanics on, it's as bad as it is in the tabletop. High level encounters are prolonged slogfests where very little meaningfully happens for most of the combat until one side starts losing pawns. One example being the Yurgir fight (it's avoidable, yes, but it is a good example of what's to come) where you take forever to actually get through it, because Yurgir's minions have so much hp, you just spend a good chunk of the time letting your big spells take care of things and hope they get caught long enough in something like Hunger of Hadad to never become an actual problem. So many fights are like this and after a while it just starts being a repetitive rather than interesting set of encounters. The early game doesn't suffer from this as much because hp numbers are normal, but by the time you're around level 7~ you start encountering enemies with 100s of hit points and it just makes battles last forever. 

You may disagree, but there's a reason why people who like this game joke about endlessly replaying chapter 1 and 2, chapter 3 is not interesting enough to want to play through and it makes me feel like this game has been a huge waste of time

Cyberpunk 2077 feels like a game that should have been incredible, but instead left me completely cold. This is exactly the kind of game I should love: a massive open world RPG in a cyberpunk setting, something that could’ve been GTA in a Blade Runner world, but it just doesn’t come together.

Even after getting past the intro and into the open world, nothing really grabbed me. The action feels slow and clunky, lacking any real sense of energy or excitement, and combat never becomes fun enough to carry the experience. Movement and gunplay both feel off, making moment-to-moment gameplay more of a chore than something engaging. And the driving flat out sucks.

The presentation didn’t help much either. While the world is detailed, the character designs and overall aesthetic lean into a kind of generic, lowest-common-denominator modern style that lacks the distinct identity you’d expect from a cyberpunk setting. Every character, for the most part, was ugly and suffering from the worst tropes of the woke gaming era. This game WILL feel aged in just a few more years. More importantly, it just doesn’t feel like true cyberpunk - the soul, grit, and atmosphere that define the best works in the genre are missing here.

The story also failed to hook me early on, which is a major issue for a game this dependent on narrative and immersion. Without that pull, there’s not much left to keep you invested - especially, not for 60+ hours.

In the end, it’s a game full of ideas that sound amazing but don’t translate into an enjoyable experience. I wanted to like it, but after just over an hour, I was bored and ready to move on.

On paper, it is everything I want. In execution, it is duller than a plastic butter knife left on a burner.

Elden Ring is obviously not a bad game. With such an overwhelmingly positive reception, it is clear that it works incredibly well for a lot of people.

But taste is subjective, and after 73 hours and several attempts to get properly into it, I think I can fairly say that this game is not for me.

I enjoyed the Dark Souls games in the past, but at some point I think I grew tired of this style of gameplay. Elden Ring takes that formula and expands it into a huge open world, which is both its greatest strength and one of its biggest weaknesses for me. If you love difficult exploration, environmental storytelling, build experimentation, and discovering things with minimal guidance, this could be an amazing experience. If you enjoy using interactive maps, wikis, and progression guides on a second monitor, it may also fit you well.

For me though, I prefer games where the story, characters, and quests actively pulls me forward. My biggest issue with FromSoftware’s Souls-style games has always been that they do not feel like RPGs in the way I personally enjoy RPGs. There is lore, atmosphere, and worldbuilding, but the storytelling is very indirect and cryptic. If you mainly want a character-driven RPG with story choices and clear quest progression, Elden Ring may disappoint you.

There are absolutely things I like about the game. The atmosphere is excellent, the world feels oppressive, and defeating a difficult boss after learning its patterns can be very satisfying. I also understand why the lack of difficulty settings appeals to many players, because it makes those victories feel more earned.

But many of the same things that make the game rewarding for others make it frustrating for me. The game often feels like it does not respect my time: there is no normal pause function, death can mean losing resources, some runbacks are tedious, and questlines can be so obscure that I often felt pushed toward using a wiki. I do not mind difficulty, but I do mind feeling like I need external guides just to understand how to follow certain quests or avoid missing major content.

The game has lore and atmosphere, but very little of what I personally consider satisfying storytelling: proper dialogue, clear character motivations, narrative agency, and quests that are understandable without a guide.

Ultimately, every time I try to play Elden Ring, I end up feeling bored, frustrated, or like I have to push myself to continue. I can admire parts of it, and I understand why so many people love it, but I do not personally enjoy the overall experience.

If you are an exploration-first or gameplay-first player, this may be one of the best games ever made for you. But if you are like me and prefer structured quests, stronger narrative direction, character-driven storytelling, actual roleplaying and narrative agency, I would advise skipping it.

Not recommended.

Going to be an unpopular opinion here, but I've tried to get into Elden Ring several times and I just can't get over some of the negatives. I know, for many people, there are so many good things about this game and I can see the reasons why its regarded so highly, but maybe souls games just aren't for me so I'm giving this review from that perspective (as someone who wanted to dip my feet into this genre). 

This has nothing to do with the difficulty of the game. I couldn't wait to "git gud" at this game or grind my way to victory if I needed to. I just had a really hard time trying to get over:

The various menus/interfaces are clunky. 

The controls: The controls feel really bad to me. I get you don't dodge until you release the button and all that stuff but just mechanically it feels clunky to me. I much prefer the layouts and more responsive action of fighting Valkyries in God of War or Stellar Blade. I first tried with KB+M and it felt clunky trying to dodge, parry, etc. People told me to try a controller so I grabbed a PS Dual Sense and it's clunky to use potions etc especially in the heat of battle. With KB+M and Controller I'm struggling to control the camera and actually see what I'm fighting properly. 

The controls again: How are there no native PS glyphs for this game? Tell me to press triangle instead of Y. Yes, I can get over it but this is basic requirement of a game this big. 

The graphics: Nearly everyone seems to say this game has amazing graphics. I'll admit the art direction is great, but graphically this game does not look great. Yes, graphics aren't everything but I expect better graphical fidelity than this. When I bumped up things to 4k it started to look decent (but like on par with Tainted Grail or some other AA game). Never was I ever thinking "woah this is impressive graphically". It messed with my immersion. Too much fog. Low textures all over the place. When you kill enemies they just sort of ethereally fade away in an uninteresting way. I tried turning on HDR and after a few computer restarts it was finally working and that did help, but why does this game have so many technical problems still? 

I've been on plenty of corpse runs in various MMOs over the years. This is a boring/time-wasting mechanic for me in a single player game at this point. 

Lore/Atmosphere/Exploration/Mystery: This was very good/interesting. I just couldn't get over the clunky controls, bad camera, and lackluster graphics.

TLDR: This game is probably great for lots of people, but if you care about tight controls and good graphics this might not be it.

The greatest achievement of this game is the feeling that you're truly living out the story and steering it beyond superficial pathways. There are so many branching pathways and different stories to be discovered within this game that it genuinely makes each play through a new experience (given that you don't do the same things over and over). 

It's also got excellent mods that are easy to download. 

Apart from the player impact on the narrative, the game also populates it's world and narrative with genuinely compelling characters everywhere you look. But regardless. The story and the characters are the main attraction here. The gameplay is also very fun and full of interesting variety. I was initially reticent to play a turn based combat game like this (I don't play many of those), but I loved it. The world is interesting, but I'm no where near as interesting the mythos or legends of the world than I am the personal narratives and personalities that inhabit it.

[b]Summary[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
I've had people recommend this game to me for years; now that I've played it I'm just utterly confused as to how anyone can find fun in this title.  It runs like it has congestive heart failure even if you have the hardware, and the gameplay is so hands-off you may as well just watch the anime.


[b]Performance[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
Short version, it's terribly optimized and getting consistent performance (60+fps) is impossible.  I've spent 4 hours in the actual game, the rest of my 'play time' has been benchmarking performance and trying to fine tune the controls so they aren't fighting me.  I just cannot find a way to stop the game from randomly cratering into the 20fps range.  The assumption at this point is that I'm on an i7700k (above mininum, below recommended) and that's the bottleneck.  The GPU is a 3070 (above recommended) and there's 32gb of RAM.  Even without any ray/path tracing enabled the game will never stay above 60fps for more than a few seconds.  With DLSS enabled there is brutal artifacting and ghosting, whether in the benchmark or the game proper, so that's not an option.  Basically, the system requirements mean nothing.

The game can go higher than 60fps, but it will regularly tank into the 20s regardless of settings without warning.  I set everything in the options to either off or low - even the level of detail and crowd density - at 1080p and it will still randomly tank into the 20s.  It'll hang in the 20-30s for a couple seconds, spend another 5-10s in the 40s, before 'stabilizing' between 50-60fps.  After a few minutes it will randomly hang again and struggle to recover.

The benchmark says I'm not dropping below 60fps at minimum everything settings, but the actual game experience is very different.  I get the same benchmark result at 720p with medium texture resolution as I do 1440p with high texture resolution (my 4K display maxes out at 60hz and i have the game capped at 65fps).  This is the biggest indicator of a CPU limitation.  Unfortunately, there are no settings for this outside of 'Level of Detail' and 'Crowd Density'.  In other words, I either live with it or move onto something else in my backlog.  Pretty easy choice.


[b]Controls[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
This was actually the most disappointing part of the entire experience.  Even if this game could get to a minimum 60fps I have my doubts about it would ever feel good to navigate.  The movement and controls are somewhere between non-functional at worst and feeling like you're under water at best.  

Walking is slow, running is slow, carrying a body gives you plenty of time to consider how you could be better spending your time.  Dashing by default is an absolute mess, and driving by default is worse than that.  In fact, driving is so bad there's an auto-drive option.  Also, it's pretty much the first thing you do after character creation.  When you're at 60fps the game feels decent, but it's usually bouncing between 50 and 60 or tanking entirely.  That variability isn't helping the controls, but even when the game is hitting that 60fps they still don't feel great by any means..


[b]Gameplay[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
The play experience is more akin to a visual novel than an FPS.  I know it's supposed to have RPG elements but I was really unprepared for how little game there is to play.  You mostly listen to other people talk, which can't be skipped and more frustratingly is broken up where characters will expect you to say something.  Sometimes you don't have to, other times they'll pester you until you respond (quips such as 'are you listening?' and the like).  You can't even walk down the street without hearing some random NPC polluting your ears with useless drek.  It all becomes noise very fast.

When you do get to do something other than respond to dialogue, it feels like executing a checklist.  Remember how people hated always having to go into detective mode in Arkham Asylum?  Here it's called scan mode and it's equally annoying.  Want to open a door?  You'll probably have to scan it and do something else first.  It's easier to steal a car - which hilariously also involves opening a door - but doing that would involve driving.  It rarely feels like you can just do something, there always seems to be a process attached to it.

The combat is fine, which is as much a criticism as much as it is a compliment.  You have guns and can shoot stuff.  The game really expects you to employ a variety of stealth and hacking techniques to overcome a lot of the challenges.  Once again, that's a process and it is rarely as simple or quick as violence.  This is probably why the combat feels so tepid.

A feature that's oddly missing is a custom radio channel.  You need a mod to have a custom radio channel, which is a feature indie companies with a fraction of the budget have integrated without issue.  I guess they really want to make sure all the money spent on copyrighted music was worth it (music is subjective, but I feel they wasted their money).

My big critique - outside of some more options to ease the strain on the CPU - is the field of view slider maxing out at 100.  This is unacceptable and makes the game feel claustrophobic regardless of where you set it.  


[b]The Good:[/b]
[hr][/hr] 
The game does have its positive elements; they simply don't matter when the overall experience is so poor.  The graphics are nice, even at low details, and I particularly really like all of the neon colours.  The character models are nice (especially with the graphics kicked up to high), and the voice work is quite well done for them.  I wish more games had an options menu as extensive as this, it's generally quite comprehensive. This game was incredibly disappointing to play.
For starters, this game is absolutely beautiful. The set pieces, the enemies, the backgrounds, the game is gorgeous to an unbelievable degree. What I find a bit lacking, however, is that a lot of the enemies and levels can feel overdesigned and clunky to a degree where the deeper thoughts of the design are unreadable. While high gothic architecture is always appreciated, it can definitely feel eye glazing at times when the developers obviously didn't care as much about a location as others. The biggest problems I found with this being the numerous catacombs, caves, forts, and mines that are present throughout the game. Although they are at numerous locations, with very distinct landscapes, there's never anything visually interesting about them that wasn't done before. It makes it feel very video-gamey and copy and paste, when I felt that the worldbuilding of this game was incredibly interesting originally.

The difficulty of the game is far higher than previous souls titles, which in itself is not bad. However, there is a clear distinction between boss encounters. There's Margit, who feel very intentionally designed, while remaining difficult in a fair way, maintaining the "I died, what did I do wrong" mindset that many of the previous games seem to hold. Then there's Knight Ordovis, which is a boss encounter stapling two mini-bosses you have already fought, then taking to precautions to make it feel like a well-made duo boss. The first knight will always cover the second's punish windows, and if you're unlucky, they will attack at such intervals where it is impossible to not take damage. The vast majority of this game is a good boss fight, followed by 2 or 3 boring to bad ones (Some of these being repeat bosses that you have already fought plenty of times before). The difficulty, then, feels less like a natural result of the game attempting to challenge you in an interesting way, but devolves into feeling like it is overly punishing and unfair because they didn't take the extra second to ensure the encounter played smoothly. It doesn't help that your rune gain is decreased if you summon additional players, so it makes single bosses crammed into a duo fight feel even worse, since you are discouraged to summon others to help even the fight out (See gargoyles and godskin duo). 

The game itself and its grandness seems impressive at first, since the selling point of over 100 bosses appears incredible, but you soon realize that the game only has over 100 boss encounters because of how much they reuse and repurpose the same enemy over and over again. I personally would have preferred a smaller world, if it meant having less repeat encounters, but the game insists on reusing things that don't make sense. For example, the tree sentinel being a returning encounter makes sense. But having an Ancient Hero of Zamor be in a catacomb makes it feel very repetitive. Why is the boss here? Because you reached the end of the dungeon. Erdtree Avatars guarding the Minor Erdtrees makes sense. Having a named magma wyrm followed by a nameless magma wyrm in another unrelated cave is boring and repetitive. Ancient Dragon Lansseax was extremely cool to find, but now, one of the later game areas throws an identical copy of the fight, thus making it less impactful. The critique here is not that the individual encounter was bad, it's moreso that the individual encounter's overall effect and impact in the game is weakened since now there are just more enemies that act exactly like the boss.

I would suggest playing this game with an open mind and a guide. Playing guideless will cause you to miss many things that the game, and most players, would deem as "important" and "required." Do not be surprised if the open world leads you to having a weapon lacking upgrades for where you're supposed to be. Perhaps, had I started the game with a guide in hand, I would not have struggled as much, but I also deem myself to be a pretty experienced souls-like player and have always enjoyed the problem solving and natural progression of the game. Sadly, it seems that this game tried to be too big, but didn't have enough things to fill the huge map.

One of the best RPGs ever made. CDPR has this somewhat ungodly capacity to bring to life worlds and stories in a way very few could. The characters, the universe they're in, the amount of little side quests you can take part in that help expand your understandking and knowledge of the world, are truly something incredible. It recently got a face lift with new graphical improvements and some extra love, preparing it for the upcoming expansion.

Hundreds of hours of content for you to entertain yourself. The game isn't free of problems or errors though. With the many updates it has received over the years, you would think it's as polished as it can get, but there are still thousands of small bugs or problems that by themselves aren't much to complain about, but they stack.

I'm talking about little details such as missing textures, wrong level of detail rendering, missing/buggy props in the world, weird AI issues and broken-ish quest paths. Nothing too serious or repetitive as to take you out of the immersion, but they're there and at least in my case, annoyed me a tiny bit both in the Next Gen version and now in the Remaster.

Combat and some other gameplay systems are very dated and it shows. Combat itself is a weird console-in-mind simplistic hack and slash mash with little build variety, you can roll/dodge away from enemies and it has a lock on feature but it doesn't really have much depth and it is a bit buggy at times. Other gameplay systems such as gear durability, lack of gear scaling, weight limitations, and such are very clearly a product of its time, but thankfully you can toggle some accesibility settings (that they introduced over the years) to QoL your way out of them, but a few still remain.

Another small problem is that the story constantly references events from the past (or the books) that you might not understand or know at first, but it doesn't affect the main story of this game, You will end up going down a few rabbit holes to learn more about the universe tho, you have been warned.

Baldur’s Gate 3 shines in its writing and characters. The narrative is well-crafted, and the world feels alive thanks to memorable personalities and engaging dialogue. It’s the kind of game I wanted to love, and the story alone almost carries it. However, the experience is held back by fundamental flaws in its combat and design. Flaws that make it hard to recommend wholeheartedly.
[h2] Combat: A Frustrating Power Fantasy [/h2]
I don’t oppose turn-based games by default, but BG3’s combat doesn’t deliver the power fantasy it promises. When facing 20 weak enemies in a single room, I should feel like an unstoppable force, clearing them in seconds, not gambling with accuracy rolls and damage dice for foes that should die to a stiff breeze. The game constantly throws overwhelming numbers at you (unless you save-scum, which shouldn’t be a core “feature”), and it feels like lazy design.
[b] SPOILERS FOR ACT 3 AND SHADOWHEARTS QUESTLINE IN THE BLOCK BELOW! [/b]

[spoiler] The basement in Act 3 during Shadowheart’s questline was the tipping point for me. I had to cheese my way through with a firewall on the stairs just to get past the relentless enemy spam. It’s not challenging; it’s tedious. [/spoiler]
[h2] Design Disconnect: Combat vs. Story [/h2] 
It’s clear the writing and combat design happened completely independent of each other. The game pretends to offer meaningful story choices, but in reality, most paths lead to minor dialogue tweaks or game-over screens. I played as a resist Durge sorcerer, expecting surrendering to the urge to open new narrative branches. Instead, I got a few lines of unique dialogue and some superficial changes. This isn’t Fallout: New Vegas, where choices ripple through the world! It’s a puddle compared to an ocean.
The disconnect extends to the game’s tone. BG3 forces you into a rigid D&D 5e simulation, complete with RNG and spreadsheet math, but it lacks the camaraderie and flexibility of a real tabletop session. As a DM, I know that level 1 goblins would cower or die in a funny, narratively satisfying way, not force the player to slog through every roll.
[h2] Industry Trends and Award Hype [/h2]
[b] Not really about the game, but important if you're considering getting the game because of it's critical acclaim. [/b]
BG3’s near-perfect scores and GOTY wins say more about the industry than the game itself. It’s not that Alan Wake 2 or other nominees are bad. It’s that awards, like movie Oscars, favor grand, cinematic experiences over smaller, tighter designs. BG3’s 96% “Overwhelmingly Positive” Steam rating is misleading (not really, but let me cook): only around a quarter of players have earned the “All’s Well That Ends Well” achievement (finishing the game). 
[h2] The Community and Criticism [/h2]
[b] Once again, not really related to the game, but still interesting imo [/b]
The most frustrating part isn’t the game, it’s the patronizing fanbase in my opinion. Criticizing BG3’s flaws invites vicious backlash. The fact that there’s a dedicated keybind for loading quicksaves speaks volumes: the developers know players are save-scumming to tolerate the combat. Yet, pointing this out gets you labeled as “not getting it” or worse. (This is not exclusive to BG3, just a flaw with CRPGs in general)
I suspect many positive reviews come from players who didn’t finish the game but don’t want to admit it. That may be out of fatigue or fear of being piled on by the community. Or maybe they just played the first act, enjoyed it but never touched the game again, which is probably the best way to experience it.
[h1] Final Verdict: A Flawed Gem [/h1]
Baldur’s Gate 3 is a game I wanted to love, and its story and characters almost make up for its flaws. But the combat is a slog, the choices are shallow, and the design feels disconnected. It’s a game most players haven’t even finished, yet it sits at near-perfect scores. That’s not a testament to BG3’s quality. It’s a sign of how low the bar has fallen.
If you’re here for the story, you’ll find a lot to enjoy. If you want satisfying combat or meaningful choices, you might leave as frustrated as I did.
Not Recommended (after one playthrough as a resist Durge sorcerer, reaching Act 3).

If you are reading this, then you probably already know the positives of Baldur’s Gate 3: freedom of choice, great voice acting, strong quest design, memorable companions, and the ridiculous amount of ways you can solve problems. I'm not going to sit here and pretend those things are not impressive, because they are.

But because those parts have already been praised to death, I want to focus on what, in my opinion, makes the game overrated.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is clearly a good game, but I don’t think it is the flawless masterpiece people make it out to be. To me, it is also bloated, clunky, awkward, weirdly horny, and surprisingly weak when it comes to the feeling of progression. I will address each of those in the following sections.

[h2]Weak Progression[/h2]

One of my biggest problems with BG3 is progression. For such a huge RPG, I rarely felt genuinely excited about my character becoming stronger.

The story moves forward, the stakes get bigger, and the locations become more dramatic, but my actual character build often felt weirdly static. Gear progression especially felt underwhelming. It is very possible to find strong equipment in Act 1 and keep using it through Act 2 and even into Act 3.

I understand that this is probably good for balance, as it avoids the usual RPG problem where every item becomes useless after two hours. But from a player perspective, it can feel boring. You defeat major enemies, explore dangerous areas, open some impressive-looking chest, and then the reward is something you instantly send to camp because your old gear is still better.

I mean there is clearly something wrong when I'm deep into Act 3 and still wearing gear from Act 1 without feeling much reason to replace it. Loot should be exciting. I should look at a new weapon, armour piece, ring, or cloak and think, "Oh, this changes my build." But too often in BG3, loot just feels like mildly interesting clutter.

[h2]Underwhelming Level-Ups[/h2]

Leveling up has a similar problem. Because BG3 follows Dungeons & Dragons 5e, progression is more restrained. Yeah, I get that it is faithful to the tabletop rules. But as a video game RPG, it can feel really underwhelming. There is no proper skill tree, no big long-term upgrade path, and not many future unlocks that made me excited.

Some classes get fun powers, but plenty of level-ups feel minor. You get one spell, a passive, a feat, or some practical option that feels fine but not exciting. Many of the coolest choices can be taken early, and after that you often just pick whatever is left or whatever seems vaguely fitting.

A skill tree would have helped. Not some bloated mess with 300 meaningless icons, but something that gives a stronger sense of direction. Something that lets you look ahead and think, “Oh wow! I cannot wait to unlock that!” In BG3, I often didn't feel like I was building towards some powerful fantasy version of my character. I felt like I was just selecting from a small menu of practical options.

[h2]Combat: Great Ideas, Clunky Execution[/h2]

Combat is a mixed bag for me. When it works, it can be genuinely great. Positioning matters, height matters, surfaces matter, spells matter, and the environment can completely change a fight. You can push enemies off ledges, block routes, set traps, summon creatures, buff allies, debuff enemies, and turn the battlefield into complete chaos.

But when combat does not work, it becomes slow and clunky. The camera is often terrible, especially in multi-level areas. Trying to click the right enemy, floor tile, ledge, ladder, or doorway can feel harder than the actual fight.

Pathfinding can also be stupid. Characters walk through fire, acid, traps, or other hazards like they are trying to speedrun natural selection. You finish a fight, relax for half a second, and then someone casually strolls through burning ground because why the hell not.

The hit chance system can also feel awful. I know missing high-chance attacks is part of D&D. But that does not mean it always feels good in a video game. Nothing kills the heroic fantasy faster than watching your trained warrior miss a point-blank attack while some goblin with the posture of a wet sock crits you from across the room.

[h2]Inventory Management: Fantasy Warehouse Simulator[/h2]

Then there is the inventory system, and oh boy, it honestly deserves its own prison sentence.

By mid-game, your bags are full of scrolls, potions, arrows, keys, books, notes, quest items, food, rings, amulets, dyes, tools, random bones, and 46 pieces of equipment you are keeping "just in case." Managing all of it becomes a chore.

The game gives you so many items, but sorting through them is tedious. You constantly move things between characters, send things to camp, compare gear, check whether some random note still matters, and try to remember which companion has the potion you need.

Somewhere in your backpack there is probably a useful item. Good luck finding it.

[h2]Act 3: Too Much of Everything[/h2]

The pacing also becomes a problem, especially in Act 3. Act 1 is strong because it has mystery, danger, discovery, and a good balance between freedom and direction. Act 2 has a strong atmosphere and feels more focused. But Act 3 is where the game starts drowning in its own ambition.

The city is impressive, don't get me wrong. There is a lot to do. But sometimes there is just too much. Every building has secrets. Every NPC has a problem. Every street corner threatens to become a side quest. You can’t walk 20 metres without someone asking you to solve a murder, uncover a conspiracy, rescue someone, investigate a basement, enter a portal, or confront a god. 

The amount of content is impressive, sure, but this density hurts the pacing.

[h2]Romance Writing: Too Fast, Too Easy, Too Awkward[/h2]

The romance writing is another big issue for me.

The issue is not just that the companions are bisexual. That alone I can survive. The problem is that nearly every companion feels player-sexual in the same way. Instead of feeling like complex adults with different preferences, boundaries, and emotional pacing, the party often feels like they all joined the same fantasy dating app and instantly matched with the player.

You meet these people, survive a few fights, avoid being completely evil, and suddenly half the camp starts acting like you are the most desirable person in Faerûn. Ridiculous.

The romance feels too easy and too fast. It does not feel like trust is properly earned. It feels like romance unlocks because you picked enough polite dialogue options. I even had scenes that felt weirdly romantic when I was not trying to romance that character at all. I was just choosing normal polite or supportive options, but the game seemed to assume I was interested.

The silent protagonist makes it even more awkward. A companion pours their heart out, becomes vulnerable, or expresses attraction, and your character mostly communicates through silent staring and vague hand gestures. Instead of two people building chemistry, it can feel like one fully acted character falling in love with a mute wax figure.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

That is why I cannot see Baldur’s Gate 3 as the flawless masterpiece people make it out to be. It is ambitious, reactive, and impressive, but also bloated, clunky, awkwardly paced, and surprisingly weak as a progression-based RPG.

I respect the game a lot, and I understand why people love it. But for me, the weak progression, messy Act 3 pacing, clunky combat moments, silent protagonist, and weirdly rushed romance writing hold it back too much.

Given how hyped this game is, I would like to give you an in-depth analysis of both its positive and negative aspects and explain to you why I don’t recommend Baldur’s Gate 3 for most players. I will break this review down into the Good, the Bad and the Ugly:

The Good:
Let’s start with what makes this game truly shine.
Characters. You’ll get up to 10 recruitable companions with lots of unique dialogues and (for the most part) their own personal quests, some of which fantastically written, revealing rich origin stories including deep character development. Add stellar voice acting on top of all that and you get a highly immersive and memorable experience! 
Motion capture animations. Another reason why this game and its characters are so immersive is the motion capture animations. I think I’ve never experienced so many characters in a single video game coming so vividly and iconically to life as in bg3. Again, the voice acting adds massively to that.
Adjusting Dungeons & Dragons rules. For those of you who are unfamiliar with the original pen and paper game, it’s extremely unbalanced, especially when comparing the different classes to play. In the community, it’s widely known that there is a huge power gap between spellcaster and martial classes which gradually widens from middle to late levels. Larian studios apparently learned from DnD players homebrewing and elegantly solved this by cutting the maximum level down to 12 (which is btw how most tabletop DnD campaigns are being played) and redesigning certain classes.
Soundtrack. It’s all you could ask for in an RPG: epic during intense moments, soft during emotional moments, dreamy during exploration and overall fantastical.

The Bad:
As cool and amazing as the good stuff sounds, there is a lot of bad stuff we need to address here.
Tutorial is very lackluster for gamers with zero DnD experience. If you’re completely new to DnD, you should probably stop here because this game won’t even teach you the basics properly. Fortunately, I have DnD experience and know the rules of 5th edition, upon which this game is based, so it was no problem for me. However, I can see a newbie getting steam rolled repeatedly without knowing why simply because they haven’t been taught well.
Difficulty is all over the place in this game. I’ve only played on balanced difficulty so perhaps this doesn’t apply as much to other difficulty levels but don’t expect a linear increase of difficulty overall. Act 1 (Char level 1-6) felt to me like walking through a minefield. Act 2 (Char level 6-10) on the other hand felt like your usual gaming experience. Most battles were moderately challenging with a few boss battles that demanded more strategic thinking. Finally, in act 3 (Char level 10-12), most battles became trivial with combatants at much lower levels than your party and subpar gear you could already loot/buy in act 1. Even some boss battles didn’t impose that much of a challenge.
Just one bad decision could screw up your whole playthrough which is devastating in an extremely long game like this (more on that later). I had to basically start over after 35 hours because I realized after a quick internet research that due to one single misjudgment I’ve completely locked myself out of recruiting Karlach, the companion who I was looking forward to the most and wanted to romance, although I haven’t even met her yet. And that's just one of many examples of how you can unknowingly and irreversibly maneuver yourself into a very unpleasant situation, which is why I advise against approaching this game blindly, as I did and as is usually the case for me with RPGs.
Mini games with mechanics not to expect in an RPG game. There have been a few occasions when I wondered whether I purchased the wrong game because it suddenly deviated from its turn based RPG formula and turned into a completely different game with completely different gameplay mechanics and those are NOT skippable. Maybe this is a me thing but when I purchase a game I expect it to be what the description says and not surprise me with in built mandatory mini games that stop the momentum and force a different gaming experience upon me.
This game is fricking looooooooooooong! It took me 220+ hours to finish it, NOT including the 35 hours I replayed. Moreover, I skipped some content at the very end of the game, just to get over with it faster. Now you might be thinking: if there’s a lot of exploration and story to dive into then that kind of length would be natural. However, about half of my playtime went into sometimes boring, sometimes infuriating downtime that could have been greatly reduced if it wasn’t for bad game design. More on that in the “Ugly”- part.

The Ugly:
The ugly parts aren’t nearly as buzzkill as the bad ones but annoying to say the least.
Level design is counter intuitive and unnecessarily prolongs the game with confusion. Most of the larger buildings like palaces, temples and forts look as if a drunk architect built them. There is close to zero consistency in terms of layout and some pathways and connections look completely out of place. I guess they tried to avoid sameness while providing intriguing playgrounds for specific battles but in the end, they just turned out confusing. I’ve lost count of how many times I got lost in a place I’ve walked past several times before because of this goofy design.
Inventory management is clunky. RPG veterans know all too well how much stuff is piling up over the course of a full playthrough when there is loot literally everywhere and it’s no different in bg3. Some games offer you search and filter options for easier management but not this game. Although you have separate pouches for alchemy, keys and food, if you want any sort of order in your inventory, you have to drag and drop every single item at a time. The “add to wares” - function isn’t helpful either because you’d still have to click on every single item in order to use it. May as well drag and drop when you’re trading. Far from elegant and again, something that unnecessarily prolongs the game.
Lootable vessels are everywhere! Why is that bad, you may ask? Because almost all of them are empty. I started this game looking into every single lootable vessel I laid eyes upon until I realized I haven’t found anything, even after opening the 100th or so. So I started using the hotkey that highlights all important lootable places on screen and went with this for the rest of the game. However, I still occasionally opened “unimportant” vessels out of boredom and to my surprise I found an important key in act 2 in one of those. So not only does the game drown you in loot spaces of which most are empty but also it misleads you in falsely believing you could save time by ignoring them and focusing on the “important stuff”! Yet another way you can waste hours and hours of playtime in a frustrating way.
Traps. It seems like traps in bg3 serve the sole purpose of wasting your time and resources. They’re not puzzles as you might think, they’re simply hindrances that require you to pass an ability check. Otherwise, you’ll have to suck up the damage. So it comes down to resource management only. You won’t get a feeling of intellectual achievement from interacting with them, but rather annoyance.
Line of sight isn’t always clear. Sometimes, I wondered what obstructed my attempt of throwing a weapon or a ranged spell at an enemy because when I adjust the camera to my character’s pov, I could see a clear line to my target. Maybe the programming is a bit clunky here or I missed something but if it’s the latter, they could have at least highlighted the object that gets in my way for better understanding. Also, for some reason ranged spells that deal damage in a straight line don’t work over stairs. Can someone explain to me why I can’t aim my spell slightly upwards/downwards?

If you made it this far, congratulations and thank you very much for your attention!

I'm so glad that I still gave a try to what followed right after (Elden RIng and AC6), because this... is easily one of the most epic experiences I've played through.

[h3]Story - 7.5/10[/h3]
Elden Ring is a legend of a big, ancient world, at its most dire moment of history. With myths of old a plenty, and legendary warriors and beasts and gods to face. Your character is essentially just a nameless chosen one; you don't really get to write the whole story, but you experience the aftermath of one long, long history. And you get to decide how it ends.
From videogame's standpoint, ER's story is built largely the same way as other souls games. You have a vague, major, endgame objective. You have a rough direction of where you're supposed to go next. But since it's an open world, you are more than free (and kind of encouraged to) walk off this path from time to time, and explore.
Exploring not only grants you additional side content - there are several branches of side quests which unlock extra ending options for the main story. Not to mention - explain the lore, giving you some much needed context for everything that happened before, and what's happening now.
Is the main story good? - It's okay. The lore is the strongest point. And the only reason I'm rating it this high is because, for once, FromSoftware bothered with making it more or less comprehensive and at least somewhat directly narrated. Yes, you'll still get a very, very solid chunk of lore and story information from nitpicking, searching for deeper meaning, and reading every description, of every item, and trying to interpret some story behind every little decoration. But even without it, you'll at least understand the main story, core characters, and the motivation of most characters, including your own.

[h3]Gameplay - 8/10[/h3]
Out of all soulslikes... I'd say I only loved Nioh 2 more than that in terms of gameplay. The combat feels impactful, animations having weight, commitment. It's still a tad limited in terms of movesets, especially due to all weapons having only one equippable special attack. But you can dual wield; you can switch between one handed grip and two-handed, unlocking extra moves; you can use some defensive option in your off-hand, or a ranged weapon, or even magic one. Plus you have extra slots for other weapons, if you really want to diversify your gameplay.
The result is still a bit slow and limited, but miles ahead of the Souls series, or Sekiro, with only one weapon and one skill slot for the entire game.
As for other aspects...
Progression is pretty standard for souls games. You level up attributes for flat stat bonuses, you don't have any skill tree, and you gather new weapons, armor and special skills that you can equip on weapons.
Open world, the newest addition to FS games, and the most controversial for many... I'm okay with it. I definitely enjoyed the exploration and the sheer scale. The best part of it is that if you feel stuck on some boss/dungeon - you can always just walk in some other direction.
The only drawbacks for me were, as mentioned, some limitations to the combat in terms of moveset. Also - restrictions to weapons with fixed, unique skills, unable to be buffed by any other element OR change the attribute it scales with. And one more thing - frequent reusing of the same enemies over the course of the game. Not enough to feel completely repetitive, but noticeable.

[h3]Graphics - 9/10[/h3]
By now, it doesn't look as impressive, but it still holds really, really well. At release, it looked incredible. There's not much to add here - characters, enemies, gear, locations, backgrounds - all of it looks amazing. The best part, in my  opinion - this is one of those games that you start, see some landmark far, far away in the background and think to yourself: "I wonder if we'll be able to actually get there? Like, normally, on foot, not through some cutscene that teleports us there." And in most cases in this game, the answer is "yes." The map is enormous, and yet you get to explore almost every inch.

[h3]Sound - 9/10[/h3]
Voice acting and soundtrack were always quite iconic to the souls games, so it's no wonder that Elden Ring also carried it on well.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
9/10. In terms of combat, Nioh 2 remains to be my leader amongst soulslikes so far. But if we're talking overall? - Elden Ring holds the crown proudly.

I do not like the direction this game and company is traveling lately.
Elden Ring is good, duh, I won't argue with that. However, there's a lot of issues that are baffling.

The Enemies:
There's maybe... 10 or so enemies in the game, with a few area distinct enemy types. It seems that without a linear world to hinge on, Fromsoftware forgot how to design challenging encounters. Expect seemingly random enemy placements outside of the legacy dungeons and catacombs and caves.
On the topic of dungeons, what a pathetic excuse for content are the copy-pasted catacombs. If you don't enjoy spirit summons, there's practically no reason to explore defeat the boss at the end of the majority of catacombs. You get shafted out of practically a third of the game's content being exciting.
Oh, also you can parry every basic weapon wielding enemy in the game for an easy victory.

The World:
The Lands Between is... beautiful. Until you get bored of the big tree and the grass that is. There is a lot of grass and very little reason to traverse it. It seems that Fromsoftware was too afraid to place weapons and armour out in the open world except in a few specific cases, perhaps concerned people wouldn't find it. Expect to find 2 dollars and a pile of crab eggs for killing a giant bear.
Legacy dungeons. These initially solved my fear that Elden Ring would be a big empty world, the prospect of exploring actual castles dotting the landscape sounds incredible! There is one castle in the base game. There is a manor with minorly hot water dyed to look like lava, an academy with one classroom in total, a city with enough housing for maybe one thousand people, and a bunch of forts claiming to be unique.
Shoutout to Redmane Castle though, definitely the best part of the game in my opinion. Too bad most people don't even fight through it, as a certain trigger caused by playing the game deletes all of the enemies in the castle and locks the doors to treasure to give players a red carpet to fighting Radahn.

The Bosses:
The best parts of the game. Well, I mean the rememberance bosses! The normal bosses are typically copy and pasted enemies from other more high level parts of the game. Shoutout to Tree Sentinel though. Most bosses are uninteresting to fight and have the same issue as the lack of enemy variety. Also, bafflingly, the least enjoyable enemies in the game are the ones repeated the most often amongst the world. The gargoyles, nights calvalry, the black knives, demi-human queens, large stone imps, erdtree avatars, putrid avatars, hero of Zamor, leonine misbegotten and those snake tree avatars. Big health pools, selective stagger response on hit, one-shot attacks, and enemy overwhelm are typical.

Rememberance Bosses:
There aren't enough of them. Its clear that Miyazaki was hands on in the construction of most if not all the Rememberance bosses in lore and gameplay.

Lore:
Its bad. Fromsoftware took the approach of item descriptions conveying lore vaguely and made it even more vague. Cool spell, who made it? No one in specific, probably some unnamed dude. Cool armour, why is it fat? Idk. Every NPC either dies or ♥♥♥♥♥ off from the game world forever or becomes just a vendor.
It seems obvious to me that Mr. Game of Thrones deeply influenced the development of the game and artstyle. Elden Ring leans heavily into the epic story of a hero conquering the world and thinks nothing deeper than that. Kill Marika's kids and then marry her or her kid, mend whatever the Elden Ring is. I have no idea what the Elden Ring is actually, I know there are great runes and they come from the Elden Ring but what a great rune itself is really quite vague. Am I holding it? or is it etched onto my soul? is it getting tattooed on my belly?

Character customization:
Good character creator. There is no personality in your character unfortunately. You stand the exact same way as every other member of whatever body type you chose. Your face is closer to a mask, an in-depth porcelain doll. You are also short, 5ft 7in. I get the issue with creating character models needing to be the same size for balance but I don't like being 5'7" frankly. All of the armour in the game makes me look fat or even shorter.

Armour:
Do you want to look like a hobo or a freak? Even when wearing high tier armour? Then this game is right for you. The metal of the world is all in different qualities or shades or glossy, hardly able to mix and match. Most armour clips with itself even just during a basic walking cycle. Capes clip consistently through sheathes with no option to hide sheathes. All armour sets are too eccentric to feel like your armour or too bland to be desireable. Most armour makes you look wide and short, leading to a oversized fit from the outside. Much like a child wearing a strainer on their head and hockey pads.

Skills and Weapons:
Medium shields are just better than light shields once you find carian retaliation or storm wall. Any weapon with innate bleed is simply better than ones that don't. Split damage still sucks. Just spam ranged weapon skills, you'll be fine. Kill a jar for one of the best talismans in the game, kill a disabled and terminally ill woman for one of the best talismans in the game, kill a masked man with a funny accent for a pair of balls strong enough to kill god easily. Kill people for their clothes? sure! its how you get the highest poise armour in the game. Kill your friends for their weapons, kill homeless people for their bell bearings (you are actually encouraged to do this, there is no penalty.) Thy kind are all of a piece... Pillagers...
Weapons are unfortunately too easy to swap and mix attributes and skills, leading to objectively better weapons than others. Like with the bleed I mentioned. Also, please make bows and crossbows stronger and faster.

Spells:
Spam em, there is no penalty for doing this. Its actually faster and better depending on the spell. Charging spells is a welcome addition, but not being able to cancel them is a poor choice. Spells are impossible to free aim properly and do not track enough to be usable in an open environment. Not to mention that most enemies past soldiers dodge the moment you cast. True PvP warriors.

Endings:
Bad. Boring. Evil. Feed a serial killer your "seed" and then take his "ring" to curse everyone and their children forevermore.

The DLC:
Bad. All of the same issues as the base game except the rememberance bosses suck too now, genuinely unfair, use a shield. At least its super pretty and the lore is interesting enough to be worthy of thought. Messmer my beloved. Thou art... Tarnished, it seems. Laggy as hell. Water will ruin your fps instantly for some reason. Did you know that you're actually supposed to kill the furnace face golems? I had no idea. 

Tarnished Edition:
Hmmm, microtransactions... the armour genuinely looks it was made by a modder. Torrent skins should have been in the game from the start, and access to a heavy armour set without murdering someone should also have been in the game from the start. A paid band-aid fix for things that should have been in an update about 4 years ago.

Final thoughts:
This review is messy, but one I've been meaning to get around to for a while. I love this game, but its flaws are very... very hard to ignore. I have very mixed feelings. The messy style of this review reflects my own conflicted thoughts on the matter.

i'm conflicted on whether i just barely recommend this game or just barely advise against it. i might change my overall rating, but for now, i can't recommend it, particularly when i've had so many people tout it as the greatest game ever made.

i'll start with the things i enjoy; 

a great story with meaningful decision making.

excellent voice acting and casting. 

a wide variety of playstyles.

beautiful graphics. 

proper atmos support that scales with a home theater very well, plus a generally decent audio mix (for a video game).

and now the things i don't like; 

poor balance with difficulty scaling where enemies just get insane amounts of health while you start dying in a couple hits and don't get enough resources like ammo or upgrade materials to keep up. elden ring is a prime example of how all games should balance difficulty. make it as hard as you want, but do not use difficulty sliders. know your audience and balance accordingly. breath of the wild and tears of the kingdom are great examples of the opposite end of the difficulty spectrum, making the game very approachable to beginners and children while still being challenging. difficulty sliders are simultaneously one of the laziest forms of game design and a nightmare to program. no one wants them; just properly balance your game. this has been long proven with time, going back to some of the earliest games like mario bros, which single-digit children could beat, or a grown adult could rage at. that is perfect game balance. a difficulty slider requires devs to finely tune like 5 versions of their game instead of 1, and almost no one puts in the time to do this because it sucks and costs a ton of money. i will never comprehend how so many video games still get this wrong today.

the combat is fairly uninteresting as well. while i enjoy the talent trees, item varieties, upgrade materials and general out-of-combat RPG elements, the combat itself is pretty shallow. not that bad, just boring and not much room for skill growth. 

poor optimization as you get into higher framerates 100fps+. changing even the heaviest settings barely changes your framerate. the difference between medium-high 4k and ultra 4k + ray tracing is like 30fps average. though if you are just aiming for 60fps this game is optimized surprisingly well given the scale of the world and how good most things look.

third party CDPR launcher every time you start the game, paired with nags to log into your CDPR account for a single-player game. blegh. 

way too much unskippable crap every time you launch the game. like two minutes between game launching and gameplay, and only about 5 of those seconds are spent actually loading into the world.

the UI and general UX when using a controller is bad. so many elements just force you to use the joystick cursor, such as the horrid menus that won't properly scroll through your items, settings etc with the d-pad. the joystick mouse SUCKS. just build proper controller support. this isn't a competitive shooter where MKB matters enough to warrant neglecting controllers this much. 

the quest tracking is frustrating and inconsistent. sometimes i'll be on a main quest, then someone will call me and start another main quest, and that will override my current quest tracking. if you're not paying attention to the quest marker moving, it can have you trek like 15 minutes across the map for a completely different quest. other times the exact same scenario will happen and it WON'T override my quest tracking even though i'm only doing main quests in both scenarios. i haven't been able to figure it out but the inconsistency drives me nuts. it shouldn't be touching my quest tracker at all until i complete my current quest chain or otherwise clear my currently tracked quest. 

while i love the decision making style of storytelling, the logic behind some of it borders on nonsensical. I've played this game and seen other parts I missed through other videos online. Despite all the great dialogue, items and spells, there's just so much that really ruins the experience.

Let me start off by saying, I played Divinity: Original Sin 2 before this, which has way less RNG, so that also probably didn't help. 

To start off with, combat: It's more unfair than challenging. Enemy ranger, (even ones you encounter at low levels) always seem to have way better odds than you do. Even if you get a height advantage on enemies, enemy rangers on lower levels always have more consistent hits than you. That with a height advantage, when you're at the same level or lower, you might as well not even try to attack. And Sorcerers... they are a lot of fun, but there's an entire act that basically makes you worthless; The Shadow-Cursed Lands. Yes, it is  only an optional path, but pretty much every other class doesn't get screwed over. I switched my class to a barbarian and straight away I was doing far better than trying to be a Sorcerer in that act. The RNG for melee isn't much better. Once again, plenty of enemy melee can hit you way more than you can hit them. Even using items against enemies has odds stacked against you. The same goes for healing too. You have a certain numbers that you can heal between. Most of time, I couldn't get above 50% of the minimum. If a healing item was 8-20, I'd consistently hover around 9-13.

The exploration: This is so poorly done. You have all these cool areas, secret locations to find and neat loot. But if you want to actually explore them, you need to pass a dice roll. You can miss entire locations because of dice rolls. And i don't mean you lose an easier way to discover them or only lose one path, I mean if the dice roll fails you just straight up don't find it.

The dice rolls: I get this is essentially a DND game, but good lord. Dice rolls on speech, certain items, finding locations, traps, treasure, it's everywhere. Unlike D:OS2, you don't find secrets from being a certain level in something, here you just get slightly better odds in the dice roll. 

The story: This is one of the few good things in this game. The characters are well written and some of the more comedic moments are amusing. But that wasn't able to save the rest of this game for me.

The game became boring for me during Act 3 (the biggest one)—including the stories, the vast majority of the quests, and the combat. Ultimately, there weren't enough good points to save the overall experience.
1) Character development is too diluted in political correctness. You can still choose to go down the evil path, but it brings no real sense of fulfillment. Most of the time, you just suffer penalties, and your choices don't truly impact the world around you. Nothing quite changes; the main story just runs its course. Character arcs are full of improbable, epic secrets, yet they still feel dull and flat. I felt no personal involvement.
2) Combat, on Tactician difficulty, is way harder at the beginning of Act 1—I would even say almost too hard, with archers insta-killing you from miles away. Then you start to mitigate things, and the end of Act 1 and most of Act 2 become enjoyable. Finally, it becomes way too easy in Act 3, with only a few hiccups here and there. It mostly becomes tedious (like enemies maiming your Mage Hand, "stun immunity" that doesn't actually work, or counterspell avalanches). Your powerhouse team breaks everything, and you just have to rest... often.
3) Quests are globally well-written but have no impact on the world. In the end, you just do them for the sake of it, like chores.
It's not the first time I've felt this way about a game that is obviously well-made. Maybe it's just me, and I can't feel the intensity anymore... or is it just gone, erased by today's lack of creativity?
