Yeah, yeah, I know, I must be crazy... But I just really didn't like it, OK? I'm sad to be this disappointed.

It's a well-made game for sure, no doubt about it. If it weren't for the great expectations, there might not have been such a great disappointment. I've enjoyed Larian's previous works, loved them even, but there was almost nothing about BG3 to inspire similar feelings.

The story was boilerplate D&D plot, stretched to 100+ hours. Meaningless, emotionless, drawn out tropes and cliches. Only Act 2 made me feel something. I put off wrapping up Act 3 for years from sheer boredom, and felt nothing but tedium by the end.

The characters were as uninteresting as they were horny, I couldn't care about them with the obvious exception of Karlach, who was an actually well-written character. Shadowheart and Astarion were ok-ish. The rest were forgettable. Couldn't decide if the late shoehorning of Jaheira and Minsc was welcome fanservice or a way to distract from the voidness Gale, Wyll and Halsin.

The 5e ruleset is not a good fit for such a game, and Larian's attempts at patching it, while valiant, were not sufficient. Some made it actively worse. The combat was plodding, the interface clunky and annoying, the abilities and items both overwhelming in number and underwhelming in the choices they presented. 5e was never meant to be a lootfest, but the magic items the game showered you with created perverse incentives and boring micromanagement. The gear-juggling was made so much worse by the abysmal stash and inventory system. That they were this bad really boggles the mind.

In the end, the game had nothing to say, nothing to offer but a fun romp that degraded into tedium by the end, Almost nothing about this game is truly memorable, artistically profound or genuinely touching. It was a 150 hour fast food meal served on a really nice and shiny plate. For all its bugs and failures, I will forever remember and cherish Owlcat's glorious mess that is Wrath of the Righteous over the slog that was BG3. Even Larian's own Original Sin games were superior.

Edit: I'm sorry for all the feelings I hurt.

I do really think that this game deserved some of its praise back in the day (mostly 'cause of lack of competition, honestly), but finishing it left such a bittersweet taste in my mouth that i can't truly call it a „masterpiece for ages“.

I think i do understand the core vision of developers. Larian tried to ensure that this game will translate pure, chaotic DnD experience: and, I'll be frank, they somewhat did it with the outstanding turn-based combat system and all the possibilities that comes with it. Unfortunately, they failed on the other aspect that makes TTRPG have it's own renown: freedom of choice, being whoever you like to be and the consequences of it.

Storyline, and thus the choices that this game is kindly offering, have been written in such a straightforward and dichotomical way that you are either Mr. Goody-Two-Shoes or a pure offspring of Satan (wink-wink) with no real choices in between. The problem is not with the idea itself, but with it realization: whatever you choose, you'll ride on the same railroad over and over again with no differences that really matters on a global, narrative scale. Moreover, this game simply punishes you for picking granted conventionally evil choices and robs you out of possible content with nothing in return. The only consequences is, sadly, the amount of XP you'll gain and alive characters that you'll meet as the main quest goes on, i'm afraid. 

The overall quality of writing dissatisfies as well, granting a generally promising, albeit not without flaws, Act One and delving deeper into mediocrity as the story progresses further in Act Two and Three, with the second being a strange, linear filler and third an unpolished disappointment with big chunks of planned content removed in a hurry. 

And the characters? Sadly, with some exceptions they all seem more like humanized, basic fantasy archetypes/alignment charts put on screen rather than living persons with interesting, properly designed backstories and character depth/development (i'm talking about you, Wyll). And if the Act One tries to keep that a little secret, enriching the game with a bunch of popping out of nowhere party banter, interactions, random events and intrigue, well... later all of it slowly starts to disappear as you'll come closer to Baldur's Gate itself. 

But does that REALLY matter in the case of enjoying that game? No, i think not. To be honest, I've enjoyed every last bit of it, playing all day and night long in search of fun that this game perfectly delivers. What saddens me the most is the possibilities of what would've been if the game was delayed for a couple of years for extra polishing, and if the cut Early Access content/story hadn't been cut so unwisely. 

Alas, it is what it is, and despite the fact that I left a negative review, I do think that's up to you to try BG3 out and decide everything for yourself, although you should severely lower your expectations if you're looking for role-playing experience and an interesting story: you'll have nothing of that. But you'll have Minthara.

One of my favourite games, and one of those that set new standards for their genre. It might even be one of the best games up there.

The story is amazing, and the game is really complex (in the best way) and engaging. It constantly keeps you experimenting and thinking, and there's almost always more than one way to approach a situation.

The characters are exceptionally well written, with only a few exceptions. The voice acting is amazing, with outstanding performances across the whole cast.

Visually, the game is gorgeous. The art style is amazing and every place feels polished and fitting for the setting. Larian did again an amazing job.

The music ranges from good to very good. My problem is that I played Divinity: Original Sin 2, Larian's previous big game, and Baldur's Gate 3's music is heavily inspired by its soundtrack, which was better overall. I must admit I was a bit disappointed.

Another important thing to add: Larian delivered a fully finished game for the current standard price. Unlike most games nowadays, where studios rush releases and finish the content later (often releasing it as DLCs and charging for it!), Larian gives the the complete experience from the start.

Two small caveats: the game can be a bit overwhelming if you're new to the D&D rules, and a better tutorial on how they work would have helped me. I also would have liked more of a middle path between a "good" and an "evil" run. It feels like you're pushed a bit toward one extreme.

Story: 10/10
Music: 7/10
Characters: 10/10
Voice Acting: 10/10
Graphics and artstyle: 10/10

Let me start off by saying that objectively speaking this is a phenomenal game, but for someone who grew up playing Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne as one of their first major gaming experiences ever it doesn't hit the same spot.

My main gripe with this is the open world. Coming from Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne I was sceptical about this being open world, because I feared that the quality of level design and unique encounters would suffer as a result and unfortunately I was right. The few legacy dungeons that this game has don't even come close to the quality of other FromSoftware entries and they are ruined by the fact that you have to traverse a beautiful but empty open world to get there. Where other FromSoftware games' levels felt coherent and rewarding and respectful to the time you spent in them, this game puts too much emphasis on the space between them. There is no big AHA moments, where you would see a new area conncet back to an old one like in other games and ultimately those are the moments I love in FromSoftware games.

As I was saying in the beginning, this is by no means a bad game, it just feels like a punch in the face for anyone who loved the aspects of other FromSoftware games that this one is missing. As much as I like how them going open world to appeal to a wider audience made more people fall in love with their games, I really hope they go back to a more linear and interconnected design for their next main singleplayer entry.

I've played only a little over 8 hours by the point I began writing this review. Here are my thoughts:

Pros:
This game looks amazing, it has a great voice acting, sfx and music. Character customization is unbelievably vast and really thought through. The setting is interesting, some of the mechanics I've come across so far are also good (like different origin stories for your character, etc.). There seems to be a lot of things you can do, but I can't really judge that, since I've only played it a little and couldn't properly explore the entire game. Story overall also looks promising, although I can't really judge that either with 8 hours of gameplay.

Cons:
Now to the cons, which for me are currently overweighting the cons. The game feels clunky. The driving is awful, it is probably the worst driving I've seen so far, feeling even worse than FC3, which already was a pain in the ass for me. The gunplay is massively underwhelming in my opinion. Like how the hell am I dumping 3 shotgun mags into someone's head and they are still alive? Enemies are extreme bullet sponges and that just ruins the experience for me. Also, the guns feel really unresponsive and the melee is just sliding around the room, slashing at people without much depth. The dialogues are really long and "draggy". The quests so far have not really felt rewarding and were rather boring. Some of the mechanics, like braindancing, were just straight up immersion-breaking for me. It took so long to finish the first braindance quest that I straight up don't want to ever experience it again. It was an interesting idea, I don't deny that, but overall it just feels dull. 

With that being said, I currently can't recommend the game. I wish I could give it a neutral score, especially since I can see the good things it has to offer. I really wanted to give it a shot and like the game, but I currently don't have enough time on my hands to force myself into playing a game that doesn't really entertain me, hoping it gets better soon. It is my personal preference though and I can deffinitely see why some people love this game so much. For me, it just didn't feel worth to continue.

I am a huge CDPR fan, especially because of The Witcher games, in which I've invested hunderds of hours across different platforms, but these games just felt rewarding, the story was gripping, the setting was even better (for me personally) and I didn't mind spending so much time on it. With Cyberpunk2077 I can't really say the same. Chances are that I will eventually change my review later, if I ever get to a point of giving it another shot, in the future, but currently I will just leave it be.

Nach nun etwa 59 Stunden und dem Gefühl, dass ich nahezu jegliches Interesse daran verloren habe, das Spiel weiterzuspielen, möchte ich meine Eindrücke teilen.


[h1]Mein erster Durchlauf – Balanced[/h1]

Ich bin auf [b]Balanced[/b] gestartet, also mit einem ausgeglichenen Verhältnis zwischen Kampf und Exploration.

Das Spiel führt einen relativ tunnelförmig von Encounter zu Encounter und treibt dabei gleichzeitig die Story voran. Zwar gibt es Abzweigungen und alternative Wege, allerdings vermittelt einem das Spiel sehr schnell, wenn man sich in ein Gebiet begibt, das offenbar „zu schwer“ ist.

Ich bin beispielsweise dazu übergegangen, solche Gebiete zunächst schleichend zu erkunden – nur um erneut vermittelt zu bekommen, dass ich dort offenbar noch nichts zu suchen habe.

Was mich dabei besonders gestört hat: [b]Viele grundlegende Mechaniken werden kaum oder gar nicht erklärt.[/b]

Nach etwa drei Stunden starb meine Gruppe in einem Kampf, den ich im Nachhinein nicht einmal hätte führen müssen. Daraufhin wurde ich wieder an den Strand am Anfang des Spiels gesetzt. Es wurde in all der Zeit einfach nicht gespeichert... >_<


[list]
[*]Wie das Camp funktioniert, musste ich selbst herausfinden.
[*]Dass man regelmäßig Short Rests und Long Rests nutzen sollte, musste ich selbst herausfinden.
[*]Dass man praktisch nach jedem relevanten Schritt speichern sollte, musste ich ebenfalls selbst lernen.
[/list]


Ich habe mich anschließend bei Freunden erkundigt, wie man eigentlich sinnvoll progressen soll, ohne ständig auf Heilung oder Exploits angewiesen zu sein. Wirklich hilfreiche Antworten bekam ich dabei kaum.

Kurz vor Akt 2 kam dann nach einem extrem anstrengenden Kampf gegen die Phase Matriarch Spider der Punkt, an dem ich meinen ersten Charakter endgültig aufgegeben habe. Ich hatte schlicht keine Perspektive mehr für meinen gewählten Schleich-Charakter. Kaum passendes Gear, kaum passende Items und Händler, die für diese Spielweise kaum etwas anbieten.


[h1]Zweiter Durchlauf – Explorer[/h1]

Also neuer Versuch: Zwerg-Barbar auf [b]Explorer[/b].

Und plötzlich ist das komplette Gegenteil der Fall.

Die Kämpfe sind inzwischen so einfach, dass ich teilweise das Gefühl habe, sie auch mit einem einzelnen Charakter gewinnen zu können. Sicherlich helfen mir die inzwischen bekannten Mechaniken, aber auch das Verhalten und die Fähigkeiten der Gegner spielen dabei eine große Rolle.

Mittlerweile bin ich fast durch Akt 2 und habe unter anderem die Githyanki Creche nahezu vollständig ausgelöscht.

Dabei tritt allerdings ein weiterer Punkt auf, der mich mittlerweile massiv nervt:

Mechaniken wie [b]Entwaffnen[/b], die einem Schlichtweg nicht erläutert werden und denen man einfach ausgeliefert ist. Man müsste das Spiel und alle Mechaniken, jeden Schritt kennen, also das Spiel studieren um darauf reagieren zu können. Bedeutet, jeder weitere Kampf, wird ähnlich ablaufen und entweder ich Informiere mich, nutze buggy Interactions oder lade Kämpfe zich dutzende male neu um sie zu überwinden. 

Meine Charaktere werden gefühlt in jedem Kampf ständig entwaffnet. Gleichzeitig kann ich meine Waffen teilweise nicht einmal unmittelbar wieder ausrüsten, geschweige denn aufheben... 

Das Problem ist weniger, dass es diese Mechanik gibt, sondern dass das Spiel einem praktisch nicht erklärt, [b]wie man damit umgehen oder sich davor schützen soll.[/b]

Im Internet findet man dann Hinweise, dass mehr Stärke die Wahrscheinlichkeit reduzieren soll. Drei meiner Charaktere haben bereits 18 Stärke – und soweit ich zu diesem Zeitpunkt weiß, liegt das Maximum bei 20. Viel mehr kann ich also ohnehin nicht dagegen unternehmen.

Und wieder stehe ich vor dem gleichen Problem: Ich muss auf eine Mechanik reagieren, von der mir das Spiel praktisch nichts erklärt.

Und die Belohnungen sind einfach nicht existent. Etwas zu überwinden das extrems schwierig war, droppt in der Regel nichts was auch dementsprechend "WoW" oder "Geil" auslösen würde.  Solche Items sind hinter weirden Interaktionen versteckt. 


[h1]Das eigentliche Problem[/h1]

Und genau hier liegt für mich das grundlegende Problem mit BG3:

[b]Ich verstehe nicht, wo der Spaß entstehen soll, wenn man das Spiel nicht vorher ausgiebig recherchiert.[/b]

Jede Entscheidung fühlt sich potentiell wie ein Fehler an. Man speichert ständig, lädt Kämpfe neu, weil man zu viele Ressourcen verbraucht hat, verliert möglicherweise wichtige Items und erfährt teilweise erst Stunden später, dass man etwas hätte anders machen müssen.

Informiert man sich vorher im Internet, stellt man wiederum fest, dass man bereits vor 10 Stunden Entscheidungen getroffen oder Items verpasst hat, die man jetzt gerne gehabt hätte.

Also lädt man einen alten Spielstand.

Das erzeugt bei mir keinen Entdeckerdrang, sondern eher das Gefühl, das Spiel ständig gegen sich selbst absichern zu müssen.

Natürlich gibt es unglaublich viele Möglichkeiten und Entscheidungen. Aber wenn die Konsequenz daraus ist, dass ich nach jeder größeren Entscheidung überlegen muss, ob ich gerade möglicherweise einen wichtigen Inhalt für die nächsten 10 Stunden zerstört habe, dann nimmt mir das einen großen Teil des Spielspaßes.

Auch die Charaktere tragen für mich bisher nur begrenzt dazu bei. Man kann natürlich seine Begleiter meucheln und auf viele Dinge völlig anders reagieren – aber das bringt mir wenig, wenn ich anschließend nichts davon habe außer Nachteile. 

[b]Karlach ist für mich bisher die einzige Figur, die ich wirklich sympathisch finde.[/b]

Und nur wegen ihrer Geschichte möchte ich mir die restlichen ~100 Stunden ehrlich gesagt nicht antun.


[h1]Fazit[/h1]

BG3 bietet offensichtlich enorme Freiheit, unzählige Möglichkeiten und sehr viel Content.

Für mich fühlt sich diese Freiheit allerdings nicht wie Freiheit an, sondern wie eine Ansammlung potentieller Fehlentscheidungen, deren Konsequenzen ich ohne vorherige Recherche kaum einschätzen kann.

Nach rund 59 Stunden habe ich deshalb schlicht das Interesse verloren, weiterzuspielen.

[b]Für mich persönlich mehr Frust als Spielspaß.[/b]

The Witcher 3 is one of those games that makes it really easy to lose hundreds of hours.

The world is absolutely incredible. There are so many places to explore, characters to meet and stories to discover that even random side quests can turn into something memorable.

And that's probably my favorite thing about the game: the side quests. They don't just feel like filler between the main missions. A lot of them have their own stories, characters and choices, and some of them are honestly better than the main quest.

The characters are also a huge part of the experience. Geralt, Ciri, Yennefer, Triss and the rest of the cast make the world feel alive, and I actually cared about what happened to them.

The combat isn't perfect and can feel a little repetitive after a while, but there's enough variety with signs, potions, weapons and builds to keep things interesting.

The game is huge, and that can sometimes be a little overwhelming, but there's always something worth doing or discovering.

Even years later, The Witcher 3 still feels like one of the best open-world RPGs around.

Elden ring i would say is a good game, but massively overrated & personally not for me. I think the game's true rating would be more along a 7/10 (good) but instead i will be rating it a 6/10 (above average) taking into account my personal preference.

Elden ring's main issue is that it takes the souls formula and proceeds to cannibalize itself in the pursuit of the desire to always get "harder" for difficulties sake rather than simply trying to make a enjoyable & engaging game that is balanced while also being hard. Rather than bosses (mostly starting in the mid-to-late game and encompassing all of the DLC) being able to be fought with a universal skillset outside of a few like in previous souls games, boss battles in Elden Ring have now become rhythm & memorization games with the skill portion largely based around the capacity to have quick reaction timing to their attack patterns. In Elden Ring, outside the basic premise of timing your rolls, what you learn from one boss rarely carries over to the next since each boss is a memory-rhythm game where learning to dodge their specific patterns is the key to victory and that must be relearned over and over again with each new boss.

This made Elden Ring not fun to engage with (to me). Additionally and equally important, Enemies in Elden Ring have every cancer thing from previous souls games cranked up to 11 alongside new mechanics to make them as frustrating as possible. Here is a list of the issues with Elden Ring enemy design that are largely absent in previous Souls:
---- Bosses no longer play on a equal field as the player. Examples include Bosses having insane tracking to the point where they can just suspend the laws of physics and redirect their attack or entire movement trajectory just to catch you and some Bosses & normal enemies being able to animation cancel out of attacks while you have to commit to yours.
---- Bosses have tons of cheap moves that have little telegraphing of what they actually do and you can only know after it happens, alongside literal "snap-moves" that are so fast it's nearly impossible to dodge them unless you knew they were coming beforehand.
---- Mix-ups in boss patterns that are designed to catch you in a roll after your iframes end & confuse you are now a universal standard instead of a rarity and the large majority of boss battles in elden ring have them. Likewise, attacks being overly delayed just to throw you off is universal throughout the game as well.
---- Instead of phases being a rarity reserved for big/important bosses, in elden ring they begin to become a universal thing given to most bosses. Not only does this make the mechanic less unique & special, only reserved for certain bosses previously to make them really memorable fights, it also just artificially prolongs many fights & makes them tedious.
---- AOE instead of being reasonable and telegraphed during boss fights & a rarity outside of them are now spammed incessantly during said boss fights and many enemies throughout the world have them for little reason. Additionally AOE attacks in elden ring rarely make sense and were clearly just added for artificial difficulty; many attacks create nonsensical artillery-explosion-esque shockwaves for no reason, AOE screams/roars being a thing now that are spammed across many enemies and which can kill you for some reason, magical explosions hitboxes being overly large, etc.
---- Many boss attack patterns & their combos starting in the late-game and through the entirety of the DLC (the DLC having broke even many in the cultish git gud crowd apon release) become overly-long and full of visual clutter that makes them hard to keep up with, alongside the DLC bosses (and DLC normal enemies) dealing insane amounts of damage. These fights along with the above, as previously said, turns Elden Ring's gameplay during boss battles into just a rhythm game of dodgeroll memorization so you can get a single hit in before dodging the pattern all over again, maybe 2-3 if you've mastered that particular boss fight.


Other issues i have with the game;
---- The souls camera starts to show its limit when confronted with with all of these large bosses & more importantly extremely fast moving bosses that often jump high up
---- The open world is good & nice as a first-time experience but overall i feel like it hurts the game more than helps it, once you learn the game you can really abuse it with it's open world and after playing it once or twice most people just speed through the open world, skipping past the large majority of enemies & environments to get specific items for their build. The open world also makes the order of things feel disjointed with many encounters not playing off the way the developers expected them to because they didn't take into account the freedom of the open world, the level & power variance a player may have apon meeting the encounter and especially the speed capabilities of the horse in said encounters. Overall though, i would say the open-world does add to the first-time experience majorly even with it's flaws during and after.
---- Following up on that, bosses are reused excessively throughout Elden Ring in various ways from dungeons to those phantom versions, far more than any souls game before it. This is primarily due to the nature of it being a open world game.
---- The decision to not include Covenants in this game & abandon them can only be described as a negative as it provides no benefits while taking away alot of the Multiplayer interaction (as well as singleplayer).
---- Speaking on the above, Cooperative play is implemented poorly and requires modding to be made tolerable and in general the invader & phantom experience is a noticeable downgrade from previous entries.
---- Personally speaking, i am not a fan of the characters in this game or the lore (i don't like anything martin writes). I would definitely grab Marika by the hair and drag her to my room though.
---- Armor feels like paper and is mostly for the aesthetic, coming from DSII this feels particularly bad.

For positives, of course, the game is beautiful, the music is dark souls music so 10/10 typically, as previously said while i believe the Open World to be deeply flawed, on a first-time playthrough i think it definitely adds alot to the experience & is worth the inclusion over it being absent. And, still, despite the souls system of combat being massively overburdened in this game due to the bosses pushing the limits of what this system can handle (in a bad way), it's still souls combat, which i love and i think has been positively ingrained into many people at this point. Predictably the build variety is also insane in this game, potentially surpassing even Dark Souls II in this field. Lastly, as much as i have to complain about the bosses and as much as many of them are reused, the boss roster overall is highly unique.
If Elden Ring is your very first proper Souls game then i can see why the experience can feel magical.

Overall, i simply don't find Elden Ring to be fun to engage with both for it's flaws and my personal preference (i'm not a fan of very fast-paced combat games period, even though i can of course play them). Maybe i would like it more if i abandoned my old-souls mindset and abused things like spirit ashes, phantoms & cheese builds constantly. Regardless, that is my analysis & thoughts on Elden Ring.

[b]tl;dr[/b] - Many times I've regretted giving Baldur's Gate 3 chances. Turn back now.

Buy only at deep discount if you're a CRPG/D&D fan. Accolades and rampant Stockholm syndrome aside, this is a painfully flawed game three years after release, still unacceptably janky. If you're even slightly bothered by poor UX or bugs, prepare to suffer death by a thousand little cuts.

Let's begin...

[h2][b]The UI - frenemy at best, always pressing its thumb on the scale against you:[/b][/h2]

*  The default camera constantly gets in the way, obstructing free views of the battlefield. At times it's so disorienting you'll struggle to tell what's going on. Just to attack somebody the game keeps obscuring, you'll have to click this over here... then that over there... then that up there...(By Act 2 I had to install a mod just to make it playable).

* In a game where every other threat triggers turn based mode, when you encounter traps that do damage based on time, does it pause? Nope. Experience low level parties perishing on the clock as you frantically try to button-press your way out of it. Worse - press wrong, and it's possible to initiate dialogue between characters _as they burn in real time_. Like some dark comedy, your party is locked behind a text based UI, discussing whatever plot point Larian decided was more important than their gradually cooking into charcoal briquettes, screams punctuating your mouse clicks.

*  Try to shoot a pesky goblin who hit you just a moment before and it'll reply 'it's not possible', beginning a new mini-game: line-of-sight-wackamole. Spend many mouse clicks sleuthing which spot will allow you to return fire without yourself stumbling through acid, poison, or fire. Don't worry, if you give up, the auto-aim is always there to masochistically drag you through things that hurt.

[h2][b]Bugs - so many still awkward or outright broken features:[/b][/h2]

*  Group pathing is excellent... at doing exactly the wrong thing. Click to go around or even jump over that obviously dangerous acid pool, and your party members follow you... stumbling through it like idiots anyway. Break group to avoid this? Enjoy 4x the number of keystrokes and mouse clicks. There's no undo function for inevitable clicking mistakes - hope you don't mind frequently reloading from saves.

*  Quests glitch, incompletable due to some decision you made hours ago, or not starting at all. You can try to hide finished items in your bloated quest log but that feature will turn itself off every new session.

*  Items for summoning assistance in tough battles... activate in the wrong place and your mercenary ogres just stand there, their AI pathing unable to navigate a giant room (looking at you, Goblin Boss fight). Then afterwards, they'll demand 500 gold for literally doing nothing.

[h2][b]Annoyances - plenty to go around...[/b][/h2]

*  Enemies react utterly inconsistently, sometimes ignoring combat right in front of them (the realtime->turn-based transitional logic deserves its own post). Today a battle 'ended' within obvious view of an enemy who'd not yet aggro'd. Then, instead of giving back control, said non-combatant enemy suddenly 'woke up,' beginning a brand new fight! ...Cancelling all my prior-battle consumables and yanking me back to turn-based mode... despite neither pressing a button nor anybody moving. Oh goodie... guess I'll have to re-bless... and spend another charge of barbarian rage... and...

*  Don't you dare keep characters together for mutual support. Most people in the Baldur's Gate universe seems to carry acid bottles in their pocket, AoE so rampant it makes the previously mentioned line of sight problems even worse. D:OS2 explodium barrels(tm) return for several guest appearances too. Stand in the wrong place and... boom, sweep up your character's residue~

*  Action bars change without your consent and the logic for placing new buttons is poor at best, dumping icons haphazardly. Hope you like futzing with everything over and over again if you're remotely interested in customizing. Every level. Every new weapon type.

[h2][b]And the rest...[/b][/h2]

How does Larian compensate for some of these problems? By shoving at you small mountains of consumables and vendor trash items until your bags nearly burst, becoming a tedious inventory. Rewards are oddly paced, progression just mildly interesting. Resources go out of wack once you recognize camp supplies are basically limitless, allowing you to long rest after every battle, far more than any D&D campaign would allow.

Too easy? Turn up the difficulty so UI flaws become downright hostile. You'll struggle to get characters to do what you want, a single mis-click frequently ending battle in catastrophe. Eventually saving before every battle round isn't cheesing - it becomes... necessary.

Sigh.

On the plus side, the story is remarkable for its many paths - no other title I've tried goes to these lengths (though expect cliche and forced moments - Shadowheart... I just met you and you're trying to jump my bones). And the many lines of dialogue, well acted, making you feel like you're part of an actual world? Solid.

But even when the best parts rise to the surface, starting to immerse you, the jank buzzes back into your face like some aggravating fly you can't waive off, reminding you're just playing a messy CRPG that will never get the polish it desperately needs. There might be a good game... buried... under all this... somewhere... but it's tiring to look. If you're not familiar with D&D 5e, it'll be twice as hard.

"Okay, relax, you're just being picky..."

"It's just a game, reload and start again..."

"...This is fun..."

<<Game Lucy-Footballs me with some new issue>>

"..."

Not sure I'll ever reach Act 3. Quit more than once, then blown the dust off months later while bored and had no other games to play. Do I hate myself? Guess so. Will I continue to fall for it? Probably - that's on me. Do I believe in this negative review? With all my heart.

Thank you for reading. /rant

The open world just destroys the flow of the game. It doesn't feel like exploring, but more like working a 9-to-5 just to reach the next legacy dungeon and finally get another taste of actual level design.

More than half of the game is made up of useless horizontal planes with different textures or, when the game feels generous, those same planes decorated with good-looking solid objects planted into the ground.

The game can often be visually impressive, but that alone contributes very little to the actual enjoyment of the exploration itself.

And the legacy dungeons aren't that much better, to be honest. Excluding Farum Azula, I don't feel like any of them really tries to propose a distinctive or interesting way of exploring in the way almost every area of Dark Souls did. Stormveil is basically a castle, Raya Lucaria is a castle with mages, Volcano Manor is a castle with lava, Leyndell spends most of its time feeling like a traditional dungeon crawler, and the Haligtree is okay but ultimately forgettable.

This doesn't mean the game looks bad. Quite the opposite: very often it looks fantastic. But visuals are only part of the job in a medium built around interaction. It's crazy to me that, despite being the first entry with a dedicated jump button, this somehow feels like the Souls game where exploration is least enjoyable.

The reward structure makes things even worse. The game fills the world with useless items in an attempt to create the illusion that wandering around is worthwhile. Half the time you go out of your way to reach some distant corner of the map only to find a crafting material or recipe whose function you'll forget five seconds after picking it up.

And then there are the catacombs and mines.

I hope you really like those assets, because you're going to see them a lot. They feel almost procedurally assembled: repetitive, unimaginative, full of dead space and absurdly unrewarding considering how much of a slog many of them are.

The entire map could have been one quarter of its current size. If that smaller space had been properly filled and given more attention, I'd probably be the happiest Souls player alive.

But thank God there are the incredibly rewarding boss fights.

Yes, I absolutely love being input-read into an AoE, roll-catching, delayed one-shot attack during a seven-hit tracking true combo. At some point you genuinely start wondering whether having somebody punch you while you're playing would improve the experience, if only because the physical pain might distract you from the spiritual hassle of fighting yet another random boss.

And that's assuming the boss isn't recycled. Be prepared to fight the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing over and over again, or, even better, a normal enemy arbitrarily promoted to boss status for the occasion. It's lazy design taken to an absurd level. There isn't a single boss in the entire game that I genuinely look forward to fighting again. Maybe Malenia and Morgott.

Regular enemies aren't much better, although their biggest problem is less the movesets themselves and more the absurd damage numbers. After a certain point, even with a full tank build, almost everything can practically two-shot you.

That doesn't mean their movesets aren't filled with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, because they absolutely are, but the damage is so aggressively overtuned in an attempt to inflate difficulty that every other problem almost becomes secondary.

That constant feeling of unfairness, combined with some of the least rewarding exploration I've experienced in this kind of game, pushes the frustration to another level.

What keeps Elden Ring afloat is its build diversity and lore. In combat, you can use almost anything and create an enormous variety of viable builds, while the world and its mythology are genuinely compelling. The problem is that the experience surrounding those strengths is often so exhausting that eventually you stop caring about what is in front of you, because everything starts feeling like another chore.

Worst entry in the series, and overall an average to below-average game.

If I also judge it against the minimum level of progress one should reasonably expect from a later installment in an established series, I have to mention how unacceptable the state of the AI is. Enemies are frequently just braindead.

The environmental storytelling has also become strangely self-celebratory. It was one of the defining strengths of the earlier games, but an open world should have been the opportunity to expand that formula and communicate the setting in more organic ways: through cities, settlements, populated spaces, or basically anything that made the world feel more alive.

Instead, despite having exponentially more space to work with, the game often falls back on the exact same formula: empty ruins, cryptic environmental details and item descriptions carrying most of the narrative burden.

At that point it stops feeling elegant and starts feeling lazy.

Once you look past the surface the veil drops as quick as the disappointment hits you because there's hints of greatness everywhere, however the story as a whole, the little moments, the world and the gameplay just don't live up to the potential. 

Buckle up because there's A LOT to say. 

The game is BUGGY. Not in an obvlivion haha look at this funny NPC exchange way, just [i] embarrassingly so. [/i]
Tons of visual bugs, flashbangs exiting menus, physics bugs, unlootable enemies, NPC's phasing through walls or spawning in and out of nowhere and the game even softlocking me a few times with unkillable enemies and that's all on the latest "2.0 comeback" patch. 
[url=https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLv4LBJ7ubTUXF34qf_S6HSCKK7Ijc0kLX] Here you can find some of the bugs I encountered [/url] (I will be adding more clips as time goes on) 

Even if that weren't the case:

The city, while pretty as I said, is empty. There's nothing to do. Only three types of activities. 
- Main and side missions, which usually are a big chain of zones to clear after listening to uninteresting dialogue for 10+ minutes. 
- Side gigs, which are usually just a big zone with enemies to clear and get -item/person- of interest.
- Police scanner missions, which are usually small zones of enemies to clear and a lootbox. 

The activities are all the same, scale being the only differentiating factor and a great part of the stories (especially in side content) is told through logs / mails which is extremely lazy and makes everything feel samey. 
The only deviation here are the races (only 4 in total) which are a joke and a repeatable fetch quest they added in the DLC. 

When it comes to the gameplay itself... again there's glimpses of greatness, it can be VERY satisfying at times, hacking away and causing mayhem but there just isn't anything to it. Whether an enemy is an "elite" or not only changes how tanky they are. Sometimes they dash around and sometimes they don't. They don't work together, they don't have any synergies between them. There's no reason to prioritize one enemy over another besides snipers. 
At some point I was going around causing everyone to suicide without lifting a finger. At first it was funny, then it just became boring, not that shooting tanky enemies over and over is all that much more exciting. 
The bosses are all lackluster, tanky and just run at you in a straight line. 
What's funny is the tankier the enemies are the more it highlights all the animation and feedback issues with the combat and I don't even know why ammo is a thing since you never run out.  
Also stealth is a joke, as in it makes every encounter trivial, even more so than it already was. 
To add to all of that, there is no reason to use anything other than Iconic weapons. You get tons of those so the vast majority of the loot you get is rendered useless besides crafting mats. Apparel barely gives stats, so you can forget about that mattering too. 

Would have been serviceable for a great story... but yeah the game is lacking there too. Besides Johnny and Panaam there's no memorable characters to speak of.  Most plotlines and character archetypes have been done better in superior sci fi stories. 
Johnny is a foil to V and only reacts to things and characters happening around V, so his character can only do so much to stay interesting. V is a non-character which only exists to ask stupid questions, everyone talks so slow as if they are mentally handicapped and / or like a angsty 15 year old. The main story contradicts the mission design. You are supposed to be dying but you can spend endless hours not only clearing the map of busy work but dabbling in the side missions which CAN affect the main stories choices. Except that side content... takes time, time you don't have yet V is completely chill just going on random misadventures with whoever asks something of him. 
Credit where credit is due, there are some decent choices in some missions but it doesn't matter when you find none of it interesting. 
This isn't even approaching how interesting and intricate the dialogue in Witcher was.

Also to add to my frustrations, ♥♥♥♥ the advertismenets. World building my ass, there's no way to turn off TV's and Radios and you are constantly bombarded by at least 5 different sources of sound blasting the same 4-5 ads over and over and over. 

I haven't even gotten to how terrible the skill tree is but alas, the review is getting long as it is. I could go in great detail about a lot of things and honestly no other game has made me want  to write a video essay as much as this due to the insane amount of undeserved glazing it receives online I'm going to leave it here. 

Would I recommend this game to someone else? 
Despite my 100+ hours, hell no.

[b]Baldur's Gate 3 is my new favorite game of all time.[/b]

I picked it up during early access and it hooked me right from the start. After about four hours I shelved it, since the full launch was only four months away and I really wanted to play it from beginning to end. Now I have over 500 hours in the game, I've played through it more times than I can count, and I've 100% completed it. That's something I haven't done with any other game in my Steam library.

[b]The Characters & Story[/b]
The narrator is amazing. Her voice work and the writing behind her lines are so well done.

The story is decent, but what really makes the game for me is the cast. Every character you meet along the way is fantastic, and they make you genuinely want to help them. My favorite is Karlach. She is such a sweet, kind-hearted character, and her questline is really good. The best questline in the game, though, belongs to Shadowheart. Her story can go in multiple directions, and you get to influence who she really becomes in the end. The romance system is decent too, though some romances are far better than others.

[b]Combat & Builds[/b]
The builds are incredibly customizable. Honor Mode kicked my butt and I had to restart more times than I'd like to admit, but my Gloom Stalker/Assassin build finally got me through it. The most fun build I've played is a Monk/Rogue. You get so many attacks, and the movement is amazing. Between the build variety and the mod support, the game stays fresh even on a sixth or seventh run.

[b]Player Freedom[/b]
You can play it however you want. If you want to be the good guy and save everyone, you can. If you want to be the bad guy and take everyone out, you can do that too. The replayability is crazy.

[b]My One Criticism[/b]
Act 1 is top tier, above and beyond anything else, but Acts 2 and 3 just don't feel as fleshed out. Act 1 gives you so many places to explore, from the open world at the start, down into the Underdark, all the way to the Grymforge. The later acts don't quite match that. Don't get me wrong, they're still better than most games being made today, and I would rather play them than most AAA releases. The drop is just noticeable.

I can't say enough good things about this game. The characters, the storytelling, and the performances from every voice actor are outstanding. If you haven't played it yet, do yourself a favor and pick it up.

[b]Final Score: 10/10[/b]

The irony is staggering, and it is easily one of the greatest examples of real-world corporate hypocrisy in gaming history. The developer became the exact villain they were warning us about.

CD Projekt Red spent years marketing a story about a dystopian future where greed destroys lives, workers are treated like garbage, and corporate executives lie to the public for a massive payday—and then they turned around and did it themselves.

1. The Corporate Exploitation of Workers (Crunch Culture)

The Promise: The studio’s leadership publicly promised their developers that they would not use forced "crunch" (mandatory, extreme overtime) to finish the game.

The Reality: As deadlines approached, corporate executives mandated six-day work weeks, with many developers working brutal 16-hour days for months on end just to patch a broken product. They literally ran a human-grinder corporate sweatshop to ship a game about human-grinder corporate sweatshops.

2. The Multi-Million Dollar Lie

The Corporate Gaslighting: To secure millions of pre-orders and protect their stock price, the executives actively lied to the public and their investors. They claimed the game ran "surprisingly well" on older consoles (PS4/Xbox One) when they knew it was completely unplayable.

Review Manipulation: In true corporate fashion, they heavily restricted review copies. They forbade reviewers from using their own gameplay footage on older consoles, forcing them to use pre-rendered corporate B-roll. It was a calculated, anti-consumer media blackout designed to milk the consumer before the truth came out.

3. Turning Rebellious Art into Corporate Slop

The True Irony: Johnny Silverhand is a character whose entire identity is about bombing a corporate headquarters to fight the system. CD Projekt Red turned that punk-rock anti-corporate icon into a marketing puppet used to sell limited-edition Porsche cars, branded energy drinks, and gaming chairs.

Night City isn't just a fictional warning anymore. The way Cyberpunk 2077 was handled proved that we already live in a cyberpunk world—where a massive company can package the idea of "rebellion," sell it to us for ₹4,000, break their workers in the process, and still walk away with a massive profit.

After decades of playing role-playing games, BG3 simply doesn't appeal to me. Larian's approach is more akin to a scavenger hunt than role-playing. Many encounters seem to be built around "you should have known" rather than organic progression, and the game penalizes you for not exploring every square inch of every map. Yes, it's well-made and packed with content, but the experience strongly favors min-maxing, guides, and meta-gaming. You'll love it if you like investigating builds and making the most of every interaction. This isn't the kind of classic role-playing game you want if you want to play your character without constantly checking every wiki page and barrel.

REVISION: After putting in more time, I’m changing this to a "Positive" rating, though with heavy caveats.

While I still find Larian’s "scavenger hunt" style of exploration and "meta-knowledge" encounters frustrating, I can't deny the sheer level of detail and craft here. If you are willing to play the game the way it wants to be played, it is a brilliant experience.

I'm still grappling with the idea that it's a universally acclaimed "masterpiece." The game is a brutal, complex CRPG that frequently punishes you for not consulting a guide or, say, a random barrel. However, it is a high-quality product that rewards a specific playstyle. It's a strong game nonetheless.

REVISION 2: After waiting a while and coming back to it, the same feeling remains: a strong start, but a disappointing follow‑through. Act 1 sets expectations the rest of the game never really meets. The pacing drops, the content quality becomes inconsistent, and many quests start feeling like chores compared to the early high‑stakes encounters. It’s worth a try if you’re curious, but overall I’m still not as happy with it as most people seem to be.

Previous Souls games made enemy encounters difficult through careful placement and unique aspects of each type of enemy, but Elden Ring is filled to the brim with rage monsters and little else. Most enemies will only permit you a single attack before their combos start up again. It's not engaging, it's an exercise in frustration and something that slowly eats away at your enjoyment of the game until the whole experience is mind-numbingly dull.

Technical issues were never the biggest problem.  And that's coming from someone that first played the game to completion on PS4 almost 5 years ago.

As a fan of CDPR games like The Witcher series, and of the original Cyberpunk 2020 tabletop RPG, I truly wanted to enjoy this game.

...what, you didn't know this game was based off a TTRPG?  That was the original concept of this game: a video game adaptation not unlike CRPG's like Baldur's Gate did for D&D.  That's why back in 2012, CDPR "promised" things like:
* a "mature RPG...set in a rich, futuristic world" 
* a "gripping non-linear story filled with life and detail"
* "advanced RPG mechanics based on pen & paper RPG system"
* "varied selection of different character classes"

If only.

Night City could have, and should have, been one of the most expansive interactive, raw, gut wrenching environments ever to exist in gaming history.  The TTRPG even says that Night City should basically be its own character with everything it has to offer.  But instead, you get city block after city block of empty buildings, non-functional store fronts and window dressing.  A detailed world of which very little can be interacted with.  Most NPC's barely have anything more to say than a zombie would, and blend in with the background.  

One of the fixers tells you not to spend all your money on "glitter and XBD's".  Which would be hilarious if it was not so sad already, because in this game there is no glitter or XBD that you can buy in any meaningful way, in contrast to what the TTRPG offers.

The world of Witcher 3, by comparison, offers far more of a "rich world" with "life and detail".  And then consider games like Deus Ex and Daggerfall which came out decades before Cyberpunk 2077 did, and yet had far more interactive worlds by comparison.

The game is basically GTA set in the future: loot, shoot and run.  Some of the new quests added in the expansion are literally just stealing a car and driving to the target destination, while escaping from the police and any other aggrieved parties.

Quests are still mostly linear and handheld with waypoints.  Only practical variation seems to be dialog choices which seem surface level at best.  One of the "new quests" added in this edition is literally just repeatable recycled dialogue and animations, not even updating as you progress in Phantom Liberty.

You have a choice of lifepath when you create your character, being either a nomad, street rat or corpo, but these only affect the first hour of the game, and then anything afterwards is just the occasional unique dialog choice.  There's no unique equipment, missions or endings based on your lifepath.  

There are no "classes" in the traditional RPG sense in this game.  There's a skill tree, and you can invest in different stats which come with different skills to specialize in specific weapons or playstyles, but there's no choosing a class at character creation like a solo, netrunner or fixer like the TTRPG.

The Phantom Liberty expansion adds a single new area: a previously inaccessible area of Pacifica called "Dogtown".  This place is a run down, almost post apocalyptic neighborhood, so it doesn't really add to the "cyberpunk" theme of this game.  If anything, it's almost poetic how reflective this is of the state of Night City: mostly empty and a shell of itself compared to what could have been.  Compare how much extra content The Witcher 3 expansions "Heart of Stone", and "Blood and Wine" added.

To give credit where it's due: the Phantom Liberty expansion does add one new ending to the base game, based on certain choices you make in the Phantom Liberty storyline.  But without regard to story choices made in that ending, there's no final mission, no final boss, or any build up; just your usual follow the waypoints, talk to characters, move on, maybe get some dialog choices, etc.  So it's very unrewarding.

While I'll admit this game is a bit of a guilty pleasure for me, there's just too many flaws to the game's design that no amount of expansion will solve.  CDPR knows how to make good RPG's with the Witcher series, and games like Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 perfected the CRPG genre decades ago with a tiny fraction of the technology available when this game was made, so there's no excuse.

The more I play this game, the more I don't like it. For a game so complete, it's missing so much. 
There's the small things, like the Dash action being the only action you can't cancel, to having no confirmation on whether or not you want to end your turn (I've accidentally hit "end turn" a lot and f-cked myself over).. and nonsensical errors, like being told "you can't fast travel" when you try to long rest while a party member's dead body is out in the open. (Why can't it just say "you can't rest while a party member's body is in the open?")

Then, there's the continuity issues. At the very first settlement in the game, I talk to a friendly tiefling because a rat led me into a storage room. The tiefling is content with my presence, but another one walks by and sentences me to prison for trespassing! 
Another time, I was accused of stealing immediately as I entered the settlement when I did no such thing. I was forced to battle enemies much too strong because of it, and essentially resulted in a forced loss. 

Next, if you don't bring some of the game's offerings of party members with you as soon as possible, you will get trampled with way too many enemies and have no chance. That wouldn't be so bad if the options weren't all so boring! None of them are fun or interesting, and some of them are a chore to have around, like Gale. 

It's also way too easy to agro people! I have to save every 2 minutes because any random conversation will end up triggering a massive battle with 20 people! 

Controls are confusing. If you click on a health potion in your action menu for example, it doesn't give you options for what to do with it. It just drinks it. You have to click 'throw item' first, then select the health potion.. that's backwards. So many times I've wasted health potions, poison, etc. because of this. 

Lastly, the battling itself is just so boring. It goes so slowly! Although it moves faster than real D&D, it just feels so flat and uneventful. And get ready for enemies to have 1HP left and every PC you have to miss miss miss miss miss miss. On enemies at the start of the game.

I never thought I’d ever rate The Witcher 3 negatively, because it’s my all time favorite game... but they completely screwed it up with the re-remaster.
The game already had Ray Tracing (which is important) in the so called “Next-Gen” version from 2022. Now, with the re-remaster, the game runs ONLY in Ray Tracing mode (so basically like the Next-Gen version), but with half the frame rate...

I have a 4090 and a 5800X3D. The Next-Gen version runs at 4K with DLSS Quality, max settings + Ray Tracing at around 60–70 FPS in Novigrad. With Frame Generation, I get around 120–140 FPS.

The remastered version, using the exact same save file and identical max settings, runs at only around 30-40 FPS with Ray Tracing, and barely over 60 FPS with Frame Generation.

I honestly wonder why nobody seems to care about optimization anymore, or why they keep pushing such an old engine to its limits over and over again. I mean, the Next-Gen version already had Ray Tracing. So what exactly is the reason for cutting the FPS in half with essentially identical Ray Tracing? This is just horribly optimized.

Then they changed the tone mapper, and the new version simply looks overexposed and almost like a camera Log profile. And that's despite the fact that I'm playing on a proper 4K OLED with properly configured HDR.

It completely destroys the look of the game and the original art style.

Anyway, I’ve gone back to the Next-Gen version. Thanks to Steam for making that possible through the game’s settings.

With a few mods, the game actually looks significantly better than the re-remaster while running at roughly twice the performance. So honestly, I can only recommend making your own “remastered” version with mods. It simply looks better and runs better.

This review is about the Remastered version.
For me, the original game is one of the best ever made. The writing and script are among the very few in video games that can boast novel quality book perfection. The art and environments are equally impressive. The original had only one major (though forgivable, given the quality of the rest) flaw: the gameplay. It wasn't THAT bad, but it had significant issues.

The Remastered:
Graphics:
It looks like they simply threw in ray/path tracing without any real tweaking or optimization. The result is that the game still looks beautiful, but the lighting behaves very strangely broken at times.

Gameplay:
I watched a long livestream where the developers emphasized that there would be many small changes, which together would ensure a better gameplay experience. That turned out to be completely untrue; unless it's a bug issue, I think they actually made the gameplay worse.
I had to disable the new dynamic camera; it gives me a headache.
Enemy behavior is atrocious. I can't tell if it's just buggy, but if it's intentional, it's unforgivable. I tend to think it's just buggy, given how poorly they behave.
It seems like the distance calculations are completely broken.

Geralt's movement is terrible and feels stiff/locked-in. It’s just like the original, back in 2015, the developers justified it by calling it "realistic," but in reality, a fat a** like me can turn, move, and sprint with far more grace, speed, and precision than Geralt.
In the remaster, it actually seems even worse somehow.
Perhaps this is linked to the fact that everything is buggy,I hope so, at least could be fixed. 
Combatting enemies has become far more frustrating than in the original.
As previously mentioned, the spacing "feels" broken, as do the hitboxes. Enemies move and behave as if they never know what to do, and not in a "tactically unpredictable" way; they just seem genuinely buggy and broken.

Audio.
The audio was generally excellent in the original, save for two issues that haven't been addressed at all here.
1. The music is wonderful overall, but after dozens of hours, it becomes truly repetitive and annoying during exploration because it is essentially a single track on an endless loop. It would have been so easy to include an option to pause the continuous music; instead, I’m forced to mute it entirely.

2. When the Witcher uses his swords, the impact sound is the same regardless of what you hit, armor, wood, or flesh. Instead of sounding like a sword strike, it sounds like a pinprick in every instance. You can't feel the impact, which significantly detracts from the gameplay experience.

Honestly, even though it’s free, I expected more care, love and polish from CDPR. I am very disappointed and hope they fix it.

I don't expect this to be seen by someone legitimately wondering if this game is worth picking up or not. I don't even expect this to be seen by anyone really but to begin: Elden Ring is at best a mid game and at worst a terrible one.

You will frequently be put in situations where you have to hope for RNG that the enemies don't move in a way that locks you into unavoidable death, bosses that deal ridiculous damage while you deal nothing, enemies that have ridiculous stats despite what they are (e,g, archers with large health pools and ridiculous damage reduction on top of that). You will get to experience the constant cycle of having to guess when an attack is going to happen because the enemy has 3 different versions of the same attack that are all identical in start-up but come out at different speeds that deal high damage. Not to mention the FromSoft special of lingering hitboxes or hitboxes that just plain make no sense, almost always to the detriment of you! Another FromSoft classic too of enemies having grabs that inflict bleed so they will 99% of the time kill you. On top of all that, enemies just plain do not follow the same rules you do, they will not run out of FP, they do not have to stop their combos at any fixed point and can string as many attacks together as they want (this is mild hyperbole, they genuinely can string together their hardest to avoid moves in one combo and I've had enemies that forced me to wait dodging through 7 attacks before I could even attempt to poke them) and speaking of stats:

Poise does next to nothing relevant in this game. It will help your attack not get interrupted if you get hit by something while charging a heavy attack but god forbid you don't want to be staggered by every pebble that hits you regardless of what you're wearing.

Level design where traps, hidden doors, and enemies are just thrown at you in ways where you'd think you'd get a grace after running low on healing despite having 10 flasks and, oops no sorry. Did you die? Make that entire slog again, bud. Oh that hole you need to dodge a trap? It's a small enemy that you're going to end up either dying to the trap trying to hit the enemy or die from the enemy somehow almost instantly proccing bleed or some other status effect on you. The Haligtree is a perfect example of another issue with the level design: Elden Ring does not do platforming well, at all. You will be put in situations where you will wonder if it's even what the devs intended before realizing, yes, they did in fact and- oh sorry you stood on the wrong part of the branch bud you will not be punished for the bad game design with death.

I think FromSoft games were what made me fully realize there is nothing more infuriating than a game over that takes way too long to get you back in the game. Ironically, for as quick as your health drains it's actually fairly long to die in this game. You get your choice of a quick death where the game still sits before finally going to the loading screen or on the opposite end: an animation that takes what feels like a full minute before you even get to the 5 second needless linger part that boots you to the loading screen.

TL;DR Elden Ring is mid at best and bad at worst. Play Dragon's Dogma or Hollow Knight for games that do the "challenging but fair" approach (in Hollow Knight's case) or the open-world medieval approach in DD's case

Cyberpunk 2077 is, in my opinion, the best story-driven RPG I've played in years. What makes it so special is that every part of the game feels carefully crafted. The main story is emotional, gripping, and filled with unforgettable moments, but what truly surprised me was the quality of the side content. Unlike many open-world games where side quests feel like repetitive filler, Cyberpunk's side missions are so well-written and unique that they often feel like they could be part of the main storyline. Many of them introduce memorable characters, unexpected twists, and meaningful choices that make every mission worth playing.

The attention to detail is simply incredible. Night City is one of the most immersive worlds I've ever explored. Every district has its own identity, architecture, atmosphere, and people. The city constantly feels alive, with crowds walking the streets, traffic moving through highways, advertisements covering every building, and countless small details that make the world believable. Even the Badlands outside the city have their own unique atmosphere, making the contrast between the urban chaos and the empty desert feel natural and immersive.

Visually, Cyberpunk 2077 is absolutely stunning. The lighting, weather effects, reflections, animations, and overall art direction make almost every location look like it belongs in a sci-fi movie. Whether you're driving through the neon-lit streets at night or watching the sunrise over the Badlands, the game is full of breathtaking moments.

The RPG systems are another reason why I love this game. The skill tree gives you the freedom to create completely different builds depending on how you want to play. You can become a deadly Netrunner who hacks enemies from a distance, a stealth assassin using throwing knives and silenced weapons, a cyber-enhanced samurai with katanas, or a heavily armored tank charging into combat with shotguns and LMGs. Cyberware implants, perks, iconic weapons, and countless equipment combinations make character progression incredibly satisfying.

Replayability is another area where Cyberpunk truly shines. Every new playthrough can feel completely different thanks to the different lifepaths, dialogue options, character builds, romances, endings, and even your character's gender. The choices you make throughout the game often change conversations, relationships, and the way certain missions unfold, giving you plenty of reasons to experience the story multiple times.

What really sets Cyberpunk 2077 apart is how all of these systems come together. The outstanding writing, unforgettable characters, meaningful side quests, incredible attention to detail, gorgeous visuals, deep progression systems, and the living, breathing world create an experience that feels unique from beginning to end. Very few games manage to combine storytelling, gameplay, exploration, and role-playing this well, which is exactly why I consider Cyberpunk 2077 the best RPG I've played in a very long time.

The first maybe 40 or so hours was some of the most fun I've ever had in any video game, and I realize I've been chasing that high ever since, and somehow it only got worse. 

Firstly, the most blatant weakness for me is the storytelling: it's a joke. I can tell there's some interesting lore and characters somewhere in there, but it's presented in a completely incomprehensible manner. 

"You must seek the Elden Ring and become Elden lord!" okay, cool. Why? You are given the vaguest of the vaguest motivations to do *anything* in this game. I meet random characters with absolutely no context or build-up, that apparently I'm supposed to care for.  I have no idea who am I fighting and why. There's barely any RP in this supposed RPG, as joining 'factions' and completing side-quests is completely inconsequential. Not to mention those aforementioned side-quests have incredibly obscure requirements to complete, some feel almost impossible without the wiki.

I understand FromSoft is known for indirect storytelling, but when you want to tell a classic, multilayered fantasy epic, this style simply does not work. It's a completely ridiculous proposition that I'm supposed to rely on vague item descriptions to understand major plot points. Again, this would be fine on some other game that wasn't heavily touted as "having a great narrative written by George RR Martin!!"

Once I realized the story was pretty much non-existent, my open world immersion and suspension of disbelief was irrecoverably shattered. I began to see cool ruins as nothing more than simple repeated 3D assets thrown randomly across the landscape. It's absolutely clear that the devs had no idea what the story behind most places in this game really was, they just expect the players to fill in the blanks. That is not even mentioning the INSANE amount of recycled areas, enemies and bosses in this game. 

Well, the story is kind of bad, at least the game can redeem itself with its gameplay right? Eh, sort of. Like I said in the beginning, I thoroughly enjoyed the early/midgame. The enemy variety was great, and I had tons of fun fighting the early bosses.

However, that's where much of my enjoyment ended. What I started realizing, is that the open world aspect of the game doesn't really work. Here's what happens in Elden Ring all the time: you stumble across a boss or a difficult area which feels way too hard and you think "okay, I'll just explore and come back later." You come back after some hours, realize you've grown vastly more powerful, and the fight becomes an unsatisfying cakewalk. It's such a shame too, because some of the coolest bosses visually were the exact ones I beat in one try. There were some bosses that I  didn't have to engage with, because I could just brute-force it by chugging down health potions. 

The other category of bosses and enemies is those that are wholly anti-fun, attacking so rapidly that you can't play in a proactive manner. There are bosses that legitimately feel like I was playing a turn-based game, since I could get in a hit safely once in a blue moon. There's so many cool skills and playstyles in this game, but it feels like you aren't allowed to experiment with any of them. My complaint has nothing to do with the difficulty, it's about the forced defensive and reactive playstyle.  

That is, if you don't use spirit summons, which are one of the most baffling design choices in this game. The spirits summons turn most fights into a joke, as they draw aggro from enemies and allow you to freely act as you wish. This is clearly meant to be an accessibility mechanic, but it almost feel like the devs designed certain encounters around them. It almost feels like the devs are constantly whispering my ears like "oh geez, this encounter sure is a bit difficult, are you sure you don't want to use the summons bro?"  

This all leads to an extremely unbalanced experience. If I died, it felt I got cheesed out. If I beat a difficult enemy, I felt I cheesed them, as opposed to feeling like a hero who has slain an epic monster. It all feels very...mechanical in nature, which is the absolute killer of my immersion.

So this is it. The Holy Grail of gaming. The Second Coming of RPGs.

Let me tell you about my combat experience. I see an enemy. I have a bow. He’s on a roof. Simple, right? WRONG. The camera said “absolutely not” and locked itself into a position that let me admire some really nice brick textures instead. I died staring at architecture. Immersive.

The turn-based combat is an incredible innovation for people who think chess is too fast-paced. There’s a goblin three inches from my face. I have a sword. I have murder in my heart. But I have zero action points because I had the AUDACITY to walk here. So I just… stand there. Menacingly. The goblin and I share an awkward moment. He’s probably thinking about his family. I’m thinking about uninstalling.

And god forbid you don’t have a PhD in D&D mechanics. Every ability has a description longer than my apartment lease. “Roll a d20, add your modifier, subtract your will to live, consult the moon phase chart…” I just want to hit things. Why is there homework?

Yes, you can do “anything.” You can talk to animals. Betray everyone. Push people into chasms. Very impressive. But between those five minutes of chaos, there are seven hours of moving at the speed of bureaucracy.

I made a stealth runner, stealth and magic, methodically crawling through dungeons, taking my time to not be seen, and by level 12 I was pretty good at it. Then for the next 31 levels nothing changed. When i turned to the internet to figure out why the downtime in my gameplay loop hadn't improved in 30 levels. I found that there were more efficient combos and perk choices that I could be making. So after some research and spending some of my in-game money, I improved my build. Or so I though. The downtime had gotten shorter, but not significantly so. So little, in fact, that I would argue that it hadn't changed. Then after more research, I found that certain resource-recovery perks were intentionally disconnected from the most popular stealth quickhack combos, without it being mentioned anywhere in the game. I can only assume this was done for marketing purposes? Because the first version of the game was such a failure (not that I had invested a lot of time into it back then, and personally dont have an opinion about early CyberPunk77) that they decided to allow only fast paced action builds to shine so that they could redeem themselves more quickly through paid youtube shillery.

Ok, fine. So i put together a Damage over Time build that used the whip to detonate the debuffs. But I found that the interaction between the skills was rarely happening and that fights would only be explosively fast. With yet more research I found that the whip's hit scan function was bugged and ultra thin, so when you were attempting to hit the also bugged hitboxes of mobs who were displaying debuff animations. So my whip attacks were hitting less than 20% of the time and enemies were dying slowly to the DoT's alone.

From my experience alone, it can be surmised that, either on purpose or on accident, no single part of this game actually works. Certainly if you don't want to play sandevistan/katana build you shouldn't spend money on it either.

The narrative is irritating. I get that V is a headstrung, insecure, dumbass, but how many story hooks can start with my character being forced by the game to do something dangerously stupid? Am I expected to believe that she grew up in night city? I've been here 15 minutes and can tell you those jerks are going to do something jerky.

Also as an accomplished netrunner, V constantly praising Songbird and "needing" her for hacking jobs felt bad. Luckily my V was a weak nerd though, because if i was a sandevistan using katana wielder, I would have been pissed that the game required me to constantly ask the help of a geriatric woman to open all the doors in that intro.

Ultimately I think I'm done with CDprokect Red for a while. Maybe they'll get their act together eventually, but at this point in time I think we can safely say that the constant development issues over there are a feature, not a bug.

Review:

Baldur,s Gate 3 redefines systemic reactivity in computer role playing games, translating tabletop freedom into a digital space where player choice consistently reshapes narrative and mechanical outcomes.

Strengths:

Improvisational sandbox: The physics engine, surface interactions, and verticality allow creative problem solving that treats spells and environment as interactive tools rather than scripted events.

Reactive narrative branches: Companion arcs and main storylines adapt dynamically to player decisions, maintaining narrative coherence across vastly different playthrough paths.

Cinematic dialogue direction: Full performance capture elevates companion writing, grounding moral dilemmas and interpersonal conflict in genuine emotional stakes.

Weaknesses:

Third act pacing: Act 3 suffers from structural fatigue, dense urban navigation, and a noticeable drop in narrative focus compared to the tight pacing of Act 1.

Encounter balance: Combat scaling flattens in the mid game, where optimized builds easily break action economy limits and trivialize major encounters.

Verdict:
A monumental achievement in systemic role playing design that sets a new benchmark for player agency, tempered by pacing issues in its final act.

Elden Ring is probably the single most overrated game of this decade and that's saying something. Do not get me wrong, Elden Ring is definitely a good game and amongst the better open world titles, yet it is still filled to the brim with problems, many of which having the same exact source: The open world.

The open world in this game feels like it's not there because Fromsoftware felt truly passionate about making an open world, but because every new game needs to have one for some odd reason. The open world is boring, static and incredibly uninteresting. Filled to the brim with dead zones, small groups of week enemies not worth engaging, mini dungeons that all look and feel the same, and so, so, so many recycled bosses. This game has somewhere between 200-300 boss encounters, yet only about 40 of them are actually unique and not recycled from a different encounter, or a basic enemy with a boss health bar. 

The loot spread throughout the open world is also lackluster. Once you have your weapon and armor, the only things you will want to look for are upgrade materials for your weapons and your healing flasks, with everything else being nigh useless, especially items used for crafting purposes, as most things you can craft have little to no actual worth in gameplay. The crafting system in general feels very much like an after thought. 

There is no way to actually interact with the open world in any way, and it doesn't really change much throughout the story. You will basically just ride from point a to point b, without actually engaging with the world in a meaningful way. Sure, it looks pretty (mostly), but it just feels so incredibly pointless. There's no villages or towns either, so everything feels very empty and devoid of life. Yeah yeah, fits with the lore and whatnot, but it does not make the world any more interesting, especially since the lore is basically just the usual Fromsoftware lore, reheated once again, with a different coat of paint.

The open world also fails at feeling like an open world. It's moreso multiple open zones arranged in a ring-like formation, connected to one or two other zones. And while some of these are alright, others are just a slog to go through and explore, especially the final ones, as the last third of the game is mostly just recycled content you have already seen, before it turns into a straight up boss gauntlet for the final stretch.

The quest design also suffers greatly due to the open world. Fromsoftware quests have always been pretty bad, as they mostly just boil down to you walking from point a to point b to talk to NPCs, before you get a mediocre item as a reward. This does not work well at all with a big open world, since you have no proper indication of where the NPCs you need to interact with actually are. Not that any of them are actually worth doing.

The open world brings about plenty of balancing issues as well, as you will most often find yourself either underleveled or overleveled for an encounter, thus meaning the game will either be way too easy, or way too difficult. The game has issues finding this balance that more linear souls games have, where the difficulty is just right, and neither too easy nor too hard.


Unfortunately the open world drags the game down quite a bit, especially almost everything else is quite good.

The game functions well (after a rocky launch that is), there is more depth to the combat system compared to the Dark Souls games, most main bosses are fun to face and take down (even if they can be a tad bit easy at times), the music is good, the game looks pretty and the big main dungeons are structured like the older souls games, and are definitely the best part of the game, as they offer actual level design with proper encounters and challenges. 

If the game would have focused more on being structured like these dungeons, added more actual bosses, and left out the dull open world, then this could have been one of the best souls games ever made. But that was not the case, and looking at Fromsoftware's current and upcoming lineup of games, it seems this game has steered the company into a very odd direction for the future.

Problems include:

*RNG Bullshi...  At a certain point it no longer becomes fun to watch your characters fail to roll above a 4.  As someone who has done alpha and beta testing on games before, I can tell you that there is something wrong with their dice rolling system.

*Camera Controls.  The way you can move and control the camera is janky as hell, and absolutely frustrating.

*Interface. It's just poorly designed.  If I'm using an item from someone's inventory, if I don't have the right character selected, it uses that item for a different character.  Absolutely asinine.

*D&D Rules.  Nevermind how it's not working how it's supposed to...  It's not working how it says it's supposed to.  For example, I've watched Karlach drop out of a rage and lose it MULTIPLE TIMES despite being attacked.

*Pathfinding.  I've never seen such poor pathfinding on a modern game.  Couple this with poor camera controls, and I've often sent people way off path because I clicked on invisible terrain that the camera couldn't see.  Which leads me to the next problem...

*Lack of a pause button.  Some of these problems could be tolerable if there was a pause button.  If I was able to stop a character running off into misfortune because of the bad interface and camera, it wouldn't be as infuriating.  


I'm off to investigate if there are any mods that fix the broken RNG of this game.  If there are, I'll try again.  But I'd rather catch a testicle in a zipper than watch the game pathologically keep my rolls under 5.
